div.p: Veda. ALBION. rame a man of aspect dreary In a time o ftrieulation. With a I,ek of apprehension. In, a vtece of dale foreboding, Distils.' eras for his country He foretold, his grey head shaking, And a shadow o'ee hlrn creepuig, As he pictured desolation, Doom, destruction, for old Albion— . Idand of the bravest, fairest, Noblest of earth's s sus and daughters, Borne f frtedem, bright tiara On the great eat th's brow. "Ancient melons," quoth the I rophet, "Who like Albion were exared. Deemed themselves exempt from downfall, Gloried in their pride and power, • And in grand, far-reaching empires— , • Where are they? Grine, gone for ever! And so Albion, greater far than Gretee ard Rene and all the splendid Empires of the past— She shall fall; her outspread standard, Floating 'mid the Arctic icebergs, Fanned by spicy tropic zephyrs, ret,.• • —• Wavieg in the winds that girdle eere Every mighty zone— This unseotted, radiant banner, ehell not keep ite.elf nsullied ; And the lands where, 'neath its shadow, Fr t edern dwells secure, Shall re) longer own allegiance To old Albion's thronel monarchs: Continents shall spurn her from them, Oceans coas-i t bear her white sails, Other livels forget her prowess, Elic-ff at what was (tree her titie, • • .iistress id the seas !' B am n and mehele, high endeavor, Eipt it of our brave ancesters, Burning love of father:wed. These shall sail, deterioration Work insidiously among U 4, • • • Sapping out our vere a hale; Gold shal, cease to fiil our coffe.s, Courale fall in tirne of battle. Wisdom .e.sve I,:gleatO)S Indolence rt,:td dt,sipetion Soon shalt rereen supyetne. Darien at gathers o'er the white cliffs Of the grand inviolate island Of the .tage and free I' " 17p arose a youttful petitiot, With a eye wherein a fire fleshed Aal a fo m rebed In enthusiasm. Aid a voice that, like a trumpet, . B rde the prophet etaee. " Shame upon such we'd: de•rpairings. Iheegh he times are full of trouble And d:rle cleu-is are on the hor:zon. These shale fl-e away. some an.: Gree-ce would ne'er have fallen If their sons had said they should mit, end while boar 3 -headed sages And their valiant-hearted eff,pring, Meet and women youths and maidens.. Thrill with patriot-IC te.vrr As they think of Alblen's grandeur, lee adore ivir stainless etandard. And, reflecting, how their fathers - Died beneath its folds, Vow to die, as thc mends have done, Boner thee Vat flag dishonored In the dust should lid; White thoy cherish love for tire hren 'Wire the' eetgues ari,ross the ocean, Teove the tined of the free, `t, A m Ad themselves woeld die 0 sip hr Frrm imeending degrafon; Wide treditions.brir..t with honor Hover round °ire am lent halts. And Ilee dia:l.stereils deck our history' - While etre hearts oats feel the impulse Of leered deeds;r within our h,mes, uefettered, Lies the ever-open Bible, While • elavcs cannot breathe in Albion' And we all may live in freedom, And in living learn to .ovr! Love it with our soul and spirit, Albion cannot fall No proud foe shall scale her whits cliffs, No usurper fill her pure throne, No seif-seeklng legislators Rule her eateve and I Sooner that, old Albion's glories Ehould expire like sinking sunsets, Everysne who loves his borne-land.' And va-t nurnb,rs love her dearly, For that laid would die ! Die we will if Fate decrees it, Bitt wbile breath is in our bodies. While oar hands can wield a sab. e Or our arms can work for Albion, Albioa shall not fall !" Warrington, 25th July, 1882.
ARTHUR BENNETT.

CONVENTIONAL Ban TASTE.—Modrn education, not In art only, bat in all other things referrable to the same standard, has invariably given taste in this had tense; it Etas given fastidionentes of choice without lodgment, super- ciliousness of manner without dignity, refinement of habit without purity, g,ratea of expression without sincerity, and desire of loveliness without love; and the modern "ideal" of high art is a curious mingling of the gracefulness and reserve of the drawing-rootn with a certain measure of classical sensuality.—Jno. Ruskin.

GARIBALDI AT THE SIEGE OF RORE.—" h writee Garibaldi, "it was a terrible night. - The artillery and fury of the ekles mingled with that of the earth; the thunder answered, responning to the cannon; the lightning ran its livid lines across the path of the bembe !" The last straggle was at band. Then was seen a thing unheard of in the annals of war. A reserve of the wounded volunteered to take their tarn in the trenebee, and men were seen with blood etreaming from their heads and breaete, bandaged, wite broken limbs and arms in slings, spending themselves in a last struggle for freedom. Garieeldi now reeolved himself to die in a hand-to-hand conffict. About midnight be unsheathed his good sword, as he firmly believed for the I last time, and went into the Aarelien trench to lead a final charge. "On that terrible night," writes his friend Vecchi, an eve-witness, "Garibaldi was great indeed; greater than , even we had ever known him. Hie sword flew like lightning, I he wee like a man inspired, every one he smote fell dead before him, the blood of one washed from his steel the blood of another. We trembled for him, but he was unwounded, he stood firm as destiny." At two o'clock Garibaldi was re- called by the Deliberative Assembly under Mazaini, then sitting in the Capitol. "When I appeared at the door of the council hall,' be writes, "all the deputies rose and applauded. I looked about me and upon myself to see what had awakened their enthusiasm. I then perceived, for the flret time, that I was steeped in blood—my clothes were pierced with balls and bayonet thrusts—my sword was jagged and stood half-way out of the scabbard, but I had not a scratch about me. It was a miracle." In all the peat crises of Garibaldi's stormy life there was a deep undertone of religious feeling: "God first and the country next," he would often say to his men. He believed that he was raised up for a special purges°, and often protected by divine interposition. He thought he saw his mother praying for him in the thick of the fight—she had taught him noble lessons of religion an 4 patriotism in his child- hood. Be believed his life was given to her intercessory prayers.—Bete H. R. Havels in "Good Words."

3.:IEDICAL VALUE OF VEGETABLES.— Asparagus is a strong diuretic, and forms part of the cure for rheumatic patients at such health resorts ts Aix-lee-B eine. Sorrel is cooling, and forms the staple of the soup which a French lady will order for herself after a long and tiring journey. Carrots, as containing a quantity of sugar, are avoided by some people, while others complain of them as indigestible; but it is the yellow core of the carrot that is difficult of diges- tion—the outer, a red layer, is tender enough. In, Savoy the peasants have recourse to an effusion of carrots as a specific for jaundice. The large sweet onion is very rich in those alkaline elements which counteract the poison of rheumatic gout. If slowly stewed in weak broth, and eaten with a little liepaul pepper, it will be found to be an admir- able diet for patients of etudiens and sedentary habits. Tutnips are often thought to be indigestible, and better sultei for cows and sheep than for delicate people; but here the fault lies with the cook quite as much as with the root. Toe cook boils the turnip badly, and then pours some butter over it, and the eater of such a dish is sure to he the worse for it. Try a better way. Half-boil your turnip, and cut it in slice like half-crowns. Batter a pie diAb, put in the slices, moisten with a little milk and weak broth, dust over with bread crumbs and pepper and salt, and bake in the oven till it gains a bright golden brown. This dish, which is the Fiedmonteme fashion of eeting turnips, is quite unszited to cows, and ought to be popular. What shall be said about onr Jettuces? The plant has a slight narcotic action, of which a French old woman, like a French doctor, well knows the value, and when properly cooked is really very easy of digestion But in our country, thoteeh lettuces are duly grown in every garden, you often Lear t 13.3 remark, "I can't eat a sal“l,' and as few cooks know how to Ins the vege- taMe which has been refused in its raw state, the lettuces are all wasted, and so is the ground in which they were grown.---Mrs. H. Beebe's " Cookery and Housekeeping!' UPRISING OF THE FINNISH COAST.—The surveyor of the Finnish Government, Herr Rodas, states that on Jane 25th this year he carefully measured the height of a hole, bored, according to authentic records, two inches above the level of the sea on the coast of Oeterbotten, on June 25th, 1755, and discovered that that part of the ersaet had risen, in 127 years, 6 feet 4 inches, or more than half an inch per year. SUBSTITUTE FOR BOX-WOOD.—One of the hardest woods in existence is that of the desert n ironwood-tree, which grows in the dry washes along the ,line of the Southern Pacific Rtilroad. Its specific gravity is nearly the same as that of lignurn tite, and it has a black heart so hard when well seasoned that it will tarn the edge of an axe and can scarctly be cut by a well-tempered saw. In burning it gives oat ae intense heat, and charcoal made from it is harelly eecoed to anthracite. It would perhaps be well for cur shuttle-makers to inquire if it would be a suitable eubstit ate 1 for box-wood, now becoming so peer, mere; and high- ! priced —Textile Manufacturer. , AUTOMATIC REGULATOR FOR SCREW STEAMERS.—A new wean-retie regulator for engines of screw steamers (to pre- vent the "racing" of the screw when out of water) teas been p --needed by Herr Windemenn. From the account in Dingier's we gather that it consists of a bell crank lever with axle at ttie abgie • one end weighted and resting, when the slip is etill, on an elastic buffer, the other end connected by chains with the throttle valve. When the screw rises, the weighted end is raised from its seat, and the chain is loosened, allowing a spring to close the throttle valve, This closure takes pleas before the lever end has cernpieted its r ' iee and before the screw leaves the water. Tbe solitary specn men is at New Haven, but was found in Bavaria in the Seine series of elites that has shown a number of famous fcssile, among them the A.rentostpteryx, a reptilian bird with feathers and a long jointed tail. The described fossil is a Rare- Demetenebus, to which Prof. Marsh has given the name of phylluras. owing• to along rat-like tail, which en is in a broad, leaf-shaped rudder. The wings of this ancestor of bats are -membraneous like those of bate, but much slenderer and more er ice! al, The head is comparatively long and large, with a formidable 'Supply of teeth. The specimen was no larger then the ordinary fox headed bats seen alive in menageries, and not so large as some of :tile living Indian and African bats. Mr. Eirikr Magnusson, of the University Library, Cam- bridge, has nearly completed hie long-expected edition of the "Saga of Thomas. a- Becket" in the Rolls Series, which will establish several points of great interest and novelty. Mr. Magnasson will be able to snow the singular veneration which Becket enjoyed in Iceland, and the especial influence of hie principles on Bishop Gudrnuni Arason. of Holar (12034237), whose fanaticism eventually cost Iceland its independence. He will also be able to *determine for the first time the dates and order of the centensporary lives of Becket, showing that the earliest, those of Fitzstephen and Benedict of Peterborough, were written be'ore Jaly, 1172; that William of Canterbury's compilation of Beckett's miracles was then' in progress ; and that the others were written before 1176, except that of Alan of Tewkesbury (1180) and Herbert's (1187). Alan's, there is every reason to believe, was derived from those "magne volurnina." which John of Salisbury states to have been left behind by Becket himself.— Atheneum. A RAINFALL RECORDER.—Au ingenious apparatus for recording the total duration of rainfall in the course of a day, or a still longer time, has been devised by M. Sclameitz, formerly professor at the Lyces de Lille. It consists of a box having a rain funnel in its top, by which the rain can enter and drop upon a band of travelling paper which passes below within the :box. This peoer is the usual Morse strip treated in a solution of sulphate of iron and dried carefully, then -brushed with tannic acid or powdered cvanoferride of potassium tnixei with resin. A roil of it is placed within the box, and it is unwound on to another roller outside the box. The latter is driven by a chain from the hour hand of a common clock, so that it rotates ones in an hoar. In this time, therefore, the paper has been pulled along beneath the rain funnel a length equal to the circumference of the -roller. The falling drops dye the paper and indicate where the rain began and left off. Cor- rection is made for the increasing diameter of the winding roller as the paper is wound upon it. The instrument is said to work well, and to indicate fine showers, which are lost upon the ordinary pluviometer.—Engineering. A CONSTANT BATTERY.—MeChIDiCII agitation has been adopted sometimes to render the current from certain vol- taic batteries constant by disergeeiog the gases which col- lect on the negative plate. Heating has been recently ap- plied by an Italian engineer, Signor Gaudini, with the like effect in the case of a cell consisting of a cast-irou pot or vessel containing a porous clay vase in which was placed a plate of certion, while a zinc cylinder surrounded the vase as a positive electrode. The exciting liquid was a saturated solution of chloride of sodium, and the depolariser-a super- saturated solietion of bichromate of potash and sulphuric acid. Whoa in a cool state this cell gives a strong but rapidly falling current on being worked continuously. If, however, it is placed over a small gas heater so as-to raise Its temperature to about 100 deg. C., the current keeps very constant and is very powerful. Crystals of bichromate of potash dropped into the depollrising solution from time to time serve to keep up the strength of the current. When cool such a cell gave an electro-motive force of 2.10 volts and an internal resistance of 0-82 'ohms. When hot the electro-motive force ross. to 2-44 volts with a resistance of 0-71 ohms. Heating, therefore, increases the7electro-motive force of the cell, and the conductivity of its solutions, while at the same time it lessens the potarisation of the electrodes. —Engineering. BABYLONIAN BOUNDARY STONES —The British Museum has lately received from the neighbourhood of Babylon three beautifal boundary stones covered all over with in- scriptions, hieroglyphs (those generally considered as zodi- acal signs), and very nice human figures. The first stone bears the name of Melisikhu, King of Babylon (whose name is contained in the list of kings discovered by Mr. T. G. Pinches), who ruled about 1175 Bc. The second is dated in the fifth year of Nalm-kaic-abli, King of Babylon, whose name has not yet been found either in the cuneiform deca- mente or in the classics, but by the style of writinn his reign ought to be placed at the beginning of the seventh century 13 C.; on this stone are the imago of the king and that of Ziria, to whom the estate was granted. The third stone is more Interesting; it has been engraved with great we, and one side is entirely covered with the so-cened zodiacal signs. We understand this care when we learn from the inscription that the stone was set up by order of Nebuchadnezzar as a memorial of the taking back of a piece of land from the Elarnites and it restoration to the country of Akkad. The document contains no date. Mr. Rassarre , who is at Bagdad, has recovered from the fall from his horsenvhich lately disabled him. Thirteen cases of antiqui- ties in all have recently arrived at the British Museum from Bagdad.—Athenceuna. . THE WEDGE PHOTOMETER FOR IUEASURING THE LIGHT OF STARS.—Mach attention has recently been directed to the use of a wedge of shade glass as a means of measur- ing the light of the stars. While in has been maintained by various writers that this device Is not a new one, the credit for its introduction as a practical 'method of stellar photo- metry seems clearly to belong to Professor Pritchard, direc- tor of the University Observatory, Oxford. Various theo- retical objections have been offered to this photometer, and numerous sources of error suggested. Prof. Pritchard has made the beat possible reply to these criticisms by measur- ing a number of stars, and showing that his results agreed very clotely with those obtained elsewhere by whelly dif- ferent methods. His instrument consists of a wedge of shade glass of a neutral tint inserted in the field of the tele- scope, and movable se that a star may be viewed through the thicker or thinner portions at will. The exact position is indicated by means of a scale. The light of different stars is measured by bringing them in turd to the centre of the field, and moving the wedge from the thin towards the thick end until the star disappears. The exact point of dis- appearance is then read by the scale. The stars must always be kept in the same part of the field, or the readings will not be comparable. By a long wedge the error from this source will be reduced. A second wedge in the reversed position will render the absorption uniformahroughout the field. Instead of keeping the star in the same place by means of clockwork, the edgec of the wedge may be placed parallel to the pith of the star, when the effect of its motion Neill be insensible. To obtain the beet results, the week Should be made purely differential, that is, freerient me-a- tares should be made of stars in the vicinity aeturned as standaide. Otherwise large errors rosy be committed, due .to the varying sensitiveness of the eye, to the effect of moonlight, twilight, &c., and to various other causes.—P eo- lesson Edward C. Pickerina.

Once . more he was unfortunate in the man he was linked to. The man wart, Devitt declares, a regular madman, a notorious character, who had the reputation among his fellow con- victs of being a "balmy bloke." On arriving at Exeter they had four hours to wait for the next train, and were locked up in the police station. There the " balmy bloke" began his tricks by stripping himself nearly naked. Convicts delight in journeys from place to "place at the expense of the country, and to be shifted about is the aim of an "old lag." In the first place he gets a glimpse of the country whilst in the train, and hopes for a job of easier work in the prison he is going to. Then at every station at which the train stops there ite a chance of a bit of tobacco or the stump end of a cigar, which sympathising people throw into the carriage window. The officers usually make a show of being indignant at such breaches of the law and of the prison rules, but if they tried to prevent it they would find their match. The writer remembers seeing a gang of about 40 Convicts standing on the platform at Paddington, waiting for a train. A mild-looking gentleman in spectacles, smoking a cigar, ventured rather too close to the party, and the cigar was coolly snatched out of his mouth, and in an instant bitten into several pieces and divided among as many convicts. Seeing this, a chap, dressed like a coster- monger, threw among them what seemed to be a quarter. pound packet of tobacco. The officer nearest to the man who caught it tried to get it, but in a twinkling he was on his back on the platform, and the angry convicts might have assaulted him load not the other officer produced his revolver and threatened to tire on the first convict who struck his brother warder. Strange as it may seem to those unacquainted with the rules of the convict service, the officer would have been perfectly justified if he load shot any convict after warning. ' It is not often that a convict has an opportunity of Com- municating with his friends outside, except by the ordinary prison letters he is allowed to write, and as every letter is road by the governor and chaplain, he cannot complain of any unfair and cruel treatment to which he has been subjected in prison. On his return from Portsmouth, Devitt managed to send out, by a prisoner about to be discharged, a letter complaining of his treatment on the journey to Portsmouth, and with regard to certain matters which had occurred at Dartmoor. The convict who took the letter risked being detained for. the whole remaining period of his sentence, forfeiting his ticket of leave ; but he was not caught. Probably the friends of Davitt took some action on ' receipt of the letter, and the fact of its having been sur- reptitiously conveyed out of the prison came to the knowledge of the authorities. Not having been detetted ere , it left the prison, Devitt could not by the rules be directly I punished. But the prison authorities hit upon a plan which they knew Devitt would regard as one of the worst and most degrading punishments they could possibly inflict. After what is known as the Devon Commission had sat to investigate the treatment of political prisoners—convicts sentenced to penal servitude for treason felony, such convicts were allowed to grow their hair and beards. One evening on returning from work, as soon as he had swallowed his seenty supper of gruel and bread, the warder unlocked his cell door and bade him "Come this way, and- bring your stool." Devitt complied, but to his great astonishment was confronted by the convict barber and lois scissors, on the landing. " Sit down ; you're to have your hair cut," said the officer with a malicious grin. Devitt expestulated, but to no effect, and finally declined to submit. But might was stronger than right, and five other warders coming to help to " poll "the `Fenian as they termed it, the six warders held him in a chair, and his hair and beard were cut as close as they could be. Next day he was taken before the governor, and awarded a day's bread arid water for dis- obedience to what was a direct breach of the law—in his , case—" insolence " being added to the charge against him, ' because he dared to challenge the right of the officers to cut his hair. The " bog-trotter screws," referred to above, were usually filled with inordinate ideas of their great importance. From the time they donned the blue uniform of the convict warden they were, in their ow-n estimetion, officers in Her Majesty's service, and, by the convicts,- they insisted on being treated with a tremendous amount of deference and respect. The "old lag," who "knew his way about," toadied, "soft- soaped," and flattered such warders to their hearts' content. But such a man as Devitt could not stoop to sucit a method of currying favour; and accateitigly he became a "marked
REPORT OF THE ROYAL COMMISSION.

The Royal Cmailission which was appointed a little over three years ago to inquire into the causes of agricultural dietreFs has at length concluded its labours. Stated very briefly, the following are the conclusions at which the Com- missioners have arrived :

The first subject dealt with is that of Amsrican competi- tion. Several of the Commissioners are inclined to discard the feara of fa.rrners on this subject, and to declare that the danger has already passed. When the Commission was ap- pointed there was a considerable scare on this subject. On all hands it was said that the imports of American cattle and meat and corn would be overwhelming, and permanently injurious to the agricultural interests of this country. is yet, not only have these fears been unfulfilled, but the im- ports themselves have become quite unimportant—so far, that is, as cattle and meat are concerned. Instead of send- ing to us, the Americans are now bu7ing from us large quantities of cattle for the purpose of stocking and improv- ing the ranches in the Western states and territories. In a few years these will be returned to us in increased snpplies, but in estimating these the wonderful increase in the popu- lation of America, and also of oar own country, must be borne, in mind. The very difficult questions involved in this problem thus led to differences of opinion among the Commissioners, but the majority agree that it is probable that, after an interval of rest, the arrivals of cattle from the United States and Can Oa will be in excess of any previous importations. The next question dealt with is the question of rent, and the result of long deliberation is that the Commissioners all agree in declaring that, in view of the altered conditions of our agrimlture, "some re-arrangement of rent seems desir- able." There is no indication given to show ho w far the Commissionas think rents to be excessive.

The chief portion of the report deals with the question of compensation to tenants for their ueexhausted improve- ments. On this point the Commissioners recommend that compensation be made compulsory, and that this shall be done by legislation based upon the present Agricultural Holdings Act—the scale of allowances and payments under that Act to be made compulsory over the whole country. But it is recognised that there are many districts—Lincoln- shire being mentioned—where satisfactory arrangements are already in existence between landlord and tenant for com- pensation, and in thene cases the Commissioners hold that compulsory legislation would be inapplicable. It is also re- commended—although some of the Commissioners do not acquiesce—that where the compensation is compulsory, it ehall only be for improvements that add to the letting value of the farm. It is also recommended that the incoming tenant shall to a certain extent approve of the improve- ments fer which compensation is paid. In the case of valua- tions of sheep stock in the North of Scotland, the Cotnnais• sinners recommend that the sheriff be empowered to name an oversman, to act as arbiter in the event of the valuers disegreeir g. The law of distress is the , subject of several paragraphs, and it is recommended that in this the landlord's power to diain shall be limited to two years. It is also recom- mended that the law of hypothec—as perpetuated by the law of seredunt, which compels a farmer six months in ar- reer to furnish security for two years' rent under pain of forfeiture of lease, should be still further modified. Local taxation is dealt with, and it is advised that the system already in vogue in Scotland, under which the local rates are equally divided between landlord and tenant, shall be extended to England and Scotland. So far as poor rates are concerned, the Commissioners recommend that the whole cost of the indoor paupers shall be taken off the local rates anO be borne by the Imperial Exchequer. These are the chief recommendations of the report. Three of the Commissioners—Mr. Charles Howard, Mr. Clay, and Mr. Paterson—dissent from certain portions of it, and their tlisnnsion will be found in Warate reports. All three dis- sent horn the proposals regarding the law of hypothec and distresa, believing that the recommendations do not go far enough. Mr. Clay holds also that the compensation must be more liberal than that laid down by the Agricultural Holdings Act, and also that rents should be reduced all over the country from 25 to 30 per cent.

Ain " with some Of the warders. Davitt fell foul of one these conceited "bog-trotter screws.". On the.arrival of the party at their working place, the warder calls Over the names of the men, to which they usually answer "Here." . This was not enough far the "officer in Her Majesty's ser- vice," who insisted that his men must say "Sir." He "was entitled to 'Sir,' and would have it." Davitt Simply repil that he had answered to his name as he had been accustomed to do, and if there was anything wrong the warder could repor it to the governor. This, of course, nso'r and insubordination, and DW.7;:: i; donstruel aS was sentenced to two days' bread and water. The parties,organgs, as they were then called, of men work- ing on the bogs, were often shifting about from one job of work to another, at the option of the farm bailiff, ;rho seem". to take a delight in caitlg a lot of trouble in that .way. Pack party had its own portable closet, which was transported from place te place by the men. One day, the warder in 's's'rearge of the party ordered Davitt to make one of a ne.:"..y of four men to carry the closet, a heavy wooden affair with two handles at each end, and not unlike a sedan chair in appearance. Davitt, in consrquence of his physical infirmity, refused to obey. Probably he imagined the governor would not uphold such tyranny, but he was soon undeceived. No matter how unjust an order may be, what the warder says must be done, and Davitt was thereupon brought before the governor, and punished by solitary con• finement in the punishment cells tor three days, at the end of which time the medical officer was pleased to report that Davitt had been asked to do more than he could perform with one hand, and he escaped bread and water. Davitt was subjected to other kinds of petty annoy- ances, and was forced to endure them, any attempt at obtaining redress only subjecting him to worse treatment. Many of the warders seemed to take a delight in showing their petty spite on every possible occasion. On one occasion, when be had reached the first class, and was therefore located on the bottom floor of the four tiers of cells, without any explanation, or any real necessity, he was transferred to the top floor, set apart for new corners and bad characters. This was when he had served nearly four years of his sentence. In the top floor he had four flights of stairs to ascend every time be came in tired from his work ; and in summer time the heated air, ascending to the top. made it almost unbearable, and very difficult to breathe.

Anotter way in which the officers annoyed Davitt was at exercise in the prison yard on a Sunday. Then the con- victs exercised in couples,and conversation was unrestricted. The convicts were usually allowed to choose their partners; at least the warders winked at it. No such privilege was allowed to Davitt ; he was compelled to walk with what- ever convicts the warder placed along side of him n ; and men were chosen with whom the warders knew that Davitt would not converse—old gaol birds, who could talk of noth- ing but the cm lines they had been guilty of the number of times they had been in quod, and the " laty " [Anglice, cunning] way they would go to " wmk " when discharged, so as not to be caught again. To be continued.
'01.1.R OLD NOBILITY,' Published by Mr. E. J. Kibblewhite, 31, Tavistock-street, London, WC., and reprinted by permssion.] THE LECONFIELDA.

The patent of nobility. held by Lord Leconfield dates only from 1859, and yet, if we take into accot nt the fact that his estates have been acquired not by 'purchase, but by matri- monial alliances, he is fully entitled to rank among " Our Old Nobility," especially as his Irish estates have descended by bequest for more than a thousand years, and the greater part of his Erwlish estates for considerably more than half that period. It is a case of "New Men and Old Acres," so far, at least, as the connection between the two is concerned; for the Wyndharns can only in that sense be regarded as new men. They are a Saxon family, anciently seated at Wymondham, in Norfolk, from which place they are sup- posed to derive their name. Mr. H. W. Wyndham w ili holds 6,483 acres in that county, and is, I believe, the son of the hero of an extraordinary case which those of my readers who have arrived at " middle life can hardly fail to remem- ber. We must not, however, look in Norfolk for-the estates of Lord Leconfield. A Wyndham in the reign of Henry VIII. obtained a good share of the spoil of the monastic houses; and his son and grandson both married Somerset. shire heiresses. Later on, the Norfolk property fell to a younger son; and the Sornersetshire property, at Orchard and elsewhere, to an elder son, one of whose descendants was created a baronet. From this latter line Lord Leconfield is descended, but we must not look for his estates in Somerset shire. The second baronet Was Sir William Wyndham, a statesman of the reigns of Anne and George 1., who, according to Lord Stanhope, held the threads of the whole Jacobite conspiracy in 1715, and narrowly escaped courting punishment through the influence of his father-in-law, the Duke of Somerset. The son of Sir William Wyndham became afterwards Earl of Egremont ; and the father of the present Lord Lecontield was the eldest illegitimate son and adopted heir of the third Earl. Succeeding as he did to 'vast estates, it was only natural that he should be created a Peer. The Egrernont titie only takes us back to 1749, but it takes us to a period when the Wyndhams succeeded to estates which had been in the possession' of great Norman houses for centuries. Lord Lecontield (Lecontied is in Yorkshire) holds estates in six different counties as follows : Sussex ..30,221 acres. Yorkshire 21,733 „ Cumberland 11,147 „ Clare 39,043 „ Limerick Tipperary • 273 „

Total • 110,720 „. with a rental of £i8,484. He also has no less than twenty-four Church livings, one of which is worth £1,538, and a house; another, £1,371 and a house; the total annual value of them all, er.clusive of residences, being £10,393. The Yorkshire, Sussex, and Cumberland estates are part of the ancient inheritance of the Percies. When speaking of the Percies, I said that for a hundred years they were a powerful family before they set foot in Northumberland. For their ancient home, where they settled soon after the Conquest, we must go to Yorkshire, in the neighbourhood of Spofforth, where they once had a magnificent mansion, the ruins of which are, I believe, still in existence. These estates are now the property of Lord Leconfield. By mar- riage the .great houses of Percy and Louvaine became united. The Louvaines acquired their possessions by an enormous Royal grant. Adeliza, Queen of Henry 1., had a brother, Joceline de Louvaine, to whom were granted vast estates in Sussex, at Petworth and other places in that county. Petworth Park, which is twelve miles in circum- ference, and the rest of the Percy estates in Sussex are now the property of Lord Leconfield. William the Sussex, granted a large part of Cumberland to Ranulph de Meschines, one of his followers, who, in turn, granted great estates at Egremont and elsewhere, in the same county, to his brother William. Prom him the Egriemont property passed by marriage to one family after another, al at length an heiress brought the domain to the Percies. The Egremont estates are now the property of Lord Leconfield. There have been a few small modern acquisitions by purchase in Sussex, and possibly in Yorkshire and Cumberland; but by far the greater part of the English estates of Lord Leconfield have passed constantly either by descent or bequest, ever since the Norman period. He certainly could not complain if Parliament should ever see fit to re-impose upon the land the ancient burdens which his forefathers undertook as the con- dition upon which. their lands should be held.

I must now proceed to show how these great ancestral estates of the Percies passed to ths Wyndhams. Charles, sixth Duke of Somerset—known to history as the "Proud Duke"—married the daughter and heiress of the Duke of Northumberland. Ultimately the Percy estates were divided between the Duchess's son's daughter and her daughter's son. Her son's daughter married. Sir Hugh Smithson, who became the first of a new line of Percies, and who was the occasion of the only witty saying ever uttered by George 111. Not satisfied with being created Duke of Northumberland, Smithson vainly applied for al Garter. "I am the first Duke of Northumberland to whom it has been refused," said he. "Yes," said King George, "and he is the first Smithson that ever asked for it." The daughter's son of the Duchess was Charles Wyndham ; Sir William Wyndham, his father, having married ,he daughter of the sixth Duke of Somerset. On the death of the seventh Duke of Somerset without issue, the Seymour title and estates passed to a distant kinsman, and the Earldom of Egremont ja brand-new title), with that portion LA estates which did not pass to Smithson, was inherited by Charles Wyndham. We must now pass to Ireland, and here we tread upon ground which has passed in unbroken succession, either by inheritance or bequest, from a time beyond which the memory of man or the records of history run not to the con- trary. The estates in Clare and elsewhere were formerly in the possession of the O'Briens, Earls of Thomond, descended froth the ancient Royal line of Brien Boroihme, who fell at the battle of Clontarf in 1014. In the wilds .of the West of Ireland the O'Briens were acknowledged as Kings of Thomond till, in the reign of Henry. VIII., that title was relinquished for two Irish peerages, the Earldom of Thomond and the Barony of lnchiquin. The Barony of .Inchiquiu is still held by the taßriens, with 21,884 acres in Clare and Limerick. The Earldom of Thotnond exists no longer, but the estates formerly appertaining thereto are now the property of Lord Leconfield. The Wyndhams, however, do not possess O'Brien's blood as well as the O'Brien's estates. The eighth Earl of Thomond marrie the siss:er of Sir William Wyndham's wife, and left his estates to a kinsman, with remainder to Sir William's youngest son, who subsequently succeeded to them, but died without issue. Thus these estates passed into the Wyndham family. The history of the Wyndhams is certainly a very curious one. At the Reformation they were simply Norfolk squires; 11 in the reign of Charles 11. the head of the elder branch had become a Sornersetshire baronet, but, by a series of matri- monial accidems, about one hundred and thirty years ago, the family had achieved a complete change of base. Prior to that time the Wyndhams do not a`Ppear to have held a sinale acre of the vast estates DM owned by Lord Lecon- field. The marriage of the Jacobite statesman, Sir Wiliam Wyndham, has resulted in the acquisition by his descondsrits of the lands held for so many centuries by the Percies and O'Briens. The Wyndharns, as a rule, have not been distinguished as tax-eilterS ; their good fortune has placed them above necessity. Yet there was one of them, the brother of one of ihe Earls of Egremont, who was a most exemplary sinecurist, This was the Hon. P. C. Wyndham, who, about half a cen- tury ago, was Secretary of the Council, Rernembrancer of_ the Court of Exchequer,,:and Clerk of Common_ Pleas it,

Ba,rbadocs, also Registrar in Chancery, and Clerk of thel Patents in Jamaica, all which duties were, of course, dis- chirked by deputy, and brought their fortunate holder an annual income of £5,500. A relative of the present Lord Leconfield, the Hon. P. S. Wyniham, has sat for nineteen years for West Cumberland, or, rather, for the 11,000 acres owned by the family. Two other W.% ndhanis figure as considerable landowners—Mr. William Wyndham, who owns 2,866 acres in Somerset and 5,734 in Wilts ; and Captain LW, Wyndham, who has 6,225 acres in Mayo,

div.head: WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.

The decision on the revision of the Baptismal service has given very great satisfaction to those who were in favour of it ; and it is not likely that any serious difficulties will arise either among the ministers or in the circuits. The affairs of the book room were brought forward and settled on Satur- day morning. The third catechism is withdrawn horn cir- culation. It was resolved to publish a new Wesleyan service book to contain all the liturgies now in use among the Wes- leyans. On the motion of Rev. 11. W. Holland, the Con- ference unanimously agreed to request Dr. Osborn to publish a letter on the study of John Wesley's writings. For several years it has been under consideration te establish an affiliated conference in South Africa; and this is now done. The Rev. John Walton has been appointed the first 'president of the new conference. A committee was appointed to con- sider what improvements can be made in the final examina- tion of the candidates for ordination.—The Rev. H. W. Holland withdrew his motion for the quarterly catechising of the Sunday scholars, and gave his support to one by Dr. Osborn to the following effect :—That the superintendents arrange with the Sunday School Committee for an examina- tion of the Sunday scholars in the Catechism in the chapel at least once a year whenever practicable.—The pastoral session was finished, and the journal signed shortly after two o'clock.

On Monday, at half-past nine, the first session of the Representative Conference commenced in the Brunswick Chapel; the Rev. Charles Garrett presiding. • The Rev. J. W. Greaves brought up the report of home missions. The following temporary grants, amongst others, were recommended :—Coventry, £35, diminishing £5 per annum; Ketley Bank, for three years, £3O, £2O, and .ClO respectively; Bromyard, £25, _diminishing £5 per annum; Crewe' £2O for one year; Liverpool (Brunswick), for two years, £3O and £2O respectively; Seacombe,l3s, diminish- ing £5 per annum; Tarporley, £35, diminishing £5 per annum ; Llandudno and Rhyl, £80; Wrexham, £3O, di,ainishing £5 per annum ; Heywood, for two years, £4O and £3O respectively; Blackburn (Darwen), for three years, £4O, £3O, and £lO respectively. The following resolution was an accepted amendment on an original proposition which'was long debated :—" That whereverthe Conference has determined, after considering the recommendation of the district meeting and the Home Mission Committee, to with- draw a home missionary minister, the committee may make a grant towird a lay agent." The Home Mission and Con- tingent Fund Committee recommend the following grants amongst others: Macclesfield, £230. Secondly, temporary and decreasing grants to circuits :—Crewe, £2O; Tarporley, £35. It 'as reported that the Home Mission Committee had agreed that the £5,000 voted by the Thanksgiving Fund tor the extension of lay agency should be divided into two equal paits, one-half to be devoted to the extension of lay lagency in country towns and villages, and the other half to be devoted to the same work in towns and cities.

At Tuesday morning's session chapel affairs occupied a good deal of the attention of the Conference. From the re- port of the committee it appears that 3.193 trusts contribute to the circuit funds to the amount of 40,6911., and. that 4,011 trusts are free holm debt. Great efforts have been nude for many years past to reduce the debts on Wesleyan trust property, and with very gratifying results. In 28 years no less than 1,572,232/. of debt has been extinguished. In the past Connexional year 117 chapels, 19 ministers' houses, 17 schoolrooms, 30 organs, and 93 alterations and enlarge- ments have been completed at a gross cost of 325,438/. Of the new chapels completed or projected 129 are for places where there have been previously no Methodist chapels, and they will provide accommodation for 24,310 hearers. buring a discussion on Methodism in the City of London, Mr. Sutcliffe, Of the Ricup Circuit, observed that from all he could gather it seemed that hundreds of Wesleyans whe went up to London from ft e country had been turned away from Methodism through the use of the Church prayers in so many of. the London Wesleyan chapels. The affairs of the Theological Institutim) were completed, the Conference agreeing that twelve men from the list of the reserve should have the Option of going to New South Wales. At the Conference on Wednesday, it was agreed that epecial arrangements should be made with the Home Mis- sionary Committee for the mainttnance and education of the children of ministers engaged in army and navy work, land in special evangelistic work. There was a long debate on the assessment ,to the children's fund, on the leases of membership, and other kindred questions. It was finally decided that the assessment by membership only should be discontinued, and that an enlarged committee should be .ippointed further to consider 'the whole question, and report o the next Conference.—The Mayor of Leeds gave an "At home "to the members of the Representative Conference .:ud their hosts and hostesses. There was a large attend. ;thee, most of the leading ministers being present, and an agreeable evening was spent.

business was made by Mr. GLADSTONE. Among the bills which would be pressed, said the Prime Minister, were the Government Annuities Bill, the Parcels Post Bill, and the Expiring Llws Continuance Bill. Then there was as yet no opposition to the Scotch Entail Bill ; anti as to the Police Superannuation Bill he could not speak decisively. Two bills, however, which were absolutely necessary were the measures providing funds for the Arrears Bill, and that making provision for the deficiency in the Friendly Societies Bill. THE NAVAL RESERVES AND NAVY ESTIMATES.-Mr. GOURLEY raised a discussion upon the state of our Naval Reserves, in the course of which Sir T. BRASSEY stated that at no previous period since the close of the great war were we so well prepared for manning the fleet as at the present time. In the aggregate we had an efficient reserve force of 44,000 men, with which, he felt assured, the country would be content.—The House then went into Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates, and Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNER- MAN stated to the House the shipbuilding programme for the year.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESIW. As soon as the House assembled, Sir S. NORTHCOTE asked if any official report had been received on the subject of the alarming rumour from Egypt which had appeared in the Daily Telograph.—There was no information to give at the moment, but in the course of the afternoon Sir A. HAYTF,R made a short statement on the subject, which, although not official, would, he thought, be found to be a tolerably satis- factory explanation. It was to the effect that a corporal and six men forming a picket at Ramleh had been attacked by 100 Bedouins. and fell back, firing at the enemy as they retreated. Sir Arthur added that he had no doubt the cor- poral and six men did what their orders directed by retiring in the face of the enemy. THE SCOTCH EDUCATION BILL.—Mr. Mundella succeeded in pushing the Scotch Education Bill through its remaining stages. The hon. gentleman announced the names of the Commissioners under the bill, who are to include the Lord Provosts of Edinburgh and Glasgow. In moving the third reading, Mr. MUNDELL& said the bill would be a blessing to Scotland, inasmuch as it would raise the whole-tone of public education in that country. and quicken the competi- tion of the public schools by offering some inducements for children to reach a higher level. After some discussinu, in which Mr. Mundella was generally thanked by the Scotch members for persevering with the measure, the bill was read a third time.

TIIE ROYAL TRISH CONSTABULARY.—On the order for going into committee to consider the authorising of an in- crease of pay to certain officers of the Royal Irish Consta- bulary Force the Land League members made a combined attack upon that body, and strenuously opposed any increase in their remuneration.—Mr. TRETELYAN defended the police, explaining that no charge of indescretion or severity against them could escape his attention. He denied that the service was unpopular or that an exceptional number •of resignations had been recently received. After a lengthy discussion the House went into committee, and the bill was subsequently reported. The Customs and Inland Revenue Bill was considered, and ordered for third reading. The Scotch Entail Bill was talked out by Mr. BIGGXR, and the House rose at six o'clock.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDAY.

TITE NEWSPAPER CORRESPONDENTS IN EGYPT.—The Earl of INIonLEv referred to the unfortunate telegram in Tuesday's Daily Telegraph reporting an alleged scare among the 60th Rifles at Ramleh.—The UNDER SECRETARY stated that so far-from there being any confirmation of the rumour, a tele- gram had been received from Sir A. Alison which completely refuted it. Three rumours of an unsatisfactory character had appeared in the papers within a week, which it was found were not based upon any trustworthy information; and as these were not only pre- judical to the public service, but disheartening to the gallant soldiers now in Egypt, he earnestly ap- pealed to the patriotism of those who had control over newspapers at hom3 to hold their hands before they published reports of this kind. The Duke of CAMBRIDGE pointed out that in times like the present it was of the utmost consequence that nothing should be stated which was not true, and after referring to the publication of the "miserable little outpost affair " as "perfectly monstrous," His Royal Highness appealed to the press not to allow sensational articles to appear in their journals with the mere object of getting them sold in the streets by a lot of boys, by whom Ile bad sometimes been taken in himself. After considerable discussion the Electric Lighting Bill. was read a second time. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY.

THE ENDOWED SCHOOL Conruisstow.—lt was announced by MIINDELLA that a separate Bill would be brought in to continue the powers of the Endowed School Commission another year, ancrthat a Bill would be brought in next session to deal with the whole subject. REPLY POST CARDS.—The POSTMASTER-GENERAL inti- mated that reply post cards would be issued to the public on Monday, October 2, and that foreign reply cards will be issued about the same time, which will be available for all countries in the International Postal Union. THE INDIAN EXPEDITION TO EGYPT.—At the request of Mr. Stanhope, the Marquis of HARTINGTON stated the pur- port of the telegrams which had passed between himself and the Government of India on the subject of the contri- bution out of the Indian revenues towardß the cost of the expedition to Egypt. The Home Government proposed that all the expenes of the Indian contingent should be at the charge of India. The Government of India unanimously objected to this proposal. It was replied that the Indian in- terests in the Canal justified the Home Government in ask- ing the Indian Government to- bear part of the charge. When the Indian Government sent the first telegram they were preparing to despatch a considerably larger force than they had now been asked to send]

R'OMAN CATHOLIC CHAPLAINS' FOR THE TROOPS.—Sir A. limmat informed Mr. Moore that five Roman Catholic chaplains would proceed with the troops to Egypt, and gave an assurance to Sir G. Campbell that two Presbyterian chap lains would also accompany the soldiers. THE EGYPTIAN REVENUES In reference to the report that money is being raised by the Porte upon the security of Egyptian revenues, Sir C. DILICE said no official informa- tion-had been received, but the Government were of opinion that such charges could not be justified. THE OUTPOST AFFAIR.—The SECRETARY for WAR was asked if there was any foundation for the report about the outpost affair, and the right hon. gentleman said he had telegraphed to know if there was any truth in the statement made, as he thought, in a most extraordinary and much to be regretted message to the Daily Telegraph, and the reply was that the facts were as stated in the official telegram from General Alison.—Colonel TOTTENHAM desired to know whether in consequence of this message, which had been most injurious to the feelings and honour of one of the most gallant regiments in the service, the Secretary for War would draw the attention of the commanding officer to it, with the view of the exclusion from the British lines of the correspondent who despatched the message.—Mr. CHILDERS declined to give a positive answer, but said he and Lord Northbrook were in communication with the authorities, and he thought the House would be satisfied with the rega- lations which had been recently published as to the functions of correspondents in the field. THE ARREARS BILL AND PUBLIC BustNr.ss.—The PRIME MINISTER stated that it was the intention of the Govern- ment to ask the House to proceed with the Arrears Bill on Tuesday next. There was no prospect of carrying the Police Bill without considerable delay ; that measure would therefore be dropped: The right hon. gentleman told Mr. Lowther that the reason why the Government had not asked for an immediate judgment upon the amendments made by the Lords on the Arrears Bill was because of the extreme importance the Government attached to some of those amend- ments, and because they wished the House to have a full opportunity of consideration before coming to what might be a most momentous decision.

MISCELLANEOUS. - Mr. CHILDERS, answering Colonel Stanley, stated that the Government had not at present any intention of embodying any of the militia battalions. The Reserve Forces Acts Consolidation Bill passed through committee, and the Militia Acts Consolidation Bill was ordered to be reported.—At the instance of Sir G. CAMPBFLL, a debate took place on the policy pursued towards the natives in South Africa.—Mr. T"REVELYAN made:a statement on the operation of the Crime Prevention Act, and defended the action of Earl Spencer in making recent arrests, which he said were absolutely necessary for the preservation of human life.
Tho House subsequently went into Committee of Supply and several voter were agref•d to.

Nothing teaches patience like a garden. You may go round and watch the opening bud from day to day; but it takes its own time, and you cannot urge it on faster than nature directs. There is no religion in making yourself miserable. God loves to make poor sinners happy. In the Old Testament He bids you delight yourself in the Lord, and promises the desires of your heart. In the New, Be says, "Rejoice in the Lord always."
