During the dinner hour on Monday. at Scot's bri zkyarcl, Gat,shead, a portion of a burning kiln fell on two boys, killing them instantaneously. At Nlonatout h assizes, on Tuesday, Denis Dolan received a sentence of 15 years' penal servitude for attempting to murder his wife by stabbing ker. Two seamen of Kirkcsldy, named Arnot and Brown, left Kirkcaldy Harbour for Leith in a small boat last Sunday, and have not since been seen. It is supposed they were drowned. The Freheit compositor found guilty on Tuesday of pub- lishing scandalous libels regarding the Phcenix Park murders, was sentenced at the Central Criminal Court,on Thursday, to three months' imprisonment. On Saturday afternoon there was a review and sham fight in Heaton Park, in which all the local volunteers and the line regiments at present stationed in Manchester and Sal- ford took part. General Cameron, C. 8., was in command. A supplementary estimate for the Civil Service is issued with the parliamentary papers. The amount required, in addition to the suns already provided, is £507,322. Three hundred thcrusand of this sum is for the Irish con- stabulary. The second section of a new line of railway from Spalding to Lincoln was opened on Tuesday for passenger traffic. It is the joint property of the Great Eastern and Great Northern Companies, and will give to London an alternate line to Doncaster. _

The last act in the sad drama of the Glasgow Bank was ended on Tuesday, when payment was made of the remain- ing balance of the debts owing by the bank. Thus termin- ates one of the most cruel and disastrous incidents of criminal folly in the whole commercial history of this country. The Select Committee upon the Agricultural Tenants' Compensation Bill met for the last time on Tuesday (Mr. Shaw-Lefevre presiding), and decided, in consequence of the late period of the year at which the committee were ap- pointed, that they could not complete their work this S The ancient castle of Pollok, near Glasgow, the residence of Sir Henry Crawford Pollok, Bart., was destroyed on Mon- day night by fire, doing damage to the extent of £20,000. The castle was 200 years old. Some valuable articles were saved from the ruins. It is covered by insurance.

On Monday morning a fire was discovered on the premises of Messrs. John Reid and Co., shipbuilders, in Port Glasgow. The greater part of the yard, including the boiler sheds, joiners' shops,and other buildings,were completely destroyed, the damage being estimated at £20,000, which is stated to be covered by insurance. Professor Blackie, the ;eminent professor of Greek in the University of Edinburgh, acting on medical advice, has resigned his chair. Professor Blaclsie has held the appoint- ment since 1852. The patronage is in the hands oi the curators. The professor was incapacitated by illness during last session. Elaborate arrangements are being made at Drumlanrig Castle, the Nithsdale seat of the Duke and Duchess of Buccleuch, in view of a visit by the Queen on or about the 23rd August. The Queen intended to visit the Duke at Delkeith Niece last autumn, but was prevented by the ill- ness of the Duke. On Saturday Mr. Bradlaugh obtained from Mr. Justice Stephen a writ of certiorari removing the trial of himself and the editor and proprietor of the Fl eethinker for alleged blasphemy from the Central Criminal Court to the Queen's Bench Division. The case is not expected to come on before the November sittings. At Brighton, on Saturday, Charles Harris Franklin, of London, a visitor, was committed for trial charged with the manslaughter of a lad named Charles Patrick. On Tuesday deceased was bathing off the pier, and the prisoner, presumably unaware of the lad's presence in the water, threw an empty bottled beer box into the water, which struck deceased, causing him to sink. The body was recovered on Saturday. The telephone has been put to a curious use at Birmingham, The Borough Hospital and the offices of the Health Depart- ment, three miles away, have had telephonic communication established between them in order to lessen the risk of the spread of infection by friends visiting patients. This method of ascertaining the progress of the inmates is being exten- sively used daily. TERRIBLE SENTENCES ON Two YOUTHS. —At the West Riding Assizes at Leeds, on Monday, Laurence Crossley, aged eighteen, was sentenced to twenty years' penal servi- tude for attempting to murder his employer, Mr. George Black, hosier, Leeds, who had discharged him for miscon- duct. Alfred Thompson, aged seventeen, who had attempted to murder Mr. Trozier, a Wakefield chemist, by beating him with a hammer, was also sentenced to twentyyears' penal servitude. DOING PENANCE IN A: CHURCH: EXTRAORDINARY SCENE.—An extraordinary scene was witnessed on Sunday evening at All Saints' Church, East Clevedon—viz., that of a man doing public penance for the seduction of a servant girl who now awaits her trial for manslaughter. The church was crowded, and, the vicar, having delivered an address on Church discipline, the penitent confessed his sin, and promised to take his place in the assize court next to the unfortunate girl upon her-trial at Wells. WIFE DESERTION BY A CLERGYMAN.—The Rev. T. J. Bailey, a clergyman of the Church of England. was brought before the Brighton magistrates on a charge of deserting his wife, who had been an inmate of the Brighton workhouse I since May. Prisoner was formerly curate of St. Michael's Church, in the town, and some few years ago removed to London, where his wife ultimately became chargeable to the parish of at. Giles. On behalf of the prisoner, it was con- tended that his wife's behaviour made it impossible for him to live with her. He, however, professed his readiness to make arrangements with the guardians, and on this under- standing the charge WAS not pressed further. EXTRAORDINARY BLOCK AT THE LIYERPOOL ASSIZE, COURTS. —About noon on Saturday business in the Crown Court, St. George's Hall, came to an absolute standstill for want of jurymen. Two sets of juries were "locked up," Mr. Justice Day, it was said having given freedom to the men who were not sworn. "I have called in the hall, I have called in the lobby, and nobody turns up," was the statement of the beadle in reply to an imperative call from Mr. Shuttleworth ; and that very practical- and able clerk of assize was heard to suggest the summoning of a jury of bystanders, a proceeding that would not have been without a precedent. "We cannot get a jury," was the last remark I that fell from Mr. Shuttleworth's lips. A Conservative demonstration was held in Bolton, on Saturday, on the occasion of opening a new club. Speeches denunciatory of the Government were delivered by Mr. E. Hardcastle, Mr. W. W. B. Hulton, Lieutenant-Colonel the Hon. F. C. Bridgeman, and Mr. A. L. Briggs; and a resolution was adopted expressing "profound distrust of the policy of Her Majesty's present advisers, which had been attended with such disastrous results at home and abroad." It had been intended to introduce Colonel Bridgeman as one of the future candidates for the borough, but, as the chairman ex- plained, "unfortunate circums:ances " in the town had pre- vented this from being done. THE HARVEST IN THE MIDLANDS.—The harvest in the central Midlands commenced in South Leicestershire on Monday by the cutting of several fields of oats. Durieg the last ten days the growing crops have made remarkable pro- gress, and with continued fine weather the crop will not only be a fairly good one, but will not he pearly so late as was at one time anticipated. Wheat in some cases is very good indeed, but in the majority of instances the ears are badly filled, and have a starved appearance. Barley is uniformly good ; and oats, although very late on old clay lands, will be a fair average crop. The potato disease is very bad. and in a great many instances one-third of the crop is only fit for pig food. The hay is now nearly all secured in good condi- tion, and has proved a most abundant crop—in fact, on the average, three times heavier than that of last year. Irecoetu TAX.—A parliamentary return just issued gives particulars relating to the income tax, under schedules A, B, and D, of the gross ' amothat of property and profits assessed in each county of Great Britain in the year 1880-81, compared with the totals in 1879-80, together with the duty charged under income tax and house duty in 1880-81. The gross amount of property and profits assessed in 1880-81, in Great Britain, under schedule A, was £174,308,104; under schedule B, £59,206,362; and under schedule D, £245,592,495. The duty charged as income tax at GI. In the pound amounted to £9,943,250 ; and as inhabited house duty, £1,887,125. In Ireland the gross assessment of pro- perty and profits in 1880-81, under schedule A, was 113,290,2-12; under schedule B, £9,950,587; and under schedule D, £9,703.414. The duty charged as income tax at 6d. in the pound amounted to £180.999. A Loy s STORY.—George Farrant, aged twenty, and Ellen Mokinan, aged sixteen, both employed at a baker's estab- lishment at Uxbridge, were on Monday committed for trial on a charge of attempting to carentlt suicl:?4,, by throwing themselves into the river Fray, a branch of the Colne. The evidence was to the effect that on Thursday evening, after dark, as a young man named Brill was walking along the bank his attention was directed to an object in the water. After partially undressing he entered the water, and in dragging the bedy of the young woman to the shore he observed that a second body, that of the young Man, also came to the side, and subsequently a broken tie was found around the waist of the young woman. On the arrival of assistance means were adopted to restore animation, and with success. The young man on recovering censciousnesss in- quired for his" dear Nelly," whom he said he should meet in heaven. Two letters were put in as evidence, in one of which, written by the young woman to her sister, the writer stated that she would never see her again except in the coffin, as she had drowned herself with George, whom she loved. 51

Tire TROUBLES OF BETTING MEN.—A rather curious action, in which two betting men, named William H. Hall and William Marshall, were involved, was tried at the Liverpool Assizes, the other day. Various betting transac-. tious had nassed between the two men, and on the Ist January, 1877, it was found that Marshall owed Hall £BOO. For this sum Marshall gave a promissory note. Subsequently Hall's aunt issued-a writ against him for about £6,000, and as part payment he handed to her Marshall's promissory note. Marshall, however, then went to Hall, and told him that if his mother, from whom he expected money, got to know about his betting transactions, she would cut him off with a shilling, and Hall, at Marshall's request, and with his aunt's knowledge, wrote to a firm of solicitors telling them to give up the note, as it was for " racing debts." Hall, however, maintained that he only consented to the note being destroyed on a promise that the money would be paid at some future time, but he admitted that he never thought of bringing his action until he was "hard up." His consent to the destruction of the note was, however, fatal to his present claim, and on the judge's direction the jury gave a verdict in Marshall's favour. This seems rather bard upon Hall, who now has to pay stiffly for sparing Marsbail from motherly censure.

On Wednesday evening, the Liverpool and Manchester express, wlwn piecing Leamington, killed one of three boys who were playinc, on the line. A conference of London and provincial letter carriers was held in London on Saturday, to take into consideration the new scheme of payment and regulations. Resolutions expressing dissatisfaction were unanimously adopted. The tlial of Richard George Wells for the murder of John Carlyle, at Fulham, in May last, was resumed at the Central Criminal Court, on Wednesday, when the prisoner was con- victed of manslaughter, and sentenced to penal servitude for life.

A man named Freer was remanded at Burton-on-Trent on Wednesday, on a charge of atlempted suicide by jumping into the Trent. the defendant said he was an Army Reserve man, and rather than light in Egypt he tried to drown himself.

Wednesday was the anniversary of Blenheim, which was fought between Marlborough, aided by Prince Eugene of Germany, and the French and Bavarians under Marshal Tallard, when the latter were defeated with a loss of 40,000 men killed, wounded, and taken prisoners, 120 pieces of cannon, and 300 standards. An Inverness telegram says that grouse disease has reap- peared in the North, and in an aggravated form. The dis- temper is only scotched, not killed, and is now assuming alarming proportions. There is a lamentable account from some of the best moors in Ross-shire. The Board of Trade report of the inyertigation into the disastrous collision between the Douro and the Yrurac Bat states that the accident appears to be attributable to the Douro, in not having taken proper precautions; but praises the officers and crew for the subsequent action. The Home Secretary has commuted the capital sentence on William Bradburn, for the double murder at Farnworth, to penal servitnde for life. It will be remembered that the jury who convicted the prisoner recommended him to mercy on the ground of his former unsoundness of mind. The Bishop of Salisbury has stated that he has placed what threatened to be a serious charge in the hands of the public prosecutor. The parish register has been found to be mutilated, several leaves having been cut out, the very leaves which were wanted in an important investigation. SAD DROWNING FATALITY: THREE LIVES LOST. On Tuesday a sad occurrence, whereby three lives were lost, occurred at Stoke Prior. Two children, aged five and four years, fell into the canal by the Half-way Houk.. The mother, the wife of a lock-keeper named -Bishop, jumped in to rescue them, and all three were drowned. A fire broke out on Saturday morning in a cotton ware- house in Oriel-street, Liverpool. The owners had in their employment a number. of women and children, and two of these—Ann Harratty and her daughter, aged eight years— were suffocated in one of the rooms, their bodies being after- wards brought from the burning building by firemen. Nothing is known as to the origin of the fire. A COWES SCANDAL.—The serene atmosphere of Cowes has already been disturbed by one scandal. The elopement of a lady of rank with a well-known yachtsman has caused much commotion and greatly shocked the Castle Club. The gentleman, who is a very wealthy proprietor of coal and other mines, and also possesses large landed estates, is grand- son to one of the best spottsmen of olden times. SAD END OF A MANCHESTER MERCllANT.—lnlelligellee was received in Manchester on Wednesday morning, from Her Majesty's Consul at Havre, that Mr. Samuel M‘Mastar, late of the firm of Hill, 111‘Master, and Plant, had shot him- self at one of the hotels of that city. Mr. M‘Nfaster disap- peared in March last from Manchester, and afterwards went to Norway. His firm was adjudicated bankrupt immediately after his disappearance. THE BATTLE OF THE NILE.—On Tuesday was the anni- versary of the battle of the Nile' which took place in Abou- kir Bay, on the North Coast of Egypt, on August 1, 1798, when Rear-Admiral (afterwards Lgrd) Nelson; with 14 line- of-battl e ships,destroyed the French fieet,under Brueys. It was during the Irish rebellion at that time that Bonaparte had embarked with a large army for the East, having, it was said, formed some plans for overthrowing the British power in India.

RUMOURED KIDNAPPING OF THE PRINCESS LOI7ISE. The rumour of the intended kidnapping of the Princess Louise is revived. It is said that the American Fenians have designs in this direction, and her Royal Highness in consequence is closely guarded. Whilst the rumour is one which is not likely to receive much credence on this side of the Atlantic, one cannot find fault with the Canadian authorities for taking all precautions for the safety of their Viceroy's Royal wife. CAMBRIDGE LOCAL EXAMINATIONS.—The University of Cambridge has, in response to invitations from the outside, avreed to hold a new examination in September, the results of which are to be available for those who may wish to enter the university this October term. These examinations are not to be spread over a number of centres, as are the others, but are to be confined to Cambridge and London. All entries for these examinations must be made not later than August 1, to the Rev. G. F. Brown, Cambridge, or Mr. Corbet, 10 Portman-street, London. Some little time ago the farmers of Aberdeenshire and other Scottish counties warmly discussed the propriety of establishing a farmers' alliance somewhat after the Irish pattern, and now it is shown that the agitation has not been without effect. A "judicial "rent is still unknown in Scot- land, but a rent by arbitration has taken its place, a farm called Nether -Hab, in Aberdeenshire, having been re-let at a reduction of nearly 20 per cent. on the former rent, the re- duced rent ,heing the outcome of arbitration. . Tint ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER BY A FARMER AT ORM- SKIRK.—The principal case in the Crown Court, at the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday; was that of an elderly farmer from the neighbourhood of Ormskilk, who was indicted for the manslaughter of Robert William Walcot, son of an Ormski; k confectioner, by running him down with his gig as he was driving on the market day.from the Golden Lion Hotel. No malice was suggested on behalf of the prosecu- tion, whilst the defence was that the unfortunate occurrence was purely an accident. The jury took this lenient view of th ecase, and acquitted the prisoner. A REMARKABLE OLD MAN.—On Wednesday the remains of a very old man were interred at Church Kirk, Church. His name was John Hindle, and he was a farmer at Stanhill. He was nearly ninety-nine years of age, and promised to last beyond the century, as he was hale and hearty until a fort- night ago, when he left his house to spperintend some mow- ing operations, and fell and broke his thigh in two places. The shock was too great, and bodied on Friday last. The previous Sunday he heard the Bishop of Manchester preach, and was warmly shaken by the hand by his lordship, whom he pronounced a right nice fellow. He tenanted the house in which Hargreaves invented the spinning jenny, and never slept out of from his wedding to his death. He was looking forward to attend the Preston Guild. LOCKED UP IN A CHURCIL—A little fellow between nine and ten years of age, living at Lower Broughton, Manchester, left his home on Sunday evening, and not returning at the usual hour his parents were naturally in a state of much distress, and caused inquiries to be made in every imaginable quarter. On Monday the river was dragged, but without success. At last it occurred to the parents that the boy went sometimes by himself to the Church of the Ascension, and they went about ten o'clock at night to the rector, the Rev. C. T. Watson, who at once cluscd all parts of the building to be searched. At last the child was found fast asleep. It seems that he fell asleep during the service, and, rolling off his seat, was not seen by the apparitor at the hour the church was closed.

CONVENTION OF THE NATIONAL LAND LEAGUE OF GREAT BRITAIN.—As already announced, the annual convention of the Land League of Great Britain will this year'be held in Manchester. It was at first intended that the delegates should assemble on August 14, but in consequence of the opening of the Irish Industrial Exhibition in Dublin on the 15th, the central executive have decided to summon the con- vention for Saturday, August 12. The convention will meet in the Assembly-room of the Free-trade Hall. On the fol- lowing day a public demonstration, at which it is expected several Irish members of Parliament will speak. will be held in the large hall of the same building. The convention this year is expected to be very largely attended, as during the year a great number of branches have been opened through- out the country. A Wires LETTER.—My dear Husband,—l got here last night all safe, and was met at the station by uncle and ..aunt. They were so glad I had come, but were sorry that von were not along. I miss you so muah. We had hot ;dolls for breakfast this morning, and the were so delicious. I want to be so happy while I am here. Don't keep the meat upstairs ; it will surely spoil. Do you miss me now ? Oh ! if you were only here, if but for an hour! Has Mrs. brought back your shirts? I hope the bosoms will suit you. You will find the milk tickets in the clock •, I forgot to tell you about them before I came away. What did yoa do last evening? were you lonesome without me? Doe't forget to scald the milk every morning. And I wish you would see if I left the potatoes in the pantry; if I did they must be sour by this time. How are you getting along? Write me all about it. But I must close now. Oceans of love to you. Affectionately your wife. P.S— Don't set the teapot on the stove. A CLERGYMAN CHARGED WITH IMMORALITY.—The Bishop of Oxfoßl, the Chancellor of the Diocese (Dr. Sweby), the Archdeacon of Berks, and Sir G. K. Rickards were occupied on Friday and Saturday in investigating allegations of improper conduct against Rev. G A. Sneyd, rector of Chastleton' with Rose Elizabeth Marnes, house decorator, who was formerly housemaid in the house of a gentleman in Chastleton. From the evidence of the Rev. William Eustace, of Chastleton, it appeared that a resolu- tion was carried at a vestry meeting at Easter this year, calling the attention of the bishop to the scandal caused by allegations against Mr. Sneyd, and asking for an enquiry. The girl herself said Mr. Sneyd was in'the habit of making signs, such as kissing his hand to her, during divine service and while proceeding from the pulpit to the vestry. This was followed by some letters making appointments, in which he addressed her as "My darling," and concluded "'Your ever loving Alfred," and in which he said he loved her better than his life, and some day would make her his wife. She gave birth to a child in March last year. .Just preN ions to the birth of the child, Mr. Sneyd endeavoured to persuade the girl to sign a paper to the effect that she had not met him from January, 1880, for twelve months, but she refused to do this. An affiliation summons was taken out, which was compromised by the payment of 100 guineas by his relatives, without, us was alleged, his knowledge or or consent. Sergeant Ballantine urged that Mr. Sneyd had become fascinated with the girl, and that his affections for her, however absurd they might have been, had led him into being in her company, but without any criminal intention. On Saturday, Mr. Sneyd, whilst admitting that he had walked out with the girl, and kissed her, declared most solemnly that he had never acted indecently towards her. After considerable deliberation, the court cAme to the con- clusion that Mr. Sneyd had acted most imprudently, but acquitted him of criminal intercourse.

_A Central News telegram, dated Berlin. Wednesday night, safe;—At Wueizburg University Jubilee to-d :y honorary degrees were conferred upon Mr. F I vrcett, pic!rnaster-genera ; Profestor Huxley, Sir John Lubbock, Sir James Paget, Pro- fessor Alexander Bell, of Edinburgh ; Dr. :-.;ietnene, and M. Waddington, ex-French Minister. The Morning Advertiser understands that the committee appoin'ed to inquire into the expediency of the completion of the Channel Tunnel have reported that it may be ren- dered perfectly eafe by the erection of fortifications involv- ing the expenditure of some millions, and a permanent fiarrison of seven thousand men It is arranged that the Duke and Duchess of Albany arrive will at Preston from the seat of the Earl of Latham on Tues- day morning, September 5. His Royal Highness will, after receiving the address of the Corporation, lay the corner stone of the Free Library with Masonic honours. Two goods trains on the Lake Shore Railway inve been in collision at Southbend, Indiana. 60cars have been wrecked and burned. Seven tramps, who were "stealing rides," were unable to get from the cars and were burned to death. Both-engine drivers were seriously injured. A secret meeting of the Irish American dynamite faction was held in Chicago on Tuesday. Patrick Crowe is stated to have declared that a school had been established near New York for instructing young men in the manufacture of explosives to be used for destructive purposes in England. Up to a late hour on Wednesday night only 800 of the Peterhead fishing boats caught in the gale had returned to port. Great anxiety is manifestel for their safety, and dur- ing the night the harbour has been crowded with relatives of the crews. Nine large boats are also missing from Kirkwall. The mail boat is still unable to cross the Pent- land Firth.

On Thursday morning, at ten o'clock, General Ham- ley, who is to command one of the divisions in the expedi— tion to Egypt, left London by special train for Portsmouth to embark for the East. He was accompanied by several officers. Sir Evelyn Wood left afterwards by an ordinary train for Portsmouth.

A shocking accident was reported to the Bolton County Police, on Thursday morning. As a collier named James Boardman, aged 30,was at work in the Ashton Field Colliery, Little Hulton, belonging to the Bridgewater Trustees, a stone weighing about a ton suddenly fell from the roof and crushed him to death. Another man named Tonge had a narrow escape. Deceavd was unmarried. Professor Beesly, ef London, addressed the annual meet- ing of the Tailoresses and Needlewomen's Society, in Liver- pool, on Wednesday evening. He said the objects of trades unions were better understood now than in the past, and they were now considered of advantage to all sides. It was for the good of trade as a whole that such societies should exist. In the past women had lacked union, and it was clear they had not the element of combination for public objects to the same extent as men, though in private life they had shown the highest example to men. He wished there were no tailoresses. It was the duty of men to sup- port women; not the business of women to wcrk outside the family. The present state of society, however, corn- pelled women to work, and it was their duty to imitate the men in trade matters, and organise for self-protection. THE "CROSBY TRAGEDY."—The "Crosby trageay " was investigated at the Liverpool Assizes on Thursday. The accused, a young man named Golding, was charged with the wilful murder of his servant, a young girl named Mary Cromer, under very remarkable circumstances. There was no dispute as to the fact that the prisoner shot the girl dead in the scullery attached to his house, but his contention was that the shooting was accidental, whilst the prosecution alleged that the prisoner had murdered the girl because she had been a party to a discreditable intrigue which her mistress carried on with men named Ritson, who were Golding's next door neighbours. The admissions which these Ritsons were compelled to make in cross-ex- amination showed them to be a couple of finished-scoundrels, and must have inspired everybody with wonder that the prisoner had not used his revolver upon them instead of the unfortunate girl who. was merely their agent. Mr. Aspinall made'a powerful appeal to the jury, and after a short de- liberation they brought in a verdict of manslaughter, with a recommendation to mercy, an illogical but eminently "safe" conclusion. Sentence was deferred. THE "Pious FOUNDER" BUSINESS.—The latest instance of disregard of the intentions of a "pious founder" has a decidedly ludicrous side. An elderly woman named Bur- dett, late of Gilmorton, in Leicestershire, by her will directed that every door and window save one in her dwelling-house should be sealed up for twenty years, and her trustees were declared entitled to certain benefits so lone. as they carried out the provisions of her eccentric will. There was no pro- vision for the eventual disposition of the property contained in the house at the end of the twenty years, and the heirs- at-law of the foolish testatrix appealed to Vice-Chancellor Bacon to set the will aside. The absolute right of a testa- tor to do with his property as he pleases was brought forward in defence of the will, and Pope's line, that a testator may " Die and endow a college or a cat," was quoted as a sort of authority on the subject; but Sir J. Bacon took a practical view of the matter, and promptly 'declared the provisions of the will to be invalid in •so far as they relate to the " blaking " of-the house. The property which Mrs. Brown had intended to seal up for 20 years will be distributed as if she had made no will. CLEVER ESCAPE OF A PRISONER.—A daring escape was made from the Birmingham Borough Gaol, on Wednesday afternoon, and a very smart cloture effected by the detec- tives. On the 25th ult. a young 111111 named Andrew Kenyon was sentenced to three months' hard labour. He was sent to Winson-green Gaol to serve his term, and, being a painter, was engaged to paint the front of the governor's house. A warder was placed in charge of him, but, during his temporary absence on Wednesday, the prisoner went into the house unobserved, put on a black coat in place of the one supplied him by the prison authorities, changed his hat for a smoking cap, and taking up a silk umbrella, left the house. Thus attired he sauntered through the yard and to the prison gates, and after wishing the attendants good day, made the best of his way towards town. On the disc )very of his esc tpe a telegram was sent to Birmingham, where Kenyan was shortly afterwards apprehended in the street. When asked his reason for escaping, he said the food was not good enough. He added, "There have been two clever things done to-day—one was my escape, and the other my capture so soon."

THE LIABILITY OF CORPORATIONS TO SUPPLY PURE WATER.—On Thursday, at the Leeds Assizes, before Mr. Justice Mathew and a special jury, the hearieg of the action in which Mr. John Jessop Manes, solicitor, Huddersfield, sued the Corporation of that town for £5,000 damages for injury sustained through drinking water 'impregnated with lead was resumed.—Mr. Willis QT.C., Mr. Waddy, Q.O , and Mr. Dodd were for the plaintiff, and the Solicitor General (Sir Ferrer Herschel!, Q.C. M.P.) Mr. Forbes, Q C., and Mr. Lockwood for the defendants.—The case, as stated on the part of the plaintiff, was that in its passage through the leaden service pipes the water absorbed lead in such quanti- ties as to become dangerous to life. Through drinking that water the plaintiff had been palsied to a certain extent. He all but lost his life. and his busiuess, through his inability to attend to it, fell off. Evidence showed that if ever the plaintiff recovered, which was doubtful, a long time must elapse. The case for the defendants was that they were only responsible for the water being wnolesome when placed in its mains. It was common ground on both sides that the mischief to the water was caused in the passage from the mains to the service taps in the plaintiff's house. It was shown that one woman had died and several persoies had had to leave the place.—The point as to the liability of the Corporation was reserved for argument in London. the jury being only asked to assess damages in case the Corporation should be held to be liable.—After a short consultation, the jury assessed damages at £2,000. MURDER BY I DOCK LABOURER.—The Crown Court at Liverpool Assizes was engaged on Thursday investigating two charges of wife murder. Francis Duffy,a dock labourer, celebrated the May Bank Holiday in a convivial manner, and, arriving at his home in a drunken condition, quarrelled with his wife because the supper was not ready. She went into the back premises to escape from his abuse, but he followed and stabbed her in the abdomen with a knife, in- flicting a wound which caused her death four days after- wards. When apprehended the prisoner admitted the stabbing, and handed the knife to a police officer. He was found guilty of manslaughter, but sentence was deferred. The second case yes that of William Turner, a collier from Skelmersdale, who was charged with kicking his wife to death. The woman was a cripple, and on a night in June, meeting the prisoner at a public-houte, induced him to go home. Arriving there, she proceeded to make ready the supper, but in consequence of deformity and weakness fell upon the floor. The prisoner who had then taken off his boots, put them on again, and kicked the poor woman in the most atrocious manner as she lay helpless, winding up by jump- ing on her face. Subsequently, when his wife was on the point of dying in consequence of her injuries, he boasted of what he had done. .Whilst engaged in kicking his crippled wife the prisoner repeatedly expressed his intention of being "hung for her before the morning." The jury having found him guilty he was sentenced to death, and there should be no question whatever as to the due fulfilment of the sentence. 'Seldom has a more abominable crime been committed. FRENCH SPlES.—There is a short cut out of French peni- tentiaries ; but it is such a dirty one that the authorities ought to be ashamed of themselves for encouraging men to take it. A moderately intelligent rc;clusionnaire who has served half his time, or even• less sometimes, may, on his private demand, became a mouton, or spy prisoner. He is subject to certain tests with a view to dscertaining whether he is sharp, and whether he can be depended upon; and if he successfully passes through these-ordaals (to which he is put without being aware of it) he is forwarded to some House of Detention or to the Prefecture de Police in Paris, where he is employed to worm secrets out of prisoners awaiting trial. To do this he must assume all sorts of parts, and sometimes assume disguises; and he carries his life in his hands, for he occasionally has to deal with desperadoes who would show him no mercy if they suspected his true character. All this unsavoury work does not give the man his full liberty.; but he may range freely within the prison boundaries. He is well paid, and he is generally allowed to go out on parole. for a couple of hours every week. In the end, he gets a year or two struck off his sentence; but after his discharge he generally remains an informal spy and hanger-on of the police, and it need scarcely be said that of all spies he is generally the most rascally and dangerous. It is fellows of his kind who lead men into planning bur- glaries so as to earn a premium for denouncing them. They are foremost in all street brawls and seditious, playing the part of agents provocateurs,-and privately nctlng down the names of victims whom they will get arrested by and by. They are, in fact, a detestable race, and it cannot be won- .. dared at that when detected by the pals whom they dupe they should be killed like verinin,—Cornhiel Magazine..
THE EGYPTIAN QIT FST lON

THE RUMOURn' SURRENDEZ OF A RUA.. THE PROPO3ED Di'..SPTCH OF TIIMISIT. THOM'S. Events in Egypt during the week lh.)7e been com- paratively quiet. It was reported at the clam of last week that Arabi Pasha had sent to the Khedive an order tg surrender on the terms laid dawn in the Anglo-French ulti- matum some months ago, namely, that he and his companions in mutiny and rebellion should leave the coun- try, retaining their rank and pay on the military es:ablish- inent of Egypt. Whether negotiations are in progrels or 'not the war preparations are not being in any way slackened. The latest accounts say there is no forward movement on the part of our troops to rersrt, and Arabi' content with maintaining his position within a few miles cf Alexandria, whirst he calls up the resourm of the country in his rear. "Great enthusiasm " is officially declared to exist at Cairo, and the army under the orders of the Dictator is continually receiving additions to ihe strength. ,

The Pont-, also at tile close a the week declaredio the Conference that it would send troops " immediately " to Egypt, and having thus acceeded to the request of the Powers, the Sultin mildly proposed that the English preparations should be stopped and cur troops withdrawn from Egypt. Lord Dufferin, therefore demanded that the Sultan should issue a proclamation denouncing Arabi as a rebel, asad the Sultan replied that such a request could only properly be made by the Conference. Contrary to His M.ijesty's hope and belief, the Conference has supported the British Ambas- sador, the German representative specially advising the Porte to give way. Ahined lltukhtar Pasha has given orders in a vague Turkish manner for the assembling of 15,000 men, but no one knows where the force is to come from, or how it is to be provisioaed, (quipped, and conveyed to Alexandria.

A special correspondent at Alexandria telegraphs some highly interesting detail, of the military force at the die- po,4al of Arabi. The rebel General has at his command, exclusive of the large garrison at Cairo, 28,000 infantry, 3.000 cavalry, 144 Krupp guns, several batteries of Gatlings, and 5000 Bedouin irregulars. At Cairo there are largo numbers of Krupp guns in readiness to be mounted. An official despatch from Cairo reports an important meeting there on Saturday of the most eminent religious i and civil authorities. Speeches of the most passionate and inflammatory kind were delivered, and the assembly pledged itself to support Arabi until either a satisfactory peace could be concluded or the English "exterminated." The decrees issued by Tewfik were declared to be nullities, and even the near relations of the Prince joined in the outcry against him. It is reported at Alexandria that Arabi has cast into prison all the provincial authorities who were known to be favourable .to tke Khedive. The plotting of M. de Lesseps, who is said to be in close communication with Arabi, is creating considerable uneasiness, but it is believed that our naval and military authorities are cognisant of the nature of the situation French agents are seeking to create for us, and diplomatic negotiations are now going on with the object of arresting the dangerous =mimes, the main object of which appears to be to bring about such a condition of things as to justify a demand for the cessation of British in- tervention. There is a statement that M. de Lesseps has long been trying to obtain a concession for a fresh canal, which was refused by Arabi. He is now trying, says the Times correspondent, to conciliate him with the object of getting his support, the value -of which, how- ever, would seem doubtful. M. de Lesseps' motto through- out would seem to be be, "Save the Canal; perish Egypt." All the measures which it may he found expedient to take to ensure the safety of the navigation of the Canal will be under the direct authority and with the sanction of the Khedive, as ruler of the territory through which the Canal passes. One of the most important items of intelligence received is the announcement that the powerful Arab journal El Ja wit) has published an artiCle fixing upon Arabi .Pasha the blame for the existing complications, and declaring that it will be necessary to proclaim him a rebel unless he submits. The Secretary of the National Mahometan Association of Bengal has drawn up a statement on the effect likely to be produced by the Egyptian news upon the Indian Mussul- man population. He points out that the Russian attack upon the Sultan was an attack upon all Islam, but Arabi Pasha's attitude of disobedience to the direct command of the Caliph disentitles him to all sympathy from his co-re- licionists. His endeavour to proclaim a jehad without the imprimatur of the authority of the Caliph is viewed by the Mahometan community as the extravagant outcome of in- sensate presumption. A telegram from Alexandria forwarded on Tuesday by the Times correspondent states that the condition of the town is causing serious inquietude. "The natives who have remained are the incendiaries ; the majority of those who have re- turned are the looters, looking after their concealed pillage. It is impossible to mistake the bitterly hostile attitude of this class, as well as of the Mustaphezin, again employed as polio., while large numbers of Bedouins are massed without the town, and the respectable natives are prevented from returning." A report from Constantinople states that Dervish Pasha is " about " to sail for Alexandria with five thousand men.

div.head: DIPLOMATIC ASPECT.
div.p: THE DIPLOMATIC ASPECT.

There is no change in the diplomatic aspect of the Egyptian question. We learn from Constantinople that Lord Dufferin has expressed his satisfaction at the new attitude taken up by the Sultan in regard to Arabi Pasha. His Excellency allows that the Sultan may have some around for irritation of late on account of his urgent demands that Alex mdria should not be bombarded having been disregarded. His Majesty is now resolved to declare Arabi a rebel, but not until after Turkish troops hare been landed in Egypt. Lord Dufferin does not assent to this proviso, but the negotiations on the subject continue, and a satisfactory arrangement. will probably be arrived at. Little can be learned from the tone of the foreign press as to the real sentiments of the Govern- ments of the respective countries ; but one journal— evidently, however, an irresponsible organ of the Opposition —holds out menaces to England in the event of her pursuing an isolated and selfish policy. The official press of the re- spective countries observes strict silence, or at least a strict reserve, in discussing the present situation. ADMIRAL SEYMOUR ON THE BOMBARDMENT OF

ALEXANDRIA. Thetlespatch in which Sir. F. B. Seymour describes the bombardtnent of the forts is published. Its contents have, of course, been anticipated by the private accounts. The Admiral thanks the captains of the fleet for the able manner in which they carried out his orders. Referring-to the op- position the fleet encountered, he says :—" The force opposed to us would have been more formidable had every gun mounted on the line of works been brou4ht into action, but in the Ras-el-Teen batteries few of the large smoo'h bores, and fewer of the French 35-pounders bought in the time of Mehemet -Ali, were manned, the Egyptians preferring to use the English 10in., Din., Bin., and smaller muzzle-loading rifl,d guns. These guns are precisely the same as those ! which Her Majesty's ships carry, and no better muzzle- loading guns could be found. They were abundantly, even lavishly, supplied with projectiles of the latest description, chilled shot; and the sighting of the guns was excellent. The same may be said of the guns hithe Neks lines, except- ing that in them the 36-pounders were more used, and that one, if not two, 151 n. smooth bares were brought into action, in additt ion to the 10in., Din., and -smaller muzzle-loading ! rifled guns fired. Fort Marabut brought two 10in, muzzle- loading guns into action at long range, shell after shell of which came up towards the inshore squadron in an excellent line, falling from ten to thirty yards short." REGULATIONS FOR PRESS CORRESPONDENTS. The War Office has issued an official code of rules for newspaper correspondents with, an army in the field. They specify that all newspaper correspondents at the seat of war must be furnished with alicence granted under the authority of the Commander-in-Chief of the Army at home, stating the paper or papers for which the correspondent is agent. All correspondents in the field are under the Mutiny Act during their stay with the army, and will not be allowed to go beyond the outposts without special permission. The use of a cypher is forbidden. All communications sent by correspondents will be supervised by a specially appointed military staff of officers. DESPATCH OF TROOPS TO EGYPT.

The Duke of Connaught, Sir Garnet Wolseley, Sir John Adye, and other officers who are to assume command of the Egyptian expedition p rid a visit to Osborne on Saturday and bade farewell to Her Majesty, returning immediately afterwards to London. Early on Sunday morning the Ist Battalion of the Scots Guards paraded at .Wellington Barracks, and, marching to Westminster Bride, were con- veyed by river steamers to the magnificent Australian liner Orient, which has been chartered by the Government for use as a troopship. The wildest enthusiasm was exhibited by the enormous crowd which witnessed the departure from the river banks and from numberless vessels in mid-stream, the troops being cheered again and again as the Orient left the dock. After casting off, a specially chartered steamer came alongside, with the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, the Duke of Cambridge, Mr. Childers, and other personages, who embarked in the Orient in order to accompany Prince Arthur some waydovrn the river. Before the Scots Guards left their barracks Colonel Knox, in command, read a letter which Ire had re- ceived from General Ponsonby in behalf of the Queen. Her Majesty regretted that she was unable to be present at the departure, but trusted that the Guards would conduct themselves as gallantly as they had always done hitherto. Colonel Knox had replied, expressing his gratitude for Her Majesty's interest in the battalion. Another movement of troops took place on Saturday, when the let Battalion (King's) Liverpool Infantry were taken on board the Batavia in the Mersey for conveyance to Queenstown. There they replaced the 2nd Battalion Grena- dier Guards, enabling the latter to proceed direct to Egypt in the Batavia. A Calcutta telegram informs us that the preparations to despatch an Indian contingent to Egypt has been so far ad- vanc-d that it is anticipated that the whole of the expe- ditionary force will have started by August 8. Three native cavalry regiments will be despatched instead of one as was orignally intended. Sir Garnet Wolseley, commander-in-chief of the expeli- tion to`Egypt, sailed on Wednesday from London for Alex- andria direct, in the Calabria, with a detachment of the cavalry of the guard. Sir Garnet's physician had advised him that a sea voyage would be bmeficial, hence the sudden change of route.

A 'eork correspondent telegraphs that the 31st Regimen', which had been stationed at Buttevant, embarked on. Wel- nesday, on beard the Dunrobin Castle, for the East. Their strength consisted of 30 officers, 10 staff sergeants, and 846 rank and file, with some WOrneU aucl children.

The squadron of the 2nd Life quards embarked at the itqyal Albert D.)eks on Wednesday-, on board the Calabria, a.-:companied ty a trop of the Royal }hi-Se-Guards. Alto- 2:ether ab:)ut 200 fflts ;mu and as Many horses were conveyed in the CiLibria, which ;eft the dock at 2-30. The band of the licrse Guard Blue played a selection of music, the 'men on board cheered enthusi.rstically.

div.head: AN "EXTRAOItDINARY AFFAIR."
div.p: AN "EXTRAOItDINARY AFFAIR."

An extraordinary affair was reported from Alexandria on Wednesday by the correspondent of the Daily Telegraph. According to his account, a detachment of the 60th Rifles, on outpost duty some distance from the c ity, had behaved disgracefully before the enemy. Charged suddenly by a band of Arab horsemen, the picket, it was stated, had " bolted " precipately, leaving arms and ammunition in the hands of the Bedouins. Other accounts show the affair was really insignificant. The picket; on being attacked, retired on their supports, as they were bound to do, and exchanged shots with the enemy. the reserve were called up, and the position re-occupied. The despat&l to the Daly Teegraph appears to have been written on an exaggerated view of the fixts.
OCCUPATION OF SUEZ BY THE BRITISH.
An Exchange Telegraph Company's despatch from Suez via Bombay, dated Wednesday, says the town has been occu- pied by the British and the telegraph office has been re- opened.

div.head: STATE OF AFFAIRS AT ALEXANDRIA.
div.p: STATE OF AFFAIRS AT ALEXANDRIA.

The Central News *teal correspondent at Alexandria, writing on 27th July says :—The Arabs are busily engaged clearine the streets. era the town is rapidly assuming an orderly appearance. Quite lisquare mile has-been burned,but it is curious that nearly all the villa residences of the Jews and natives have escaped. The looters have made such a clean sweep as I have never bofore fe,en. Nothing now remains for the pillagers but bundles of rags, broken chairs and furl niture, and other worthless debris. We are all anxiously awaiting the opening of the campaign against the rebels, and the arrival of Sir Garnet Wolseley will be welcomed by all The Aboukir Forts are full of Egyptian soldiers, and operas tions may commence at any moment. The white flag is conspicuously hoisted over the fort. The Inflexible, Temeraire, Alexandra, Sultan, and Agincourt are the men-of-war detailed for the bombardment of Aboukir. The Sultan is anchored off the fort ready to open fire at any moment. The war ships are lying off at a great distance, and none of the sailors are allowed to communi- cate with the shore for fear of inflaming the native mind. The blue jackets have, however, been ordered to make pre. parations for a prolonged stay on shore. A naval brigade is now in readiness to land, the Agincourt having brought in 110 marines and 300 blue jackets. The mess stewards, in going ashore for provisions, are always pi.ovided with an escort. The Orion has gone on to Ismailia with a naval contingent ready to land. In consequence of her light draught the Orion is a most useful vessel here. The fol- lowing is a list of vessels at present at Port Said :—The Penelope (flagship), the Agincourt, Tourmaline, Iris, Salamis, Beacon and Coquette. Foreign ships: French,' Legalissoniere (d ' igship), Bison, Alma, Asper Sarthe, and Allier, and Hirondella, the despatch vessel ; Spanish, Arragon ; German, Mowl;. Greek, Hellas. Sub-Lieutenant Chas. Annon, of the Helicon, has ben appointed to the ' a ting vacancy caused by the death of Lieutenant Jackson, of the Inflexible. THE FEELING- AT PORT SAIDe

The Central News Port Said correspondent writes ;—The feeling against the English here is very strong, and a fearful catastrophe may occur at any moment. RUMOURED IMPENDING MASSACRE. IMPRISONMENT OF PASHAS.

A telegram from Alexandria, dated Thursday- , 11-30 a.m., says: Last night and this morning alarm was caused here by rumours of an imptmding massacre. The patrols were con- sequently ordered to use increastd vigilance and activity. The police now -confiscate the bludgeons and sticks carried by the natives. Town criers have proceeded through the native quarter enjoining the people to remain in their houses at three o'clock this afternoon, this being the hour reported to have been fixed upon for the intended massacre. Intelli- gence received here from Cairo to the 30th ultimo states that 17 pashas were itnprisoned in the citadel, including Ali Sherif Pasha, the latter having been arrested on the ground that he employed Greeks to guard his house.

div.head: ARABI CUTTING TRE RAILWAY LINES.
div.p: ARABI CUTTING TRE RAILWAY LINES.

A train armed with Gatlings, Nordenfeldts, and 7-pounders was proceeding to Malabar with marines and blue jackets, under the command of Capt:iin FiEher and Major Phillips, when it was found thar Arabi had again destroyed the rails. The enemy, however, made no attack.

div.head: FOREIGN POWEAS AND THE SUEZ CANAL.
div.p: FOREIGN POWEAS AND THE SUEZ CANAL.

A Central News telegram, dated Jlerlin, Wednesday night, says Germany, Russia, aril Austria have given their adhe- sion to the proposal of Itals for an International Com- mission to deal with the ffairs of the Suez Canal.
On Wedneslay Admiral Seymour latidcd a naval brigale and occupied the Mex forts in order to keep the Belouins in check.

According to a telegram from Alexandria, it is estimatcd that 550 Claristians have been murdered at Damanhour, Tanta!), and Mihella. A correspondent in Rome learns that Ricciotti Garibaldi is enrolling volunteers for an expedition to Egypt in aid of Arabi. The movement is not likely to lead to anything, as It is impossible the Italian Government can allow it to proceed. The Ministry of M. de Freycinet as been defeated on the proposed vote of credit for the expenses of a force to guard the Suez Canal. The question was made one of confidence, or no con idence, and the Chamber on Saturday rejected the Imposed vote by 450 votes against 75. The Cabinet forth- with resigned._ _ _

. A despatch from Washington states that the conduct of Admiral Nicholson in landing the troops to assist in the saving of life and property at Alexandria is fully approved both in the official circles and by the mass of popular opinion,—which means that the great majority, probably the whole, of the " genuine " American community approve the part which their officer took on a critical occasion, and that the malcontents are to be found only among the im- ported patriots. 'rho Times says :—" We understand that the Prince of Wales has been desirous to accompany the headquarters of the expeditionary force to be sent to Egypt, but tbat, in de- ference to the wishes of the Queen, he has abandoned the project. Although, no doubt, there are good reasons for the decieion of her Majesty, yet that his Royal Highness should have been anxious to share the labours of this important enterprise will enhance the respect and esteem with which he is regarded hy all classes of his countrymen." An "official " telegram from Cairo states that the captured midshipman, Mr. de Chair, was conveyed on horseback to Arabi Pacha, who conversed with him for nearly half-an- hour with great kindness, and subsequently sent him by rail to Cake), with instructions that he was to b 3 well treated. It is added that Mr. de Chair has been provided with com- foltable quarters, and that two native officers, who speak English, have received orders to keep him company. The Daily .Arctes special correspondent in Alexandria telegraphs that the long-talked of return of the Arab depu- Lion to the enemy's lines took place on Tuesday morning, and afforded a_ most interesting trip to those who accom- panied the special train sent to the front with Reouf Pasha and his companions. On reaching the front the visitors got out, and the train proceeded beyond with the members of the deputation. When they had alighted sit backed until it was within the British lines and then returned to Alexandria.

div.head: CRIMINAL ASSAULT- AT ST. ELYNS. EXEMPLARY PUNISRMENT.
div.p: THE CRIMINAL ASSAULT- AT ST. ELYNS. EXEMPLARY PUNISRMENT.

At the Liverpool A ssivs, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice North, Joseph Foster, 20, labourer, Wm. Rimmer, 19, labourer, Laurence Birminzham, Id, labourer, Wm. Water- worth, 19, labourer, and Geo. Fillingham. 18, labourer, were charged with having committed a criminal assault upon Mary Forrester, at Eccleston, on July 2od. Mr. McConnell, and Mr. Shee, were for the prosecution, and Dr. Commins, M.P., defended the prisoners. The prosecutix, a girl of 18, living at 34, Havelock-street, St. Helens, was on the evening in question walking with a young man named Neckton. She remained in his company till ,late in the night, and ultimately left him and proceeded towards home. When she was near the railway station she was accosted by the prisoners one of whom said "Good night." She walked on and the prisoners were about to follow her when one of Qaem said "don't touch her, it's little Mary." Rimmer said she was no better than anyone else, and seizing her threw her to the ground. The whole of the prisoners then committed the assault which tbe prosecutrix described. She also had some money and several articles in her pocket, which Foster took and appropriated remarking that he had got her money. She was also kicked violently in the side by some of the pri- soners. When she escaped from the men her face was covered with blood and sand, and her clothing was all torn. Some one in the crowd which came bapit with Nockton, wiped her face, and rescued her from the prisoners. The defence raised was that the identity of the prisoners was not conclusive. The jury returned a verdict of guilty, and all the prisoners were sentenced to 10 years' penal servitude. An indictment for robbery with violence was not proceeded with.

He sold the handkerchiefs, by 8 unPle, to measure about 23 inches at the sem% time explaining that they were a job lot, and being a job lot, they are known in the linen trade to be irregular in size, and occasionally to have il avvs in them. He had seen Mr. Uns- worth since he received the order for the goods, and defend- ant admitted the delivery. —Mr. Unsworth said that he gave the plaintiffs an order for handkerchiefs in December last, and when they arrived he returned them because they were not to o-der. • The order given at the beg'nning of April ' was given on conditions that they were to be to sample. lie gave the plaintiffs an or for ten dozen 23-inch hand- kerchiefs, but when they arrived Arne were found to measnre 21 7-Bth inches, some 21, and some 22. Not one of them masured 23 inches.—His Honour thought the con- , tract had not been fulfilled, and gave judgment for the de, fondants.

TEE NEW CONGREGATIONAL MANSE.—The new Congre- gational manse, built at the corner of Clifton-voad, from designs by Mr. John Wilson, and costing some £7OO, has been occupied this week by the Rev. I. D. Thomas, pastor of the Congregational Church. TRADE OF RUNCORN PORT.—The aggregate registered tonnage of the 60 vessels which entered the port of Run- corn last week was 5,378. Amongst them were 14 light vessels, while the imports amounted to 7,600 tons during the week. For the corresponding week of last year the number of vessels entering the port was 49. The exports of salt and coal from Runcorn and Weston Point for the Jive weeks in the month of July amounted to 39,736 tons, as entered by the custom house.

SUDDEN DEATH AT THE BOARD SCHOOLS, WIDNES.—A very sudden death took place at the Board Schools, Widnes; on Friday morning. About a quarter-past nine in the morn- ing James Clunie, a caretake at the schools, was beard hy his wife to fall in his bedroom. She went in, and finding him on the floor apparently ill, she called for help. Dr. McDonald, who lives quite close, was at once sent for, but before he could arrive life was found to be extinct. The deceased was about 39 yearsof age, and leaves a family. He has not been attended by any medical man for about two years. At that time, however, he was seen by Dr. McDonald, who treated him for heart disease. The deceased was, we are informed, at the temperance lecture on Thursday night, and went home in seeming goad health. SHIP BUILDING AT WESTON POINT.—The building of a screw tug at WeStln Point creates hopes of an addition to the trade of the busy little port on the Mersey. The new boat will be somewhat larger than those presently employed at the port, but will be engaged in like manner. Mr. Jos. Parkes, of Northwich, is the constructor; Mr. Edwin Foden, of Northwich, has charge of the machinery required; and Messrs. Stubbs and Son are the carpenter's. The effort is looked to with sonic interest, the prospects of development in this particular branch of labour being received with great favour.

HAIM ON WIDNES RAG SELLERi.—Michael Boyle was charged at the Widnes Petty Sessions, before Messrs. E. Gibbons and W. D. Holt, with having in his possession a set of scales which were half a pound against the customer and also with using a weight which was not denominated. He pleaded guilty "but not to his knowledge." Superin- tendent Barker proved visiting the defendant's premises, which he occupied as a marine store dealer in Grenfleld- street, Widnes, and on examining the scales in use for weigh- ing the rags and bones defendant bought in, found them 121 b. against the customer. A weight was also found in use which was without denomination ami which was considerably short of a pouud. A fine. of 40s. and costs was inflicted.

NOT ASIIA:sIED OF HIMSELF.—At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Catherine Roberts and Eliza McGee were charged with using threats towards Patrick Lawley such as to cause him alarm and fear of his life. The complainant, a strong looking man, said the case had arisen out of the two woman being summoned last clurt day for using bad language to his wife. After the summonses bad been served, both defendants began to make a great noise on the wall which divided his house from their's, so that he was afraid the wall would come down. They afterwards came to the street and challenged him to come out of his house and tLey would give him "something worth summon- beg for."—The Clerk: They made you afraid of what they might do ?—Complainant: Yes, sir. A Defendant: Are you not asharnecl of yourself to say so ?—Complainant : No, I am not.—The magistrates did not think there was any- thing in the matter, and dismissed the case. FEMALE CRITICISMS AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Catherine Welsh was sum- moned by Margaret Dailey, for having used language towards her calculated to create a breach of the peace. De- fendant had called the complainant a police informer, which seemed to be a term held in the utmost abhorrence, and other names of an equally scandalous nature.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace.--Catherine Cronfield pleaded guilty to using exciting language to Catharine Mar- tin, at Widnes, on the 26th July, and was also bound over to keep the peace. The criticisms, as described in this case, were quite unmentionable.—Catharine Fallon, another Widnes woman, was bound over to keep the peace, she hav- ing been found guilty of using provoking language towards Ellen Martin, on the 29th July.—Defendant had remarked on the complainant's character in the choicest Billingsgate, and made it extremely difficult for ker to refrain from active
