IT:"—At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Tikiinas keatir4, a labourer, bionging to Widnes, was charged with being drunk and digclaerly Oh Lite 26th July, and also with assaulting Mary Ann Bird, A married woman, residing in Appleton-street. Defendant pleaded guilty to the first charge, but said in reply to the second, that complainant bad struck him with a brush. The Supe.intendent said that defendant had been fifteen times before the Bench, having on one occasion been imprisoned for a month for stealing, and on another occasion, for two months for assaulting the police.—Complainant, when called, stated that defendant on the day in question had come to her door and belayed in an improper manner. Se " rebuked " him for it and he went away, but coming back' in a short time, entered her house and hit her on the face with a large stone, the result, as she phrased it, being quite visible to the Bench, her face having been severely cut and bruised.—Defendant acknowledged throwing the stone, which he intended to hit the door. Complainant, however, most unfortunately put out her head at the moment, and the stoue struck her instead. The magistrates—Edward Gibbons and W. D. Bolt aquires—sentenud the prisoner to a month's imprisonment for his drunken conduct, and two months for the assault.

WARNING ' A DISSATI,FIED CUSTOMER.—Mary Cilley was charged with assaulting Fanny Wigley, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday.—From the evidence it appeared that Mrs. Wigley had sent her girl to purchase. a "pair of kippers" at Mrs. Colley's shop. When the girl liatought them Mrs. Wigley did not like their appearance, and sent them back with the information that they were not fit to eat Mrs. Colley would not take them back unless complainant came herself, which sit'b accordingly did. When in the shop she repeated her remark as to the edible unfit- ness of the articles, and the husband of Mrs. Colley, who came in at the moment, remarked that they were fit enough for the complainant, anyhow. The latter was leaving, *hen Mrs. Colley threw the "scoof " of the scales at her, bitting her on the neck. She was hurt by the blow, and went into the shop of Mr. Noon, the butcher, to rest, but was not allowed to do so; Mrs. Colley comisg up and pulling her our in a very rough manner. The defendant afterwards, as declared by a witness, who protested independency, struck Mrs. Wigley "scandalous."—.l fine of 20s. and costs was imposed.

DISTURBING TIIE SALVATION ARMY: UPROARIOUS CON- CT or A WIDNEs YOUTH—A young man, named James Riley, belonging to Widnes, and judging from .appearaace of the order denominated " roughs," was charged at the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with conducting him- self in a riotous manner during divine service in the ' Wesleyan school-room Widnes.—" Captain'" William Elmes said be held that rank in the Salvation Army. On Monday night the "corps "in Widnes was holding a service in the Wesleyan school-room. They had as usual com- menced the service with singing, and thereafter two of the " soldiers" engaged in prayer. The defendant then began to conduct himself in an obstreperous manner, shouting at the top of his voice, keeping his cap on contrary to all Salvation Army "orders," and otherwise making himself prominent by an cntire absence of what was right and proper for the occasion. When asked to take his cap off and stop his "row " he ordered "Captain " Ehnes to "get out " "go on " ttc., and interlarded his remarks with phrases more forcible than polite. A police. constable (392) had finally to be called in, and to him also the defendant was very violent, using language of an offensive nature. The constable took him in charge and brought him to the Police-station. In reply to the Bench defendant said he had no excuse for himself; and thit he had not tasted beer that day. It was stated that he had been before the court previously, and had just completed a term of 10 months' imprisonmentfor house breaking. He was sent to gaol for la month with hard labour.
FIRE IN A. RUNCORN CONFECTIONER'S SIIOP.—On Wed-

uesday night about ten o'clock, the very unmelodious •sound of the tire bell "startled the dull air," and alarmed the inhabitants of Runcorn. The streets 'speedily showed an animation for which at that hour they are by no means distinguished, and inquiries were the order of the evening, the question "Where is it ?" being about all that could be heard for some ticie. A. considerable number of people found their way to the fire station, no sign of fire anywhere being visible, and here it was discovered that the tire was in a shop in the High-street. One or two firemen, who seemed to have thrown on their helmets and run out began to arrive, and a more was made to get the engine out. 'Ere it could he effected, however, a messenger aerived with the intelligence that the ,fire was out, a piece of information which made a number of people w*nder what all the cow had been about, seeing that the whole affair had not lasted much over ten minutes. It appears that about ten o'clock Mrs. Webster, who occupies a shop 39, Higlz-street, as a confectioner, had been attending to a customer, end by some accident a large paraffin oil lamp, which stood on the counter, was knocked to the around, setting fire to a quantity of straw lying there. An alarm was at once given, a young girl taking fright at the leiaze and smoke ruehing out into the street, and by her cries attracted the attention of the neighbours. Water was luckily at Land in plecty, and the fire was almost ianmediately got unkr. The shop is composed largely of wood, and if the fire had got a fair hold the damage Clone would have been seriotze. As it i much at the centents of the shop are in- jured both by the water and the smoke, • which was very dense. It is stated to be insured. The excitement won enhAided, and many jokes were cracked in the course of the remaining part of the evening about the nnneessary trouble c which many had put themselves to. One matter -deserves cominent. Short as was the time during which the fire had an active existence, Mr. Robert Wright and a number of his subordinates were at the fire engine eation, and considering it the duty to make "assurance doubly sure," got out the hand reel. They were just on their way with tills apparatus when reliable information was brought of the extinguish- ment of the fire. The town is to be complinveate4 on the promptitude of the local fire brigade.

At the Edinburgh _ University on Tuesday, the degree of "Doctor of Medicine," was conferred upon Donald Urquhart M'Lennan (Scotland, MB., and C.M., 1878), and 31 other gentlemen. Dr. M'Lennan practices in Widnes.

RUNCORN PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL: ANNIVER- SARY SERVICES. Anniversary services were held in this chapel on Sunday—the Rev. William Inman, of Blackball, occupying the pulpit. Good congregations were present during the day. The collections amounted to close on M. ST. MARY'S CATHOLIC SCHOOLS. SerTHOIIS in aid of these new school's were preached in St. Mary's Catholic Church, Widnes, on Sunday. High Mass was celebrated at eleven, and the Rev. Father Sheehy, vice-president of St. John's College, Waterford, preached at the morning service. The evening sermon was preached by the Rev. Father O'Callaghan, of St. Michael's, Liverpool, fairly large con- gregations being present at both services.

DEPARTURE OF SALVATIONISTS FROM RUNCORN. Captain Gibbs, who has been "commanding "the Salvation Ara ‘v at Runcorn for some time, has, with his " hallelujah wife and child," departed for Australia. The " soldiers "at Runcorn held a number of services of a valedictory nature in connection with the departure of the "gallant captain," and otherwise commemorated the event. On Sunday the ser- vices were of a very animated nature, ar.d were largely attended, the band of the army also parading the streets at an early hour. A farewell address was given by Captain Gibbs, %bleb visibly affected many members of the army. A public tea meeting was held on Monday. which was largely attended, and a procession was afterwards formed, and a parade through the streets engaged in. Great enthusiasm wc.s manifested in-the entire proceedings.

SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A Bo Y AT WIDNES.—A rather serious accident happened on Tuesday, to a young lad named Thomas Macaulay, residing with his parents at 14, Caro- line-street, Widnes, and employed as plumber's boy at Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s chemical works. He had been engaged on the "high level " shortly after twelve o'clock, and it is supposed that he had in a fit of boyishness, attempted to reach the lower part of the work by sliding down the bannisters of the staircase. He was found lying at the bottom in an insensible condition, and must have slipped or overbalanced himself in some way, coming down heavily on the metals beneath. He was, as soon as discovered, conveyed to the Accident Hospital, where he was seen by Dr. McDonald. On examination it was ascertained that he had sustained severe injuries to his left arm, while his facu was very badly cut, the nose being much injured. The eyes had also received severe injury. He lies at the. Acc- ident Hospital in a very precarious condition, and without regaining consciousness. •

TIIE ROYAL COLLEG3 OF MIIsIC.—By direction of the Prince of Wales, the following letter has been addressed to the beneficed clergy of England and Wales:—" Duchy of Cornwall Office, S.W., 30th July, 1882. Sir,—l am di- rected by the Prince of Wales to send you the following communication on the subject of the Royal College of Music. His Royal Highness is fully aware of the large demands on clergymen, which often makes it impossible for them to give pecuniary aid, even in the best cause. On the other hand, they have peculiar opportunities for bringing subjects requiring such support before their parishioners, and by forming committees can obtain small subscriptione from those who, though not wealthy, are willing to assist a worthy object. The Prince of Wales, tiler close, desires me to ask your aid by bringing the subject of the Royal College of Music under the notice of your parishioners and acquain- tances, and by inviting them to contribute to it. I airs also to express the hope that you will be able to form a com- mittee in the parish, with the view of collecting smaller contributions towards this national object. I forward a packet of collecting cards for the latter purpose, and am directed to state that, as the widest possible support is desired, small contributions will be gratefully received. Music increases the sum of harmlees and elevating plea- sures, binds families together, alleviates the sorrows and quickens the joys of life, and not only enlivens the social meeting, but is the best accompaniment to the worship of Almighty God. AU this the Royal College of Music will assist. The foundation scholarships of the college may, it is hoped, often be the means of ie .evokin talent in quarters where otherwise it would have lain 'dormant. On these grounds his Royal Highness commends the college to your I early and best attention, and I shall be glad to hover for his information whether and, if so, in what way it will be in your power to assist the object in view.—l am, dear sir, your obedient servant, CHARLES MORLEY, Hon. Secretary." AN EN MICEMAN SENT TO GA.OI, AT WARRINGTON: A SAD CAsß.—John Gandy, described as a shonniker, brought before Messrs. C. Broadbent and F. Monks at the! Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, charged on warrant I with having, on the 19th May, neglected to maintain his *family, whereby Ws wife and five children became, and still I are, chargeable to the Union.—The prisoner pleaded f. y remarking that he had not been able to provide for them.— Mr. Shearer stated that on the 19th May last the prisoner's wife and family were admitted to the Workhouse, and al warrant was issued against him on the sth June. Prisoner I was brought before the magistrates anti committed to gaol for 14 days. He come out of gaol on the 25th June, and the Guardians gave him to the 12th July to take the children away. This, however, the prisoner drd not do, and the ease came before the Board on the 12th July, when they gaTe him a few days longer, and he was instructed if the prisoner did not take his family away during that time to take out another warrant. Prisoner Aid not take his children away on the 28th July, and they were still in the Work- house.—Mr. Monks: Is he a Warrington man P—The Assistant Clerk : He is an ex-policeman,—Prisoner said he was born in Penketh.—Mr. Shearer said it was very ex- pensive for the Guardians to maintain the wife and five children.—Mr. Monks: He has been used and com- mitted to gaol, and he seems to he incorrigible.— Mr. Shearer said he wrote to the prisoner to ask him to come and make some provison for his children, but he did not come near.—Prisoner said he had not been able to work, as he had erysipelas in his leg, but ;! he was able now, and he would make things all right in a ' few weeks.—The Chief Constable said he was sorry to see the prisoner in the position he then was. He had a drunken wife, and tiee police had done all they could to help him, but he had gone from bad to worse. He had no borne for ' his family. His wife was a well-educated woman, and used to be a goes:nuns, and she had relatives in a good peeition in St. Helens, who had helped them until their patience was I thoroughly exhausted. The prisoner used to have a good home, but he had spent it large fortune. He came-et a very old Penketh family. He was a very fair penman, and could get hisliving in several ways if he would only buckle to.— Mr. Broadbent said it was a *very painful case, hut they had to deal with it in the interests of the ratepayers:, and as a warning to other people. These cases, the Guardians told The magistrates, were becoming too numerous, and when the I Guardians pressed for committal the Bench felt bound to Icoteviet.—The prisoner 'gat sent to gaol for a month.

LEAGUE HALL,. WARRINCIVOX.—On Sunday night tke last of a series of lectures on total abstinence was de- livered in the above trail by Mr. Thomas Campbell, before a crowded audience, the following gentlemen being on the .platform : Mr. Mullins (in the chair), Mr.. Campbell, Mr. , McDonald, Mr. Houghton, and Mr. Kilduff. The Chairman said that Mr. Camptell's stay amongst them was drawing to a close, but he hoped that in a very short time they would have him with them again because he had do* a great work in Warrington=during the mission. They had on the list names of something like 250 persons who had come up during the mission and taken the pledge, and he sincerely hoped they would +keep that pledge. Mr. Houghton and Mr. Kilduff having made a few remarks on the importance of the pledge those present were asked to take, Mr. Ca mobeit rose amidst great applause, and in the course of his lecture he said that at the present day they ha l in England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales associations almost of every kind to better the condition of the working classes. they had political associations, religious associations, and even the licensed victuallers' association. Well now, if the licensed

victuallers had associations for the protec-taon of what they called their rights and 'interests, surely they would not begrudge them, as c'body of workingmen, irom forming an asslciation or associations, whether it be iatkconnection with the Catholic Church, the Church of England, Wesleyan., or any other denomination, to protect their interests in the best possible way, and that was what they were doing there that night. He aekod if there was anyone there that was ignorant of the dark specks that surrounded them. Mr. Chamberlain, President of the Board of Trede, said in a speech delivered by .him on the 13th March, 1877, "that during three houriof one Saturday evening, 35 public-bouses in different parts of Birmingham were watched, and during those three hours there was a total of 838

drunken persons alleged to have been sten corning out of the 35 houses. In Birmingham there were 1239 drinkshons, and, Vet, although there were 833 persons reported as coining drunk during the ,three hours out of 35 houses watched, the police reports for that day gave only 29 cases of drunkenness as coming from the whole of the 1,839 houses. If the remainder of the drinkshops gave an equal proportion of tirunkards with the 25 houses which were watched, it would give 44,136 case of drunken- ness for three hours on a Saturday everting alone, instead of :29 for the whole day as reported by the police. fie (Mr. 'Campbell) asked his audience to consider what an amount of good might be done with the money that was spent in.drink, and went on to say that the number of deaths caused through drink was something enormous. On this topic he quoted the opinion of Dr. W. B. Richardson, and said if that opinion was well founded, the drinking habits of the country were responsible for upwards of 230,000 deaths yearly. If, said Mr. Campbell, there were 230,000 slaves through drink, there never was a massacre took place in history either in .the present or past ages that eat down so many lives. It was a terrible thing to think of, and yet there were some people who thought them a lot of fanatics in going into this ques- tion: Pe3ple would not defend them, and why that was so he did not know. He appealed earnestly to his audience to swell the ranks of the League of the Cross, and follow the example of such great men as Cardinal Manning, Sir Evelyn Wood, and many others who take great interest in this im- portant work, for drink had been and would be so long as it existed, the disgrace and the wreck of thousands of happy homes. A large number of persons signed the phdge' and a vote of thanks having been passed to the lecturer, tll2 pro. (peelings termin4,ted.

BOY BURGLARS AT WARRINGTON.—eit the Liverpool Assizes, on Saturday—before Mr. Justice North—William Linaker (17), labourer; John Thomas Carroll (15), labourer and Peter Wilson (13), were charged with having, at War- rington, on the sth July, committed a burglary on the pre- mises of James Varlet, and stolen therefrom ss. Mr. Sutton prosecuted. Carroll pleaded guilty, and his statement im- plicated the others. All were found guilty. Mr..Cotting- barn spoke on behalf saf Carroll, who, it appeared, had a good character. Linaker, who had been "in trouble " before, was sentenced to six months' imprisonment. The two others were sentenced to a month's imprisonment, to be followed by three years in a reformatory. WARRINGTON FORESTERS IN LIVERPOOL.—On Saturday last the members of the P.C.R. Court Ancient Order of Foresters, Warrington district, held the seventh anniversary by an excursion to Liverpool. The members came up in good force accompanied by a number of their wives and friends. In the afternoon they met at the dining rooms of Mr. J. Howcroft, 10, Myrtle-street, and late of this town, where an excellent tea was found ready for them, and it gave general satisfaction. After partaking of the good things set before them, the members held a short meeting on the subject of their society, under the presidency of Brother D.C.R. L Davies. The party shortly afterwards separated to enjoy themselves in the town, and on t!)e river, returning home at night much pleased with the day's out. CiLklaGr. o RESI,TING TTIZ POLICN.—At the War- rington Police Court, on Monday, John Duane, a young man, was charged with obstructing P.C. Evans whilst acting in the execution of his du ry in Horsernarket-street, on Satur- day night; and further with resisting the constable by at- attempting to rescue a prisoner.—The prisoner pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Evans said that about 20 minutes past 11 o'clock on Saturday night he was in Horsemarket-street, and took in custody a man who was drunk and disorderly. He was bringing the man to the police station, when the pri- soner called out " You won't well „take him. Now, boys, set on, and let us take him away from him." They took hold of his prisoner awl pulled him away. Ha fol- lowed Duane, and took him into custody.—The Ex-Mayor: Did you get the prisoner again ? P.C. Evans: No, sir, I did not; but I think I shall.—The constable in reply to the Bench, said he had no witnesses, and cotd not remember anyone who was present at tYie time.—The prisoner said he did not know who the man was that the constable had in custody, and did not know anyone who was in the crowd.— As there was no corroborative evidence, the Loch dis- charged the prisoner.

PRESENTATION TO A SCNDAY SCHOOL TEACHER AT I PENKETIL—On Friday, July 2 Ah, the teachers and officers of the Wesleyay Sunday School met for the purpose of pre- senting to Mr. H. Booth, a family Bible, and also a copy of the Wesleyan hymn book, both handsomely bound and covered in morocco. Coffee and refreshments were provided, and after all bad done justice to the good things, Mr. R. Garnett, the superintendent, in making the presentation, referred at great length to the services of Mr. Boath, who has been the trepeurer of the sick club for a period of 26 yeare, He (Mr. Garnett) could hilly say that Mr. Booth n,,ver hal been absent from the Sunday school during the 26 years, unless through sickness or some other unavoidable, cause. He hoped Mr. Booth would long be spared to enjoy comfort from the sacred pages of the books he was presented with. Mr. Robson read the inscription on the frontispieces. Mr. John Atherton and Mr. Thomas Wilkinson also spoke in feeling Wr!ls of thi long services of Mr. Booth. Mr. Booth, in returning, thanks, said he was extremely obligel to all for their kindness. He did not linow that be deserved such a handsome present, for he had only done his duty. A very pleasant evening *AS spent. TIZE VOlr_lEs OF A WARRINGTON Buosert.—Wm. Piir.4tot, bcoker, was charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with being drunk on Sunday afternoon, with furiously driving a horse he was riding, and further with violently assaulting P.C.'s Clynes and Baxendale, whilst in the execution of their duty, in Mersey-street.— On Sunday afternoon, about a quarter past three o'clock, P.C. Clynes was at Warrington Bridge in company with P.C. Baxendale, and saw the prisoner on horsebacklsoming from Arpley Station. He was driving at a very furious rate, giving the animal the full length of the rein, and driving his heels into it, Near Marsh's shop there was a great number of harvest men, who had a narrow escape of being knocked down. He got on the footpath in Bridge- street, and on getting off he continued at the same speed as far as the Lion Hotel, where be turned round and came to the Roebuck Inn stables. Thezonstables followed him into j•the stables, and prisoner came out in a few minutes with the horse, which a little boy was then leading. P.C. Clynes asked prisoner for his aNress, and he said . he lived in j Edinburgh. The constahise ordered P.C.Baxendale to take I him into custody and he came quietly es far as the end of Hall-street, -where his friends lived, and prisoner then set the I policemen at defiance. He knocked both the constables j down, and when P.C. Clynes got his 'hand in his pocket to I get out his snaps the prisoner turned round on him like a dog and it his fiugee. P.C. McLaren tben came up, and with great difficulty 'he was locked up.—The prisoner coin- plainedeof violence haying been used to him, and asked "Do yen think thtt fair treatmer,t to a man who helps to support, you ?"—The Ex-Mayor-said there might hive been ! some violence used, and no 1110 n than was really necessary. The prisoner war tined ss. and costs or 7 days for being drunk, 108. and-costs or 14 derye for furious driving, and 1 40s. and costs er one month for the assault on the officers.

WHOLESALE ROBBERY Ot BACON AT WARRINGTON.-- At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, before Alder- man Burgess-and Captain litton, Peter Grounds, living et I:the Moan Cow Public-houte, St. James's street, Latchford, was charged with stealinefrom the premises of his father, Joseph Grecnds, pork butcher, Bridge-street, on Tuesday, August 15t, four sides of bacon, and at divers other •eimes 'during the last four weeks, live sides of bacon, of the Tdue ',altogether of £lO, or thereabouts; and John Woods, 54, Old- road, Latehford, wag charged, in company with Teter Groands,-with stealing, on Tuesday, the four sides of 'bacon, valued at £4 123.—Greunds pleaded guilty, and Weeds not guilty.—Mr. Hunt sick', that Grounds was 23 years of age I and had a wife and one child, and he lived with his mother- in-law at the Roan Cow, St. James's-street, Latchford. , Woods was a brush maker, and worked for •Mr. Parkinson. On Tuesday, Inspector Berry received informative of the ' sale of a lot of bacon. He made enquiries, and then went to see the prosecutor to impart some information he had re- ceivedas to a Mr. Sohn Stirrup. Mr. John Stirrup is .a tobacconist and umbrella manufactuner. in Bridge-street, and also occupieo a provision shop in Bewsey- road, which his son John managed. Enspector BerrY's information went to show that about a' month ago three sides of bacon were sold by the prisoner : Grounds to Mr. Stirrup, senr. Four sides of bacon were taken to the Roan Cow, and remained there until it was• c3nvenient to dispose of them. On Monday last two sides of bacon were taken from prosecutor's shop in the day time, and in the evening were sold to Mr. Stirrup, by the first named prisoner. Again on Tuesday night four sides were taken from the shcp by Grounds, assisted by the other prisoner. The, first four sides of bacon weighed 1681h5., 1 which at fid. a pound came to £5 7s. St The four sides 1 taken on Tuesday weighed 1481b5., and at the same rate were 1 worth £4 153. 7d. One of the sides stolen on Monday or 1 Tuesday night weighed 381 b., and had been sold by Mr. Stirrup jour. at7d. per lb. It had been a question with him whether there had not been some rec Avers. Mr. Joseph Grounds when in the box would state that the bicon bad beereeold much below its value. Peter Grounds was simply a servant to his father, who did not miss the bacon owins to the large quantities he had on his premises.—The prisoners were remanded until Saturday, and Woods applied for bail, which was refused.

ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT ON THE CHESHIRE LINES. Au alarming railway accident took place yesterday morn- ing on the Cheshire Lines Railway at Hough Green. The 845 a.m. passenger train from Stockport stops at Hough Green, being due there av 9-29 a.m. Yesterday it stopped at the station as usual, and then proceeded to back into a siding in order to Itt the private express of the Midland Railway Company pass. While so engaged the rear car- riage struck the points of the siding the concussion causing the four end carriages to leave the rails. Considerable abrm was felt by the passengers, but none of them were injured save in sustain- ing a severe shaking. The occurrence netessitat,ed the delaying of the Midland express for about 45 minutes. The Stockport train did not leave for a full hour. But little damage was done to the plant.

DEATH OF A CHILD AT RUNCORN.

NEGLECT BY THE MOTHER. On Tuesday, at the Runcorn Sessions. House, Mr. J. T. Ridgway, district coroner held an inquest touching the death of Ellen 011)lin. a child aged one month, the daughter of Thomas and Sarah Giblin, residing in back Mersey-street, Runcorn. The child died on Sunday morning last. Sarah Giblin, the mother of the deceased child, and aged only 18, deposed that her husb ind was a dock labourer, and that deceased was her first child and had been weakly since its birth. Dr. Bagnall attended her when she was confined. She took &ceased to Dr. Bagnall's on Sunday, the 23rd inst., and he told her that the child wanted some medicine and that she must fetch is. ad. before he could give her any. He, however, gave her some arrowroot and a powder, but the child seemed to lie no better. She did not go to see Dr. Bagnall again because she Lad no money to pay for medicine, and the child died at an early hour on Sunday morning lAst.—Crosszexisnined by the Coroner : She knew there was a parish doctor in Runcorn, and did not take her child to him because she did not think that he would give her anything. Samuel Freeman Bagnall, physician and surg,,on, practis; lug in Runcorn, said that she was with the last witness when she was confined. There was nothing wrong with the child when it was born. The mother and another woman brought the child to him on the 23rd ult. It was then diseased, and appeared to have been very much neglected. -The mother was quite incapable of attending to the child. He gave her sotne dressing, and told her distinctly that if the child died he could not grant her a certificate unless she had the seen to. He had not seen the child since its death.

Jane Owen, 4, King-street, stated that she nursed Mrs. Giblin during her confin y ument. The child was a very healthy one. She visited Mrs. Giblin eight times, and she was in a very delicate state. She saw the child after it was dead, and thought it bad died in convulsions. Elizabeth Murray- said that she lived in the same house as Mrs. Giblin, and was with her every day aft.:r her con- finement. The child seemed right enough in the day time, but at night it was always crying. The Coroner, addressing the prisoner, said that it was a matter for them to decide whether they thought the negli- gence had simply been from ignorance on the part of the mother on account of her youth, or from illness, weak health, or other causes. Probably they might think that the child had died suddenly from natural causes; but if on the other hand they thought the child had really died through carelessness and from want of proper attention, then he thought it was a case for a post-mortem examina- tion. He thought there was some blame attached to the mother, but the father was_niore to blame than she was.

The 'hey returned a verdict to the effict that the child died from neglect, arising from the ignorance of the mother and the persons assisting her. The Coroner, addressing the mother, said : Da you hear the verdict that the jury have returned ? They said that your child died, they considered, through your neglect, and that further, they think that the neglect was causal by your ignorance. Now, I may tell you that if the evidence Ina been a little stronger, you and your husband might probtbly have been standing charged with manslaughter. Lot this be a lesson to you. If you have any more children do not neglect them, and if you hove no money, go to the parish doctor for assistance. The jury also say that your husband, your mother, anti all yonr .filend? ought to have advised you, and that they are also guilty of negligent behaviour towards your child. Addressing Mrs. Murray, Mr. Ridg- way went on to say that the jury thought—and be quite agreed with them—that she ought to have seen that the mother had the child taken care of, and obtained a doctor's assistance. It did seem to him that there were a good many people who did not care a bit how their children died, so long as they got over all responsibility, and so long as they got a death certificate. The jury and he (the coroner) thought that Mrs. Owen did all that was necessary for the child. He was much obliged to Dr. tiagnall for having refused to give a certificate, and he thought, supposing the mother bad bad more sense, they might possibly have taken a different view oC the whole case.

div.p: REFUSING TO SELL MILK TJ TRE • INSPECTOR. TNTERESTING TO WIDNES MILK DEALERS.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Messrs. 'Edward Gibbons and W. D. Holt on the Bench, a caae of some interest to milk (.rcalers cime up for consideration. Jdlya Bennett, a farmer and cowkeeper, in Peelhonse-lane, war, summoned by Superintendent Barker, as inspector under the Food and Drugs Act, for baying, on the 14th Juty, at Widnes, refused to sell one quart of new milk to him when -recuested to do so for the purposes of analysis. Mr. W. T. 'Husband defended. I Mr. Barker stated 0:14 be was in Peelbouse-lane on the 1 •day stated, and saw a woman with a number of milk cans, -such as are used to v..-pply small customers, in her hand. :He asked her if she was carrying it oat for sale, and she i,replied that she was. •He asked her name, and she said that 1 it was Sarah Shooter, -and told him that she was•c trrying the j'milk out for John Bennett, up the lane. He said, '"1 want 1 a quart of that milk;:i want it for the imposes of analysis." i She replied, "I won't sell it you; bat you can have as much as you like if you go Lack to Bennett's farm" He said no, as he wanted a quart of the milk she was-carrying. She i again refused to sell it to him, when he told her that she had !.batter sell it, or he should summon her for refusing to do so. I She continued her refusal. At this time two carts .came down the road, and he nude purchases of milk from each °I • them, one of the purchases being exactly the same as he wished to make of the woman—a quart can•full. She stood . and looked on, and saw him pay for each. He told her who Fite was—the inspector of weights and measures—and repeated , to her the purpose for which he wanted the milk, but it was i c no use. . .

Cross-examined ',Jv Mr.liusband : This took place about ,NO yards from Mr. 'Bennett's farm. This was•the first tiro.e he had worked in Widnes under the Milk Act. Mr. Husband: Are you aware the Local Board have taken samples of milk hitherto? Witness: I don't know anything about the Local Board. You are aware that they can do so by the Act?—l am not aware of it. You have read up the Act—Yes; but not-referring to that. You have told us all that hit.ppened that is of import- ance ?—Yes. We Lre to take it that you have nothing left to tell us?— Yes. What•sort of cans were they thatais woman had f —They were such as tnilk is usually delivered in. She said clic was delivering milk to customers. I do not know whether she had meass-re or not. I asired her for one of her qua:t cans full. _
What did she tell you az.ie was?—gbe saki she was a servant of John Bennett's, I have sine ascertained that she is his wife.
Well, you know a wife is supposed to b 2 her husbanrs ervant.

The Chairman (Mr. Gib':ons): I question whether the husband will always find it so. (Laughter.) Mr. Hush ind: Yes; but you uudei:stand Abe is supposed to be under his orders. To Mr. Barker—You know the woman, and understand that she is peculiar. Mr. Barker: Yes, she is rather peculiar. I have seen her since. I asked her if she was John Bennett's wife. She replied," I suppose I sin Bennett's wife, I do not know that I am not." (Laughter.) This concluded Mr. Barker'f7 evidence. M. Husband then addressed the Bench for the defence. He read the clause which referred to the matter, and based his defence on a contention that the woman was not exposing milk for sale as understood by the Act—in a public manner. Mr. Ilirker also had not complied with the requirements of the Act inas- much as he bad not tendered the price of the. milk. The woman also had no authority to sell the milk as required by

r Mr. Barker, and the case altogether was of an unimportant nature. They were not afraid to have their milk examined, as Mr. Bennett lived in a very respectable neighbourhood and had a very good connection. having.. the honour of sup- plying a great many members of the Local Board with milk. Part of the mistake had arisen from Mrs. Bennett being accustomed to Mr. Dickinson, the Board's Inspector, coming to examine her milk and her not knowing Mr. Barker. Mr. Husband then proceeded to call his witnesses. Mrs. Bennett was the first called, some amusement being ecca- sioned by the defendant sharply ejaculating "Sarah " in order to bring her more quickly to the box. She remem- bered the occasion on which she spoke to Mr. Barker. She told him the milk was sold, and that she was not to Ed i it over again. She had no authority from Bennett to sell the milk. She had no quart measure with her. She hid had the inspector, Mr. Dickson, up before but niver the police. She denied being offered a shilling by Mr. Barker. She I did not see him with a measure, but he had a jag which he i used when he made the purchases from the carts. She did not know that it was to divide the milk. She saw hipn give money to the people he bought the milk from. Mr. Dickson wai called, but could give no evi.leece with , regard to this ntse. The magietrates dismissed the case.

div.head: TEMPERANCE LECTURE AT WIDNES.
div.p: TEMPERANCE LECTURE AT WIDNES.

A lecture, enlitlid " England Heaie and Beauty," was delivered in the Waterloo-road schoolroom, Widnes, on Thursday evening, under the auspices of the Widues Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, the Rev. T. G. Madden, of Christ Church, Liverpool, being the lecturer. The Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar of Widnes, occupied the chair, and there was a very large attendance. The CHAannaer, in introducing the lecturer, said they had again assembled for the consideration of the most im- portant question of the day so far as England was con- cerned. (Hear, hear.) They were there to consider the drink traffic. Many present were members of their society, and they did not wish that lecture to be a flash in the pan. Instead, they wished that night to gain over new adherents to their cause, and he concluded by asking them to stow that they were heart and soul in the matter by taking the pledge and joining the Church of England Temperance Society. (Hear, hear). The LEC rURER, after a few introductory remarks, pro- ceeded to state that the drink enemy at home was much more dangerous than any enemy we had abroad. Hidden, it was mere to be feared, and in his belief was ruining the commerce of the country. To intemperance was largely to be ;attributed the present heavy taxation, and be believed with Lord Derby, that if workingmen really knew the fact that out of every 6.1. they paid for beer, sd. went for taxes, they would not meddle with it. Referring to a week which he had spent in Kirkdale gaol as chaplain in that gloomy institution, the lecturer said that he found a large propartion of the inmates had come there through drink. The money spent in the traffic was enormous, and if only spent in legitimate trade, what an increase in industry there would be, what a quickening in the veins of the chemical trade. (Hear, hear.) Corning to the more practical part of the subject, the social part, he hoped that there were many happy homes in England, homes to which the soldier, battling for country, whether on the plains of Egypt or in the mountains of Afghanistan; or the sailors amid the dark waves of the stormy ocean, would look back to with pleasure and pride as real British homes, happy, glo- rious, and free. (Applause.) There waseliowever, the other side of the picture where the home which should have been so happy wasruined, and become a curse. Through drink mothers had left their children to die, and husbands brut illy abused those who should have been the nearest and dearest to them. Speaking of the third bead of his lecture, he said he thought there was a tendency sometimes to' despise the bodily tem- ple. Man must have been very beiutiful in his first state, when after the ruin wrought by sin, "He was still so physically beautiful." But drink destroyed the body, and not only the tody but the soul, for they would all remember that upon the golden gates of Paradise was ayritten, "No drunka;d shall enter the Kingdom of Heaven." In con- cluding, he urged that the remedy must be a personal one. All must take a part in the struggle, and fight for "England, home, and beauty." "[he temperance problem was coming within the realm of practical polit:ca, and he expressed a belief that Sunday closing would soon be an accemplished fact in England. (Hear, hear.) Votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

To:aibta Pasha is at KAfr DOWak. The only tluropean with Arabi Pasha is a Swiss named Ninet, formerly a secret agent of Haulm Pasha. Three officials of the Land and Mortgage Company, stationed at Kafr Dowar, have been &dd.), escorted to Ismailia by order of Arabi Pasha. The reconnaissance made bn Thursday satisfial Sir Archibald Alissu that the enemy has no force worth mentioning near Alexandria. There is no foundation for the c)nstant alarmist reports of an impending sutprise of the city. Arabi cannot attack without executing mommts which would give ample warn- ing of his intentions. TECEGRAPIIIC ARRANGEMENrs.

The Centr;l. N;ar's ia enabled to state that it has been decided by the Government to connect Suez, Port-Said, and Alexandria by cab'e ; and arrangements have been made for that purpose with the Eastern Telegraph Company. The work will be completed at an early date. A Lloyd's Port Said telegram, rec deed via Alexandria, and dated from the latter place, 3c.1 Aug., 7-20, p.m., states : —No eommunic ttion with Sn:•z, either by post or wire dur- irg the last two days. Telegrams via Gaza greatly delayed, if not suppressed at Cairo. Sending this message by steamer to AlQxandria. Great surprise is expressed here that the British authorities have not laid a cable from Alexandria which wouk be beneficial to the shipping interests. Canal traffic still clear. Europeans here anxious.

div.head: CF.TEWAYO IN ENGLAND.
div.p: CF.TEWAYO IN ENGLAND.

Cetewayo remained quietly at home yesterday. During the evening he received several visitors, both military and civilian, who bad known him in South Africa. Some officials from the Colonial Office were presented to His Majesty and graciously received. Cetewayo is very favour ably impressed by our climate, and by the appearance of tha part of London in which be is staying, having been led to expect something different. Three policemen have been Posted eu:side the house to prevent inconvenience of the crowd.

The " tirstfruits" of the harvest in Suss(tx made their appearance on Thursday morning, in the shape of a loaf of bread produced from a Brighton b.tkehouse from this year's wheat, cut on Monday. On Thursday evening a little child named Sarah Mitchel, four years of age, the daughter of a labourer living at Elton, Bury, was so severeley burned that she died shortly after- wards.

Most of the fishing boats caught in the gale of Wednes- day, had returned to port last night.,lohut several are still un- accounted for. Many have returned in a disabled condition, and the loss of life and nets has been Rerions. Four fisherman were drowned during the gale—one off Aberdeen, and one c,fl Rosehearty, one off Buckle, and one off Wick. Nothing has been heard of the Kirkwall boats. The -Press Association is informed that owing to the determination of the Treasury to call Connell, the captain of the Cork " Moonlighters," as a witness against Wash, application will be made on the part of the dence to have the trial postponed until the October session of the Central Criminal Court.

Ilarvest reports from Sussex, Surrey, Kent, and Ham shire, state-that under the most favourable conditions the wheat crop will not exceed an average, and barley but slightly. Oats in many places are' a splendid crop. The hay is almost in, but it has been greatly injured by the rains. Roots promise well. A Limerick telegram says :—" The strike mania has now become general throughout Ireland in the constibulary, and telegrams in reply to circulars sent from Limerick to every statien in Ireland are being received hourly, stating that if the Government do not at once comply with the demands of the force they will all, on the day mentioned in the circular, lay down their arms and refuse to do any .more duty." - -

Another death occurred at Bolton yesterday morning through the dangerous practice of leaving pans of scalding water on the thor. A womin named Millward, of Slater- fi,ld, went into the yard to hang out some clothes, when a little boy natnul John Mil'ward Brown, aged four years, walked backwards against a pan of boiling water, which was on the floor, and fell into it. He was dreadfully scalded, and died in a few hours.

Captain 1-Immersley, chief constable of Cheshire, has re- ceived information of a serious oatbreak of swine fever on the farm of Mr. Furber, of Audlem. Mr. Furber possesses a large heard, and the deceased first attacked three pigs. A veterinary surgeon clndernned three others, and the next day the disease attacked nine more, and they were immediately slaughtered. Saliaequently three more were attacked and killed, making over fifteen out of he herd that have had to be de,stroyed. _ .

A sad affair has -just occurred at Basterley. A. child named two years old, was playing in a garden adjacent to Ih?r father's house, when the lid over a deep well, upon which the cnild got, suddenly gave way, and eleceased fell to the bottom and was drowned. A verdict of "Accidental death" was recorded, the jury censuring the parents for allowing the well to remain so unprotected. At Sedqley, yesterday, Thomas Poole, a labourer, charged with causing the death of his coulin, Thomas Meredith, bv throwing him over a wall at Gospel End. on Snnday night prisoner met deceased in the lane, and, wi,hout „changing words, threw him over a garden wail. The fall caused the spinal card to he injured, and death subwinently took place. The prisoner, wit° said he was only "larking" with the deceased, was remanded. Bail was refused.

FALL DOWN A COAL PIT SHAFT. An inquiry was held on Thursday at Moxhy, near Coss v', resrcting, to death of Harriet Fletcher, who had been married five months. On Tipsday the deceised, whilst in in intoxicated stafe went across a fi:dd, rln.l when walk fng near a disused coal pit she staggered and fell Jon the shaft. Her dead body was subsequently found terribly mangled.
The jury considered the shaft was not properly fenced, and the inquiry was adjourned for the attendance of the Govern- ment inspector.

CLOSE OF THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE. The Wesleyan Conference re-assembled yesterday morni ing in Brunswick Chapel, Leeds. It was announced that - the Bey. Jabcz i'aikyn, one of the newly-appointed military ' would embark wi h theitroops for Egypt. A - variety of matte, haying been disposed of, the reading of the .1 journal commenced. A large number of leading Methodists in Leeds and neighbouthood were present to wan, ss the closing act. Votes of thanks were presented to ffends en. tertaining ministers, to the President of the Conference, the secretary, awl others. Devotional exercises followed, and at noon the conference came to a close.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
UOUSE OF LORDS.-FRIDAY.

THE EGYPTIAN QCESTION.—EarI GRANrILLE corrected a statement he had made as to the number killed in the first massacre at Alexandria. The number should have been GO.—Lord LAMINGTON asked whether the Government would endeavour, through the Khedive, to obtain a peaceful solution of the Egyptian question.—Earl GRANVILLM declined to reopen the question after the debate that had taken place upon it. CETEWAYO.—EarI KrAteEntEv-said Cotewayo would have no official reception in this country. He would simply call at the Colonial Office, and they would hear what he had to say.—Adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMOAS.—FRIDAY.

DISESTABLISIIIIENT.—MT. DICK PEDDIE gave notice that early next session he would move a resolution for the Cs- endowment and disestablishment of the Church of Scotland. —Sir J. HAY said he should oppose the resolution. FLOGGING IN A SCHOOL.—Mr. DODSON, replying to Mr. O'Shea' said when he was furnished with the name of the school he would make inquiries into the statements made that four chi:dren had been severely flogged for refusing to conform to religious duties different to that professed by their parents.
PREVENTION OF CAME ACT.—Sit W. HARCOURT, reply- ing Mr. Tottenham, said no steps brd been taken against any person under the alien clauses of the Prevention of Crime (Ireland) Act.

ARMY RESERVES.—Mr. CHILDERS, replying to Sir W. Batellott, thought the returns of the Army Resreves were quite satisfactory. TIIE IRISH POLICE.—Mr. TREVELYAN sail the reports of the thre deflect strike of Irish police in Limerick were very much exaggerated. There was nothing to create apprehen- sion, and the dispute was being arranged.—Mr. CALLAN said he had a telegram quite of an opposite nature,•and insisted on addressing the Chair until he was twice called to order. THE RUSSO-TURKISH WAR INDEMNITY.—Sir O. Diucr.„ aplying to Baron de Worms, said the Government had na information that tha Russian Government had surrendered any instalment of the Russo-Tarkish war indemnity, but the Turkish Government had raised a loan on the security of the indemnity. AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS IN IRELAND.—Mr. GLAD- STONE, replying to Mr. McCarthy, said he could not promise the appointment this session of the Royal Commission to enquire into the c,ndition of the agricultural labourers in Ireland.

EMIGRANTS.—Mr. A. MOORE called attention to the state of the law regarding emigrants. He showed the disgraceful manner in which poor people were treated on board emi- grant ships, and the other hardships they encountered by frequently being detained five or six weeks in London in disreputable lodging-houses awaiting the sailing of the ship. He moved that the Passenger Acts require revision and re- form.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN objected to the resolution. He said considerable improvenient had been made on board emigrant ships. He thought friendly connections with the , owners of vessels would produce better results than compul- sory legislation.—The motion was negatived. The SKIE CROFroM.S. —Mr MCFAIMANE called attention to the con lition of the crofters in the Isle of Skye, and advised the appointment of a Royal Commission to make enquiry!

div.head: PAINFUL DISCLOSURES.
div.p: PAINFUL DISCLOSURES.

At the Liverpool Assiz =B, on Monday, before Mr. Jastice North, Eliaibeth Kerr pleaded guilty to an indictment charging her with having, at Widnes, on November 21st, married one John Harrison, her former husband, John Kerr, being then alk'e. ; Prior to the passing of the sentence, Mr. Woodard, who appeared for tlie prisoner, said she had been married to Kerr when she was about 17 years of age while be was 43, with a family of several almost grown-up children, and from the time of the marriage she had been shamefully ill-treated. , On one occasion she had been ill-used by her husband, and ' laid up for live weeks. He had turned her out of the house, and threatened her lit. She then went to Widnes, whither he followed her, ran after her with a large knife, and attempted to stab her, but the knife was wrenched from him. The prisoner was really driven into this act, and did not really appear to know the wrongful nature of the act she was com- mitting at the time she went through the form of marriage. He (Mr. Woodard) hoped bis Lo:dship would be able to deal lightly with the prisoner, Mr. Lumb, who appeared for the prosecution, said he was instructed that the statement made by Mr. Woodard was not altogether correct. The man she married the second time had been a lodger in her husband's house, and improper relations had arisen between thew'. Annie Kerr, a daughter of the prisoner's husband, 15 years of age, was called, and was examined by Mr. Lumb. ' Mr. Lumb: Did yea ever see your father ill-treat this woman? Witness: Not unless she was drunk.—Did you ever see him strike hitr on the head with a bottle? /Co, sir. Harrison was a lodger in the house, and when he left she went with him.—Cross-examined by Mr. Woodard: She said her father had thrown a salt-cellar at her on one occa- sion ; it was the result of Ler " carrying's on."—Mr. Wood- ard: Did you ever see your father throw a paraffin lamp at her ? Witness : Yes, but it did not hit her, and she took a clock from a wall and threw it at him.—Mr. Woodard: Did you ever see him strike her in the face with a scrubbing brush ? Witness: No, sir. Another witness having spoken to the effect that Kerr was a good husband, two witnesses were called by Mr. , Woodard in support of his allegations. I Ultimately His Lordship deferred sentence till Tuesday. On the latter day Kerr, in extenuation, said that it was only cruelty on her husband's part which had driven her to do what she had done. His Lordship said the offence was one which could nct be looked over. The prisoner. must suffer three tnonths' imprisonment.
