MUSIC AT RUNCORN.

Sir,—Your correspondent, "Flaccus," made a suggestion in your issue of the 15th instant, to the effect that the brass bands of Ituncern should play in some public place once a week. Will he kindly tell the members of those bands where the mus;c is to be obtained, as they will want a larger quantity thau they have at present. He reminds them of Widnes having two concerts a week; but is "Flacons" aware that the Widnes band receive some kind of pay for -their playing. If the Runcqrn bands received but a trifle of the enc,iur.l•L;ement received by the Widnes musicians, I feel lure they would oblige their townsmen occasionally. I night say a great deal more on the subject, but I fear to intrude on your valuable rpace.—Yours, 28th July. 1852.
A BANDSMAN.

" ANGLO-SCOTUS :" A HUMOROUS REJOINDER. am afraid my Newten friends and myself are un- consciously and unintentionally drifting into cross-purposes. One of your latest correspondents says, "We felt a little disappointed with " Anglo-Scotus " for saying that he dis- liked the study of entomology." All I paid was, that since a certain cccurrence entomology suggested to me unpleasant reflections. If my friend will take the trouble to look at a good encyclopmeia, he will find it related of the Cimex lectularius that when crushed it exudes a disagreeable odour. I dare say he is an ardent disciple of Eamelus, dtc., but I venture to affirm that if ever he should, by accident, get a fat specimen of the wineless insect with the oval body be- tween his teeth, entomology will certainly suggest, even to him, unpleasant reflections. It will possibly then he of little interest or curiosity to him to know whether London or Ella.sgow deserves the credit of introducing into Great Britain the insect Norfolk Howard was called after, before he re-christened himself; whether the insects Lady Murray's "infallible mixture" failed to exterminate, reached Glas- gow about 1727 by means of Dutch wood, or came to London after the great fire, in the American timber then imported. I should like to discuss the subject of entomology with my friend over some mild tobacco, and a nice brew of the liquid the women went to War about in the United States in 1874, from the apotheosis of ants into men in the , time of lEacus, to the change of colour of bees from white to black and brown at the fall of man. Juet fancy a Scotch- man having an aversion to the study of entomology! lam afraid the real character of the ant was not fully known in ' Solomon's days' or he would have been chary of sending people—especially careless persons--to study its ways. As Sir John Lubbock has shown, the ant is a careful insect, but it is also an unscrupulous, selfish, and cruel one. I hope my friend, if he is a married man, a native of Lan- cashire, and a honey grower, did not neglect to give the bees notice of his marriage when it took place, by tying a piece of red cloth to the hives, as is the custom of the county. I wonder also if he has heard the story of the hunter, the bear, the wild cateand the bee's nest. The latter was situate 4 in the hollow of a tree ; the bear was sitting en the ground in front of it, cogitating a plan whereby it might get at the honey; the hunter made his appearance on the scene, fired at the bear, hut missing his mark, had t. take refuge in the tree, before he could essay a second shot. Presently he heard a growl overhead, and looking up, he saw a large wild cat waving its tail preparatory to a spring. He fired on the cat, and the wounded animal in its fail . dragged the unlucky hunter down with it, on to the top of the bear, which, to a certain extent, broke their fall. By good fortune the claws of the cat fixed in a sensitive part of the bea4 and made him furious; and while the four- legged combatants were locked in a savage embrace, the astonished hunter beat a hasty retreat. Next morning curiosity prompted him to visit the spot, where, although the ground bore the signs of a sanguinary struggle, there remained nothing very distinct but the ears of the bear and the tail of the cat. "That is something like the store- of the Kilkenny cats," I fancy I hear some one remark. ,lust so, my dear friends. There are two sides to every question; and every form of a word or version of a story has its own application. "Yes, we admit all that," I fancy I hear others say. "We also know the bear is fond of honey; but what the deuce has the cat to do with bees? Surely the feline representatrve is a false factor in this sum ?" I will defer an explanation of the relation the cat bears to the honey-bee, with the Editor's permission, for another letter, as also a few words on etymology,—l am, sir, &c, • ANGLO-SCOTUS.

div.head: WARRINGTON To-WN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON To-WN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. Present :—His worship the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) in the chair; Aldermen Chandley, Harrison, Kean, Holmes, Davies, Burgess ; Councillors Monks, Brown, Platt, Wright, Mackie, Caldwell, Woolfall, Broadbent, Pierpoint, Whittk Ashton, Barker, Fairclongh, Dixon, Jeans, Litton, Francotnb; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), and C. Chorley (borough treasurer).

div.head: WATCH COMMITTEE
div.p: THE WATCH COMMITTEE
The MA.YOR moved the adoption of the Watch Com- mittee's minutes.
Alderman HARRISON seconded the motion, which was carried.
THE FINANCE COMMITTEE AND THE COST OF FORMING
STREETS.

Alderman liormEs moved that the minutes of the Finance Committee be passed, and Councillor W00r..r,t1.1. seconded the motion. r, Councillor PIERPOINT, alluding to a recommendation of the committee that it be an instruction to the Town Clerk in all cases where owners of property hare neglected, after the three months allowed by law, to pay their proportion of the Gest of street construction, to take immediate proceedings against them for the recovery thereof, asked whether, if that were passed, it was to act as a hard and fast line. He ex- pressed the opinion that it would press somewhat heavily upon some of the small property owners, who would be put to a very great expense to meet requirements. Councillor MACKIE remarked that the same thing to which Councillor Pierpoint had alluded, had struck him, and he sug- gested to the committee that afternoon the words "recovery thereof," these should be added "so that a charge of 5 per cent. should be made upon the unpaid money." Before they put a man into the County Court and took out a warrant against him he thought he should have a fair time allowed him, bat if more time was allowed to him than his neighbour it was only fair that he should pay to the lorough fund the interest upon the money that the Borough kad absolately let to him. Alderman liormr.s remarked that they did that already,

Councillor PLATT ob:ervect that there WAS no intention to deal differently with the property owners than hitherto. The resolution was simply to put the committee in a legal positian with regard to the recovery of their money. Alderman HOLMES ; Perfectly. Councillor PLATT believed that it was a fact that they were obliged to take proceedings for the recovery of the money within a certain time or they could not recover it. He did not anyone could object to the committee taking that pt caution. Aldei sian HOLMES thought the cash was not so hard on the small property owners as Councillor Fierpoint had sag- Teed. All persons engaged in the erection of property knew that one of the things they would have to do was to make a street in front of it, -and, therefore, when they en- gaged in the work if they did not take its cost into consider- they ought to have done, that was all. (Hear, hear.) In the first case they had three months allowed for the con- struction of the street, and the property took something like three-quarters of a year to erect, while they had three months allowed to dispute the apportionment of the coot, so that they had 12 to 15 months credit on all accounts before ey began to pay. COM:Miller PIERPOINT remarked that it was not that time from the outlay. Was the work paid for?

Alderman liorzrEs replied that the work was paid for by the Corporation. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH added that they had 15 months from the first notice given of the construction of the street. Alderman HOLIES observed that the recommendation was made with the view of strengtkening. the hands of the Town Clerk. Councillor Mackie had suggested that they should charge interest on those acconnts that were not paid within a certain time, but they already did so. • Councillor 7.4Acrun : Are they charged, Mr. Holmes? Alderman HotmEs : Oh, certainly. We give them three months' notice to pay the money. In reply to Councillor Pierpoint, 'Alderman HoLMEs said six months was the limit of time in which proceedings could be Instituted for the recovery of the money. The minutes were then passed. HE STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. Councillor BROADBENT moved the adoption of the minutes of this committee, and Councillor PLATT seconded the motion. Alderman KEAN remarked that he had handed to Coun- cillor MU a memorial from ratepayers in School-street, wanting additional light there. He had no doubt that it would receive the attention of the committee. Ho knew a short time ago Mr. Platt revested that any member of the Council pointing out where light was required should hand in a memorial.

Councillor PLATT : We will pay a visit on the very next occasion we have a meeting. The motion was then carried. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMUITTEE. THE QUESTION OF FLAG AND TILE FOOTPATHS. Alderman lixax, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, remarked that they had had more trouble owing to frequent floods in lower parts of the town, and they had instrucred their Borough Sur- veyor to make a report, and see if they could not obviate the difficulty. They had done all they possibly could to get such a plan, so that if possible they might prevent those floods. The Council would be glad to find that the tenders for the cast-iron cylinders for the Latchford sewerage were accepted, and the Borough Surveyor hoped be could have the work completed by the end of August. They were push- ing on the work as well as they could. Councillor WOOLFALL seconded the motion that the minutes be passed. Councillor MACEIE, alluding to a recommendation that a tile footpath should be constructed in Latchford, remarked that he thought tiles must have been the invention of some shoemaker anxious to increase his own trade—(laughter)— but he had great faith in the good old-fashioned flag. (Laughter.) If flags did cost a trifle more he thought they would do wisely not to have recourse to the barbarous With respect to the resolution about frequent floods. He slggested that the matter should be allowed to stand over at the present time until they saw what was the result of the ,movement in connection with the proposed widening of the

Mersey. He noticed in connection with a recommendation that a tender for drain pipes be accepted, it did not tell whether it was for £5, £5OO, or £l,OOO. Possibly there might be some reason for it, but it was not according to the ordinary course. Alderman CHANDLET remarked it would be more congenial to his own feelings to substitute flags in place of the abom- inable tiles. He thought the adoption of tiles tended very much to deteriorate the appearance of the street. Flags, be thought, had a look of more solidity and dignity about them, and he exceedingly regretted that tiles had been used to the extent they had been. He felt conscientiously bound to coincide with the remarks of Dr. Mackie, for he abominated them. Flags, he understood, would cost little or no more than tiles did. (Several MEMBERS: Double the amount !") He regretted that a cheese-pairing economy should be shown, land with all due deference to the committee he protested !against tiles as compared with fligs for the leading streets of Warrington. Alderman BURGESS said he thought there was a resolution passPd some years ago which had determined the question of tiles or flags in newly-formed streets, and until that resolu- tion was rescinded he thought they would go on very wisely as they were doing—(hear, hear)—in allowing the use of tiles in newly-formed streets. (Hear, hear.) It had been shown by experience that the Corporation were no losers by them, and that the people who had to form the street were considerable gainers. He thought the resolution had worked admirably for the town, and he hoped it would be retained. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HARRISON asked if tiles were more durable than flags—if so he did not think there was anything more to be said ahout them.

A MEMBER said he would not like to see them in their leading streets. (Several MEMBERS: It is not attempted to lay them there.) In newly-formed streets and in by-streets it appeared to him that the reasons in favouriof tiles were overwhelming. In the first place they got them at half the cost, and they lasted twice as long. The objection taken against tiles now was quite new to him—he never knew any objection to them before. They were perfectly clean and appeared to be respectable enough. Councillor BROADBENT expressed the opinion that those who thought so highly of flags, as compared with tiles, had a perfect right to hold that opinion, but no one ought to stigmatise as cheeseparing such judicious economy as using tiles which cost one•half the price of flags, and which were also more durable. .11 Mr. Alderman Chandley lived in Latchford he would find something worse than tiles to walk upon—big " cobble " stones of the old fashioned sort. In Latchford they considered tiles quite a luxury, and without expressing a very strong opinion upon the two sorts of pave- ment, he thought the general public in Latchford would be very well satisfied when they got the tiles laid where it was proposed to lay them and when they had the "cobble " stones replaced by tiles. (Hear, hear.) Councillor DIXON expressed his astonishment at Alderman Chandley speaking in the manner he had done. Councillor PLATT ageed with Councillor Mackie that the amount of the tender for the drain pipes ought to have been stated. He had been told that the proper time to object to any amounts was when the tender was accepted and the amounts appeared in the minutes. Now, however, they had a tender accepted, and the amount was not in the minute at all.

Alderman DAVIES remarked that it was a fact not generally known to those who had nothing to do with the committee, that the wear and tear of flags was beyond the conception of anyone. The wear and tear that took place in re-laying from time to time was one of the most serious items of the committee. Their late borough surveyor and the present borough surveror had reported to them from time to time, and he thought that tiles were far more suitable. It was a fact learned from experience—(A MEMBER : "And more dignified.")—but he did not think they were exactly becoming in main streets after all. He thought they, all agreed on that, but it was quite time they bad them in Latchford. Alderman KEAN observed that after the discussion that had taken place he had hardly anything to say although at one part of the discussion his task might have been a some- what difficult one. With regard to tile footpaths he liked them very much himself. There was a diversity of opinion many years ago as to which were best, and which looked best, and that Council came to a resolution that they ought to adopt tile footpaths. They had done so ever since, and as Alderman Burgess said they must do so until that resolu- tion was rescinded. But he hoped that would not take place. (Hear, hear.) Tiles lasted as long again as flags, and the cost was one half. With reference to the sugges- tion of Dr. Mackie, on the question of flooding in the lower parts of the town, he did not think it would be wise on their part to wait until the Navigable Tideway was made. He thought they should have the opinion of the Borough Surveyor, and make the best use of it they possibly could. With regard to the tender accepted by the Committee for tiles and drain pipes for Latchford, it was simply im- possible to give them every p trticular about them as they did not know how many would be wanted, or what the final price would be. Therefore it was not in the books. If any Councillor felt himself short of information he had only to go to the minute book and they would see the exact price there. In reply to Councillor Platt, he contended that before any money was paid it would cotne before them in its proper form. Councillor MACKIE asked if they were submitted in com- petition in the usual way. Several members replied that they had been. Alderman KEAN remarked that he wished Councillor Mackie had been at their committee meeting when they were inspecting the various pipes and tiles. He was sure they had plenty of competition before they accepted any- thing.
The MAroa said he thought it was a case in which the committee had exercised a wise discretion, he had no doubt: (Hear, hear.) • The minutes were then adopted. THE MUSEUM AND LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
The minutEs of this committee were passed, on the motion of Councillor BROADBENT, seconded by Councillor CALD- WELL.
THE PRIVACY Or THE PARE: ALDERMAN HARRISON RESENTS AN "ATTACK." •

The Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee, at a meeting held on the 6th July, recommended that the tender of Messrs. H. J. Ward and Son, of Manchester, for 12 band- stands, conductor's stand, and drum stool, be accepted. On the 20th ult., the bath keeper reported that the income from the baths for the past four weeks was £25 Po. 61, and for the corresponding period of last year £36 Me. 61.
The M&YoR mWed, and Councillor WHITTLE seconded the aloption_of the minutes. _ _

Councillor MAorctE said he had no wish to reiterate the statements that he made at the Ilast Council meeting in connection with the public park, but in looking over the accounts he found that it cost the town something like £420 a year to keep up. He had no doubt its share of the money the Council expended on those buildings over and above the magnificent -donations that they had, would make it worth something like £5OO a year to them. He was not going to re-open the question about the blank wall 'in front of the Town Hall. The Council came to the unanimous conclusion that in better times, when the income tax and some other things were less, the change would be made. But he thought they might utilize the Park much more than they did at the present time. It fell to his lot as a young man to live near a paik, and he also for several years lived close to Hyde Park, and he had been in both parks at a very much earlier hour than Bank ' Park was opened. He was not at all aware of that until some time this Year. He was an early riser, and liked to take a walk, but he -found, excepting the small portion leading up to the Town Hall, all was under lock and key. Thus the place was sealed against nine-tenths of the ratepayers until seven o'clock, and when a workingman finished in the evening—and he was in the same position as the most ordinary workingman —by the time he got home, had his tea, and was prepared to go out, the shades of evening were drawing on, with the ex- ception of two or three of the best months in the year. He would therefore strongly recommend that there should be some re-arrangement of the hours of opening so that the Park should be open during the summer months at 5 o'clock or 5-30 in the morning; and that on Sundays they should not keep it closed to one o'clock, but open it from five in the morning to nine o'clock in the evening. In making the latter suggestion he had no wish to interfere with the hours of church services. But he was sure there were thousands of workingmen and others engaged in trade who never had an opportunity of going through the Park on week days, owing to the arrangements to which he had alluded, and who would be glad to have a laic° place where on Sunday mornings they could have a nice walk. He also respectfully urged the committee to do something towards thinning those very luxuriant and close-planted trees and shrubs all along Crosfield-street. It was very hard to think, after £5OO a year was spent on the Park. the townspeople could not even look at it unless they went in, and that they could not get in until the hours when they had to go to business. He hoped the committee would reconsider the matter, and that the public Park would be thrown as fully open to the ratepayers, both on week days and Sundays, as was consistent with decorum and safety to its contents. The opportunities for going in the Park were sadly incommensu- rate with the money that was paid for keeping it in its present condition. . Alderman HARRISON said Dr. Mackie had complained that it was a pity to shut the Park up from public view after an expenditure of £5OO a year, and he said it was equally a pity that that Hall shoat! be shut up from public view also. He thought in the Town Hall they possessed a building that would do honour to a town of 200,000 in- liabitante,—(hear, hear)—and it did seem a pity that it I should be shut up by a high wall. (flear, hear.) When a I private family lived there it was natural to suppose they I would like some seclusion from public view. Inasmuch as lit was now a public hall it seemed out of harmony that they i should see that ugly excresence of a wall excluding it from i public view He hoped the committee would see their way Ito take the initiative towards effecting the suggested im- provements. He was satisfied with the expen- diture of a very few hundred pounds that could be done. He hoped the committee would give the matter consideration. i nay could at once destroy its ugliness and could make it 1 attractive to the inhabitants. If they did so, by putting , down a pair of gates and making a broad walk, they could : then devote the ground, which was, strictly speaking, the recreation 'ground, and from which the public were now ; excluded, to the purpose for which it was originally intended ! —the use of the public. It would extend the advantages of ; the Park very considerably. ! Councillor Wuirnai here interrupted, and 1 Aldermon HARRISON said it was very unmannerly, and he ishould have hoped in these days of education and-progress gentlemen would wait until a speaker had finished. (Hear, hear.) He proceeded to state that he was satisfied that the

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 5, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 5, 1882.

expenditure of a very small sum of money would make the front of the Town Hall a very attractive and a very pleasant place for the inhabitants of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BROADBENT remarked that although he agreed very heartily with a great deal Dr. Mackie had said he would like to show where he differed from him. He agreed with him in thinking that the Town Hall gardens might be open to the public as long as possible on week days and most frequent ontSundays (hear, hear) when the working people were at liberty to enjoy its attractions; while he differed from him and Alderman Harrison in their desire to lay the place open by lowering the walls and cutting down shrubs. (Hear, hear.) He was afraid it would not be very lon, that they would have to complain of the luxuriant thickness of the trees and shrubs in Warrington, and he thought they had better let them grow while they would. (Hear hear.) A short time ago there was a gentleman came over from one of the rich Lancashire towns, and he said " We have been spending half a million of money upon the Town Hall, but there is nothing to compare with this. Money cannot buy the attractions of this place." The attractions consisted of its quietness and privacy, and these Dr. Mackie I and Alderman Harrison wanted to sweep away. Let the Park be open as much as possible every day in the week, but what the ratepayers wanted was the quietness of the place, and that they got in the Park shut out from the buzz and turmoil of the street. The committee should be very cautious indeed as to laying the place open, and their object should be to make the Park contribute as much as possible to the rest and recreation of the people of Warrington. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH was amused by Alderman Har- rison's speech, for if he was not mistaken he thought the alderman was one of the most bitt3r opponents to the pur- chase of the Park. His reason for that opposition was the great expense the town would be annually put to to keep the place in order, but now he wanted the Corporation to spend a great deal more money. The Park was very much better for its quietness; and he did not think if the Council laid it open the public would frequent it any more. Alderman HARRISON said an attack had been made upon him, and he felt sure the Mayor would be the last to pre- clude him from Standing up— The MAYOR: Do you consider it an attack ? Alderman HARRISON: I do consider it a very unwarrant; able attack. He has done his best to show I was quite in- consistent in the way I Councillor WHITTLE: You always are! Alderman HARRISON: I could give that Coun- cillor Whittle a flagellation if I thought fit, but I think him beneath my notice. The Alderman went on to state that he,was sorry Councillor Fairclough was not more correct in his facts. If he would look over the minute book for a certain minute that they should purchase the Town Hall, he would find his (Alderman Harrison's) name subscribed as one of the supporters, and permit him to say that he never opposed to purchase the Town Hall. He defied Councillor Fairclough or anybody else to say he did. What he opposed was the purchase of the recreation ground. When it was suggeste I that the Council should purchase the Town Hall and the land on the opposite side of the road where the printing works waa, he supported it, but when it was proposed to take the recreation ground at what he considered to be a large sum of money, he simply retired and did not vote at all. Councillor Fairclough's statement as utterly at variance with facts in stating that he was now support- ing that which one time he opposed. He did nothing of the kind. He had always considered that Hall with the five acres of land a great bargain, and had never taken excep- tion to it. He would advise Councillor Fairclough to be quite sure of his facts before he made an attack upon any- body. Alderman HOLMES said this was a very unpleasant sub- ject, and he was sorry it had been introduced; but after Councillor Fairclough had spoken in the way in which he had about Alderman Harri: on's opposition to the purchase of the Hall, he could corroborate Councillor Fairclough's statement entirely. (Hear, hear.) He remembered very well indeed they had to call a statutory meeting in reference to the purchase, in the Public Hail, during the Mayoralty of Alderman Davies, and he remembered Alderman Harrison came to the meeting and denouriced the purchase of the Town Hall in very strong language. Alderman HARRISON: Never, never in this world. _ . .
The MAYOR: This is a subject which has not the slightest connection with the minutes before us; and I desire we do not have anything farther on this subject. Speak to the minutes.

Alderman BunbEss thought tEe Council would be very glad to leave to the committee the question of lowering the wall, and if it was to be lowered the time that it should be done. He sincerely hoped if it was to be done that the approach to the Town Hall would be kept as private as it was now. (Hear, hear.) He suggested if this work was to be done it should be done at that period of the year when it could come in the estimates. It would be a larger work than some of the members led the Council to believe; and be thought the proper time to bring it forward was when the half-yearly estimates came in, so that the Council would know what they were doing. (Hear, hear.) • Councillor MoNirs agreed with Councillor Broadbent. He held an entirely different opinion to those gentlemen who advocated the separation of the shrubs, and the laying open of the Park. He did not see how they could very well im- prove it, although they might put tho band-stand in front of the Hall, and encourage music iii the Park as much as possible. He confessed be was rather surprised to hear those who at other times were economists advocate the ex- penditure of a few thousand pounds on the Park. The money would be wasted, in 'his opinion. He did not agree pith the remark that the Park was rot frequented as much as it might be. From enquiries he had made, and from what he had soen personal! he was satislie 1 the Park was much frequented by all classes, and that the Cour.cil would make a mistake if they touched it. Councillor St-TToN also agreed with Councillor Broadbent that it would do away with the privacy of the Town Hall if they pulled down the wall. Councillor PLATT was of opinion that an extension of the hours of opening the Park would be a considerable boon to the public. He did not approve of it being closed on Sun- day morning until one o'clock, and by keeping the Park closed until that hour they would not drive the people to church.

Councillor FeancLouGu: The Park is always open. It is only the gardens that are closed.. Councillor PLATT said that was the nicest part of it. The greater portion of the inhabitants went to church before nine o'clock on the Sunday morning, and had the time after that hour at their disposi I. He thought the more private they could keep the Park the more it would be enjoyed by the inhabitants when they came to visit it. Its privacy was one of its great attractions to his mind ; and the more private and secluded they could keep it so that people when inside would forget the outside world and turmoil of the streets, the more the Park would be. enjoyed and appreciated. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR nbeerved that the subject had been before the Council on several occasione, and on many occasions before the cemmittee entrusted with the arrangements of the Park and Town Hill. He must say he did not see the necessity of the Park beimg opened before six o'clock in the morning or for it being kept °pm after nine o'clock at night. The committee had often had that question before them, and after taking everything into consideration they were quite of opi lion that if they were to keep it in order and keep bad characters out it should be closed at nine o'clock. On fine summer evenines a little latitude was allowed, and it was then kept open align 9-30 and 10 o'clock. Referring to Councillor Platt' S remarks, he said the Park was closed on Sunday morning to allow those who had the manage- ment of the Park, and who had to be there when the public were admitted, to g to church or chapel once on Sunday. That was the great object. There were various opinions on the question of opening on Sunday other places besides Parks. Some said there ought to he a certain time allowed for all persons to go to a place of worship on Sunday, and he certainly thought Mr. Gredn and his assistants ought to be allowed at least half the Sunday to themselves. The Council would not-for- get that the Park itself was always open, and it was only the gardens, a cAmparative small portion, that were kept closed to one o'clock, and he thought properly so. He hoped the gentlemen who advocated the remorral of the wall , would next year be on the committee, but in the meantime he could not hold out any hope that it would be removed, as there were several things which went against it, not only the viers of the majority of the Council, but the want of , money.

Co Incillor ITACKIE : Will you give us an official intima- tion when the Park is open ? Conncillor FAIRCLOUGH: Always. The MAYOR said that although the notice board stated the Park was opened at seven o'clock in the morning, it vraq. as a matter of fact, always open at six o'clock.
The minutes were then confirmed. THE MARKETS.

The minutes of the Markptq Committee were confirmed on the proposition of AldPrMall CITANDLEY. Alderman KEAN said he had had several complaints about the closing of the gafes in Flag-lane. Councillor CALDWELL spoke of the great inconvenience caused by the gates being closed.

Alderman CITINDLEV replied that the M trkefs Committee did not wish to mike it a public thoroughfare after reason- able hours. They wished to encloee the market as much as possible, to keen it more protected in the evening.,

SANITARY COMMITTEE : THE REMOVAL OF TRE PAILS. The minutes of the Ssnitary Committee comprised, be- sides the letter from Councillor Crosfield given in our last i.,sue, a resolution that the members of the committee be requested to go to Birmingham on Monday to inspect the health works.

Atierman BURGESS, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the deputation went to Birmingham on Mon- day and made an inspection, a report of which would be given in the minutes of the Council when the report was matured.

Councillor MONKS seconded. Alderman Hormrs said he had been spoken to by one or two townsmen about the removal of pails during the day time, and it had been uvested they should be removed in the night. He htd no opinion to offer, but he thought he would bring the matter to the notice of the chairman of the committee. -- -

Councillor NfecruE asked whether it was possible for this committee, which now seemed to be in full working order, and no doubt enjoying perfect happiness and peace, to supply the Council with a line or two in the minutes stating what amount of business they had been able to transact dur- inz the previous month. He thought, as they were a very expensive committee, thy ought to give the Council some idea of the amount of business they were doing. Councillor BROADBENT thought every member of the Council knew something of the admirable services rendered

to the town by the Sanitary Committee, and something of the great difficulties they had to overcome. He was sure the Council did not *aut to pass any unfavourable criticism on these matters or anything else; still he could join with Alderman Holmes in bearing testimony to the number of complaints about the nuisance caused by the large vans con- taining pails moving about in the day time and emiting, as they all knew from personal experience, a very offensive odour. The Sanitary Committee could not be ignorant of that, and if they could devise some means by which the smell could be subdued it would be more satisfactory to the inhabitants of the town.

Alderman BURGESS, in reply, said when the report was presented it would contain accounts of visits to Birmingham and other towns where similar works were carried on. So far as Birmingham was concerned, he did not hesitate to tell the Council they were going backwards—(" Oh ")—but that would come at the proper time. He told them so at Birm- ingham on Monday, and he did not hesitate to tell the Council what he told them. They would beat Birmingham easily enough. As to the remeval of pails in the night, gentlemen who were members of the Council would easily understand the difficulty which attached to the removal of pails in the night time. At the same time the committee were quite as much alive to the disagreeableness of the removal in the day time as any member of the Council; but they found that, in perhaps five CASt.S out of six, the pail was in the yard, which was locked up when the family retired to rest, and they could not call the family up to let them into the yard to remove the pail at any unreasonable hour. It was a matter of serious difficulty to alter the time of removal. The question was asked at Birmingham on Monday if the collection was made in the night time, and there was any difficulty in the matter. The reply was that where the pails were easy of access, and in the majority of cases that was the condition of things there, they were collected in the night, and those that were locked up were collected in the day time. But the opinion was that the collection in the night time added very largely to the cost of collection. (Hear, hear.) In Warrington it would add largely to the cost of collection, and would be attended with considerable difficulty. The committee had always been gorging the Council with in- formation, but they had repudiated it. (Loud laughter.) They had tried to 'furnish the Council with information that would enlighten them, and make them knew a great deal more than they appeared to know; but the Council would not accept that kind of teaching, and told the com- mittee to be content with printing less, but if they did print to never mind having it read. If the Council had altered their mind the committee would let them know how every- thing was going on—that was if the Council would pass a resolution to the effect that they wanted the information. The minutes were agreed to. GAS COMMITTEE.
Alderman HoufEs moved, and Councillor MONKS seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Gas Committee, which contained nothing of public interest. _ _ _

Councillor DIXON asked hOw much the committee had lost by a certain firm, and Alderman DAVIHS, in reply, pointed out that as a busi- ness firm they set aside a certain sum of money to meet di!- counts and bad debts, and that sum had been sufficient to meet both of them.. (Hear, hear.) As regarded the reduc- tion in the price of gas, he was satisfied if the works had been in the hands of the Gas Committee they would not have had a reduction at all. During the past four years the committee had been sinking and saving a large sum of money with the view of eventually paying for the gas works. But beyond that they had been enabled to reduce the price of gas 3d. per thousand. It was, however, his opinion if they had reduced the price to 6d. people would have wanted 91, and if the committee had reduced it to nothing they would have wanted them to insure their houses from fire.

_ Councillor MAcnn most strongly repadiated such whole- sale statements as Alderman Davies that made, which were intended to reflect upon the Ratepayers' Association, which asked for the question to be considered. He maintained that -the gas question was a very serious question to many per- sons. He had no doubt Alderman Davies went in for wax candles, but some of them did not ; and that gas was always to be sold at a price which would be remunerative according to the price which they had purchased the gasworks and erected others, was a heresy which ought to be cut in its earliest conception.

Alderman HOLMES remarked that a great number of cus- tomers were now cooking by gas, and the hiring out of stoves was getting common, and he thought it would be (notifying to the Council and the public to know that all the persons who had taken stoves to cook by gas were very much pleased with them. The question of a reduction in the price of gas was not before the Council. He thought the Coancil were satisfied with the amount of reduction the committee were able to make, but whenever they had a favourable margin so that they could reduce the price of gas, they would do so. As to bad debts, they were published at the end of the committee's statement of accounts, but he did not think it at all desirable thy should go into particulars. The minutes were confirmed. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE: THE avo:rEn SUPPLY, AND THE POLICE BILL.

The proceedings of the General Purposes Committee con- tained a minute that the Committee, in conjunction with the Street Improvement Committee, considered the desirability, of nurchasinc,, the property in Sankey-street, in the occupa- tion of Messrs. Benson, Sharp, and Garnett, to be sold by public auction on the 10th day of July, when it was resolved that the Borough Surveyor and the Town Clerk be in- structed to attend the sale, and offer a sum not exceeding £4,000 for the property ; also a minute, that the subject of the water supply was diccussed in detail, and postponed until after the sub-committee had again had an interview with the Waterworks Company. It was resolved that the Council be recommended to petition against the Police Bill now in Parlia.meat, and that the member for the borough be reqnested to present the petition and oppose the bill. The Me-You, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the members would observe that the committee considered the desirability of purchasing the property in Sankey-street. He dared say they were all aware that the property went for more than the amount stated, and of course the Corpora- tion did not becomt the purchasers. Referring to the sub- committee which was appointed to meet the directors of the Waterworks Company, he said they had had several interviews with them. They had a,reed with the directors of the Waterworks Co. on certain terms : and there were a few details connected with the question which were left to the Borough Surveyor and the secretary of the company, Mr. Ross. The matter would corns before the Council at the next meeting. The committee thought it wise to oppose the Police Bill which was now before Parliament. (Hear, hear.) There were several things connected with the police regulations in the Bill now before Parliament that the com- mittee considered they were not fully justified in accepting, and they thought they should petition against the Bill. Alderman DAVIES seconded-

Alderman HOLMES hoped it would be made known that the Council were in earnest in their opposition. The MAYOR said they would ask the member for the borough to support the petition, and do all he could to oppose the Bill. He b.?lieved the Bill would not be brought forward again this year, but it Was well to be prepared, and they would send the petition. Councillor 11.1Actrisl remarked that the Home Secretary stated in the House of Commons the previous night he fully expected to be able to carry the Bill, and he thought the Council would do well to take immediate steps as far as they could to put a stop to it. The Bill would take the control of the police virtually out of their hands by taking the headship from them ; and rather than do that it would be well for them to repudiate the whole grant, and pay the police themselves. (Hear, hear.) He had no doubt the time would come when the county and borough police would be worked in a more systematic manner than at present; but there were many insidious paragraphs in the Bill which made it absolutely necessary that, as a Council who had the care of the police and the preservation of the peace of the borough, they should give the Bill their Most strenuous opposition. (Hear, hear.)

Alderman BURGESS observed that as to taking the control of the police into their own hands, they sold their birth- right long ago. But while he should not be unprepared to support the proposition before the Council he could not help thinking the police superannuation fund did really require inquiring into. They had now over £4,000, which had been contributed by the police of the borough within about 20 years, and very little had been paid out of the fund, whenever there had been a demand made upon it. He thongbt there had been demands made upon it which had not been very generously responded to. There had always been a disposition to under-estimate the value. of services rendered by the officer who applied. (" Oh.") They would pardon him, but he was telling them what he knew. That £4,000, a sum of money taken from the pay of the officers, might be better applied than it was, so far as the officers themrielves were concerned. He was sure a better method could be devised than the present—that the Watch Commit- tee, guided by the Chief Constable, should have the distribu- tion of the fund or any portion of it. It should be placed upon a much more equitable basis than it was now. It was only necessary for an officer retiring from the force or being dismissed to have incurred the displeasure of his chief—he was not speaking of Mr. Hunt—and he lost every chance of benefit which might aecrue to him from the fund. He might have been contributing for a dozen years, but he lost every penny of the money. Something should be done and he thought gentlemen who took upon themselves, to move the rejection of the Bill should be prepared to recom- mend a better method than obtained, for he was sure nothing could be worse. Alderman DAVIES hoped they would let the borough member know the Council were unanimous. Councillor BROADBENT understood the opposition to the Bill arose from the desire not to allow any more interference on the part of the Government than existed ht present in the management of the police force, (hear, hear) —at the same time he entirely disagreed with the heroic policy suggested of throwing up the moiety paid by Government for the maintenance of the force. Speaking from a large experience on the Watch Committee and in other ways, he had not observed any officious inter- ference on the part of the Government or which was hurtful. On the contrary, be though the part which the Govern- ment toek was beneficial to the force. At the same time he quite agreed with those who did not desire any further centralisation in the management of the police force. Councillor PLATT stated that the proposed petition had his hearty concurrence in every respect. No good reason had been shown why such a Bill should be introduced, and he thought they ought to oppose it by every possible means. He thought such a Bill would open the way for an extension of that system of centralisation which was carried out by departments of the Government, and he hoped the Council would resist by every means in their power not only this, but every other case where it was sought to be promoted,

Councillor Prznroprr said he had it on very good authority that if it was necessary to make a street ot any- thing of the sort by the property the Corporation wished to purchase, the property could be obtained at a very reasonable price. He had it from Mr. G trnett himself that he would not stand in the way of any improvement the Corporation desired to make.

The MAYOR, replying to Alderman Burgess, said whenever an officer came before the committee with the 'expectation of receiving anything from the superannuation fund the case was taken on its merits, and from his experience generally got a very liberal allowance. (Hear, hear.) They had had no very serious case lately. They had had two or three anplications,in the last four or five years, and he had no doubt the fund had been very beneficial to those who received it. If Alderman Burgess had any suggestion to Make the committee would give it consideration. The Town Clerk and himself would do all in their power to get the petition brought before the notice of the House of Com- mons by the borough member. The minutes were agreed to. _ _
On the motion of the MAYOR, it was agreed that the peti- tion, a copy of which appeared in last week's Examiner, be forwarded for presentation to the House of Commons.
STATE VISIT TO CHURCH.

The MAYOR wished to say as that would probably be the last quarterly meeting over which he would have the honour of presiding, he begged to intimate that he intended to go to church on Sunday next, in accordance with the cus- tom adopted by his predecessors. He thought it was a very good thing for the Mayor and Corporation to occasionally observe a ceremony of that kind, and go either to church or to chapel. (Hear, hear.) He was a Churchman, and, there- fore, went to church, and he would be glad if the members of the Council would accompany him to the Parish Church im Sunday morning.

div.head: TIDAL NAVIGATION SCHEME.
div.p: THE TIDAL NAVIGATION SCHEME.

As the Council were about to rise, Alderman DAVIES asked the members to remain in their seats for a short time as he had a very. important matter to bring before them. It was a matter of vital importance to the town. In the beginning of the last century anyone looking at an old picture of Manchester would see vessels with their sails set that had gone beyond Warrington even from the sea. Navigation was carried on in this river with little or no im- provement. The river was tortuous in its way, but notwith- standing these difficulties vessels sailed from the sea to Runcorn and Warrington and right up to Manchester. There were some little improvements carried out in the river, but very few. He thought there were only three weirs and three locks: but those vessels navigated the river in its then condition. In the middle of the last century, as they were aware, the Duke of Bridgewater, with the assistance of the great Brindley, constructed the Duke's Canal, which was carried from Runcorn to Manchester at one level. But he wanted to call attention to the fact that there was a navigation before that, and that was the reason why it was called the Old Quay. In 1790 there was an improved navigation which was called the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, and that was called the New Quay. It was a puzzle to many persons why the newer navigation should have been called the Old Quay. The reason was that the vessels he had spoken of sailed to a quay in Man- chester called the Old Quay. A gentleman said to him the other day, "After looking at your town I must say that I have never seen any place in England that possesses such ' natural advantages. It is a constant disgrace to your town that you have almost a sea within reech and that you have not taken advantage of it." (Hear, hear.) Of course, the Council could quite understand that he was leading up to the question of the Manchester Tidal Navigation Scheme. In the advantages of the river they likewise had diasdvant- ages, and Warrington was no doubt a low-lying town and subject to floods. When in 1854 the Council ob. tamed an Act of Parliament with a view to .battle with the low-lying parts of the town, and endeavoured to effect a good sewerage scheme, the question was strongly put before them as to how far they were going to be successful. When , the Council began the sewerage works at Bank Quay, and worked towards the town, they should have dug a deep reservoir at that point deep enough to hays received the whole of the sewage of the town, and then to have pumped it over a dyke which should have been erected at the same time. The Chairman of the Paving and Sewerage Commit- tee hod stated that it was possible if the tidal navigation scheme was not carried out, the Council would have to do almost all their work in the town over again as regarded the sewerage. They must be aware of the fact that there was not sufficient fall in the sewers. The Council had done' all they could in the matter. During the past year especially they had had storm waters ; and Councillor Francomb could tell them that the whole system of sewerage from Church- street to Bank Quay was not sufficient to take those waters, and not even the ordinary storm water, because there was not sufficient flow. "(Hear, hear.) That was a little beside the question he had introduced; but he thought they would admit that, if such a thing as a tide] navigation to Man- chester could be carried out, the Council would have ample opportunity of completing their sewerage works. With the view of showing thet the Corporation had been looking after the river, he stated that in 1880 the Council carefully watched the passage through Parliament of the Liverpool Water Bill, because they were going to carry their pipes •under the Mersey, two miles below Fiddler's Ferry. They were going to lay those pipes at the bottom of the river in such a manner as would have entirely stopped navigation; and therefore the Corporation of Warrington, in the interests of the trading community of the town and neighbourhood, very properly petitioned Parliament. The traders likewise' petitioned Parliament to require the Liverpool Cor- poration to lay the pipes 15 feet 13-low the level of high water when high water was eleven feet below Oh a Dock Sill. That was what they prayed for. It was a happy thing that the Liverpool Corporation fought them on the question, with the result that instead of having a clause whereby the pipes were required to be ftvel at the depth the Warrinton Corporation a,ltoi for, it was eventually agreed that the depth should be left entirely with the Board of Trade. That was a very happy conclusion; and the re- sult was that to-clav they wee in the happy positlon of , asking the Board of Trade to require the Liverpool Corpora- tion to lay the pipes of a sufficient depth to enable the Man- chester Tidal Navigation scheme to be carried oat. (Hear, hear.) Lord Winm...rleigh was heartily taking the matter no, amongst others ; and he was glad to tell them those who were promoting it had raised three times as much money as was required to ascertain whether it is neceseiry and practicable to carry out the work. He therefore begged to move—

That this Council views with satisfaction the promotion of an 'improved tidal navigation of the river up-to Manchester, and that support be given to the scheme, feeling assured tint any such improvements will be conducive to the lute - est, of the town and the trale of Warrtnlton, and be the be ;t me-ins of enablng the Corporation to prevent the floods to which the lower parts of the borough are subject..

(Hear. hear.) He also moved that the following memorial be presented to the Board of Trade : T the Right Honourable Joseph Chamberlain, M.P., PreF.i. dent of the Board of Trade. The respectful memorial of the Mayor. Aldermen, stud Bargesses of the Borough of Warrington sheweth—(l.) That the river Mersey, after being joined by the Irwell and other tributaries, fiwe througn the Borough of' Warrirreon, and the low-lying parts of the borough with the houses•and manuf ,ctories thereon are subject to diastrons floods. The area so affectert comnrises more than 100 acres. (2 ) That the liability to such floods is now aggravated by the vast extent of slated roofs and improved sewerage works in Manchester, Salfo,3, and other large towns in the uplands of this rainfall basin which precipitates the storm water into the r:ver. (3.) That the river eve-, in its normal c-nrlition,` and especially when so flooded, is highly charged with sewage and other off,nsive matter, and the stench given off is intolerable and provokes nausea. (4 ) For years past your memo- rialist= have been endeavouring to take steps to prevent the nuisance and damage caused by the floods, and have pre- pared several schemes and reports with the view of effecting wo-ks to remedy the eel's, but have been unable to accompli=h them. (5.) That your memorialists have heard with great satisfaction of the proposed scheme for rendering the rivers Mersey and Irwell navigable no to Manchester for vessels of large tonnage, and your memorialists believe that the construc- tion of the proposed tidal navigation will prevent die serious floods caused by the overflow of the river. (6.) That, by the Liverpool Water Act, 18'l0, your honourable Board are authorized to determine at what depth the aqueduct from the Tyrnwy to Liverpool shall cross the river Mersey, so that such aqueduct shall not interfere with the present or any proposed improvement of the navigation Your memorialists, therefore, humbly pray that your honourable Board will be pleased to rerpfre that such waterpipes. aqueduo. and any works in con- nection therewith. or otherwise, shall be effected at. such a depth, and in such a manner as will not cause any obstruction to the carrying nut of the proposed improved navigation. A.nd your memorialists further respectfully ask that they may be allowed to appear and be represented before your honourable Board in the interests of the prayer of this memorial." (Hear, hear.) Alderman KHAN seconded the motion.

Councillor MACKIE said it would have afforded hint great pleasure to have had the chance of seconding the resolut ion, from the fact that three or four years ago he had the honour of bringing over the engineer who was now eximining the plans—he referred to Mr. Fulton—and getting some infor- mation which convinced him that, at any rate, what they were now aiming at was thoroughly practical and practi- cable. He cong-atulated Alderman Davies upon the able speech he had made and upon his previous efforts at the Chamber of Commerce. His own conviction was that this was one of those momentous affairs, which, if taken at the flood, would really lead to the honour and advantage of Warrington. He hoped the Council would join in it, and take the advice of Cicero, when he exhorted men to endeavour to leave their mark behind them, and to feel that they had something to live for beyond the mere gratification of them- selves. In fact, the feeling,on the minds of the members of the Council was evident. A great amount of solidity and solemnity (if he might use the word) had sat on their brows since the worthy Alderman introduced the subject. He certainly felt from what he had read on the subject, that this was one of those things they should engage in most h Wordsworth of spending their time p spoke of as "The I upon m as an a thingsow n C os uu no ch i l a, s i handywork of craftsmen, grooms, and cooks." It was grati- fying to know that Alderman Davies had substantiated some of the facts connected with the early history of the river. In 1722 they had a noble attempt to make the river not only navigable to Liverpool—it was always that—but to Man- chester; and in connection with that the names of many of the forefathers of present townsmen were to be seen. He pointed out that in anything that was done, they should take care that Warrington reaped the benefits of its position as a town on this part of the Mersey. Their, forefathers, in 1722, secured as a condition for all time, in the then river scheme, that there should be no dues whatever charged upon any vessels going between Liverpool and Warrington, because the river was deep enough up to this point; but that charges should begin at Warrington and go on to Manchester. He sh2;gested to Alderman Davies as a member of the Central Com- mittee that that point should not be overlooked, and that they should not be treated as merchants who were at the top ' of the dirty stream known by the name of the Irwell. In

Warrington they had a riyer which eyen within the memory of the youngest was able to carry a noble vessel c tiled the Tayleur down to Liverpool, a vessel which, no doubt, would have been followed by the building of many other iron ships of as majestic a size as she was, had it not been for the un- fortunate end to which the Tayleur came. It cast a damp over the shipbuilding In Warrington, and it expired. Their river was competent for that kind of work; and what they wanted was to give a long pull, a strong pull, and a pull altogether to support the object now occupying the atten- tion of Manchester and other men. There was ne doubt that there were difficulties in the way. Those who were familiar with the Clyde., to which so many references had been made, thought that because the Clyde was deepened and made a source of eternal wealth to Glasgow, the same would follow" by making the Mersey deep to Manchester. Those who believed that most seriously consider the local differences. The one was practically connected with the canal which cut Scotland right across, between the Forth and the Clyde, and it was made before railways and various other improve- ments in road-making were attained. However, they had before them a noble scheme, worthy of the highest support of each and all, and he most heartily supported the proposi- tion Alderman Davies had made, and would hope that if money were required from them as a Town Council, that they.. would give it, for they could not more worthily spend the public money than in an endeavour to promote such an object.

Councillor MONIC9 lived the Council would support the proposition most heartily, as he thought it would consider- ably help the scheme. Whether the scheme went through or not he hoped they would not lose sight of the fact, that even at a very moderate cost it could be made prac- ticable and navigable. He believed it was the opinion of the most practical engineers that the difficulties really be-an at Warrington, and continued up to Manchester. For all practical purposes they admitted the navigation could be made to Warrington at a slight cost, and he sincerely hoped that the Council would give the scheme the most thorough support. Even in the event of its not being pushed through in the way it was anticipated, he hoped they would not let the matter drop as far as Warrington was concerned, but strive to make a port for vessels of from at least 500 to. 1,000 tons. He thought that could be done at a small cost, and if they did it it would considerably facilitate the trade of the town. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Dixoti said the difficulties commenced before they got to Warrington. He had chartered small vessels in Liverpool, and they had been detained before reaching Widnes.
Councillor LITTON From what cause? Councillor DIXON: Want of water.

Counciller LITToN : You can get to Runcorn any time. Councillor DIxoN said only during the last fortnight Ile had a vessel detained, and he knew a Widnes firin who contemplated selling their steamers because of the want of water.

Councillor LITTON hoped Alderman Davies would bear in mind the question of vessels coming up free of tonnage to Warrington. (Hear, hear.) At the present time, he under- stood, it was in contemplation to make such a charge upon those who had free access to Warrington, and if it was the case there would be opposition from those who would other- wise support the scheme. Councillor PLATT was sure the motion was one which would receive the hearty support of all. (Hear, hear.) It was a great scheme, and would do wonders for Warrington if carried out—perhaps more for Warrington than even Manchester. With regard to its geographical position War, rington was hardly second to any in the kingdom. (Hear, hear.) There was good railway accommodation to every part; and if they could have vessels of large ton- nage coming to Warrington, it would snake the town increase more rapidly in the future than it had done in the past. (Hear, hear.) The scheme would be watched by the Rivers Committee of the Corporation, and he was sure they would promote it to the utmost of their power. The Corporation no doubt would as a whole assist them in every possible way. Alderman BURGESS said it was very gratifying to hear the proposition by Alderman Davies. There were gentle- men in the Council Chamber who knew the deep interest he had taken for many years in the river as far as it referred to the interests of Warrington, with a view to an improve- ment of the navigation. It was his lot to ask the Council to appoint a new committee, namely, the Rivers Commitee, and he hoped it would be found to be A useful committee. The proposed scheme was fraught with the most important interests as far as Warrington was concerned ; and it would be a duty of the Rivers Committee to carefully watch this gigantic question, and see that the interests of the town were protected. The Council must also afford all the as- sistance they could to the promoters of the scheme, and he hoped the Council would take care whatever could be done to further the scheme should be done. (Hear, hear.) Few of them ever dreamt, however much they might have talked about it, that the Scheme proposed would ever have assumed the shape it had, and which was likely to be carried to a successful issue. Most of them would have been content with a less thing. A straightening of the river from Howley to Wilderspool would have been considered a great thing, and it was pro- bably as much as they had hoped for. He hoped the Council would unanimously support the proposition. Alderman HARRISON observed that every expression in favour of the scheme added weight to the influence which would be brought to bear upon it. This was a new scheme, for it had been talked about extensively for the last ten years. Difficulties were at first seen which seemed to have been swept away. Dame Nature did not seem to place diffi- culties in the way of the carrying out of the scheme; vested interests seemed to be the great difficulty. Did they not remember what was achieved by the great man who desjgned the Suez Canal? It was deemed to be impossible. Nothing was more ridiculed than that. Even the son of Robert Stephenson, the great engineer, said it was impossible. Lord Palmerston said it was impractic- able, and nonsense, and the work of a visionary; and every discouragement that could be thrown upon a great scheme was thrown upon that. But notwithstanding that the Suez Canal had turned out a great success both financially and in every other way. He ,was of opinion that the-tidal naviga- ion scheme, if carried out, would be of great advantage to all the towns of Lanca- shire. There was no doubt the centre of gravity of Enzland, as it were, was marching in this direction. They had far more important towns in the North than in the South. All the towns between here and London were practically of little importance—simply agricultural towns. In Lanca- shire there was Bury, Rochdale, Manchester, Liverpool, Old- ham, not excepting even their own town. Any one of them was sufficiently large to be the capital of some of the conti- nental countries. There was no doubt if the scheme could be carried mat it would be productive of untold advantages to the towna of Lancashire. He did not anticipate that any member would raise the least objection to the scheme. No doubt the vested interests would oppose it, such as the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company, and the Bridge- water Navigation Company, and Liverpool. Still vested interests, he should hope, would not prevail against what would be a great national good. He hoped they would live to see the scheme carried out.

The ICIA.ron said there was no doubt that Warrington was one of the principal places that would he benefited by the scheme. He was sure that if they passed a unanimous vote on the subject they would be supported by the whole of the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) He thought they were much obliged to Alderman Davies for bringing the matter so well before them. (Hear, hear.) The resolution and memorial were then unanimously agreed to, and the Council rose.

div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENGE.
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENGE.

Serious damage has been done to the crops in Hungary by heavy rains, which have fallen since Friday in the Central and Western Alps, A Berne telegram announces that the compulsory Vaccina- tion Bill and the Bill for the Protection of Inventions have been rejected by the popular vote. The Turkish commander on the Greek front,er 'reports that a Greek force has crossed the line and occupied the Ottoman village of Z Irta. No eiplanation of the movement is given„_

The Siberia Gazette states that a regular steam service has been established between Wlad uvostok, Nicolaijewsk, Japan, and China. The Chinese are building a fort on the Ressian frontier, and the Chinese Governor of Chuntchun has forbidden the sale of provisions or horses to the Russians, A new military department has been established by the Russian War Office in the newly conquered territory east of the Caspian. The territory is placed under the control of the Commander-in-Chief of the Caucassian military dis- trict. The seat of the Central Administration will be at Askabad—the limit of General Schobeleff's conquests. The quarrel between Spain and Uruguay has been arranged, and the persons who were guilty of barbarities on Spanish subjects in Monte Video are to be punished. A dispute which may lead to serious consequences has arisen on a frontier question between Brazil and the Argen- tine Republic. A Central News telegram from St. Petersburg states that after the recent extensive arrests of Nihilists M. Koskoff in- formed the Czar he was prepared to guarantee him from any attempt at assassination for three months, and advised the Emperor's immediate coronation. A council of the Imperial family is convoked for the Empress's fete day to consider the question. EAs a procession was walking through Trieste, on Thurs- day, in honour of the Arch Duke Charles Louis, who opened the Industrial Exhibition at Triest on the previous day, a petard was thrown in its midst, which woulded several persons. , ATROCIOUS MURDERS BY A PRIEST.—A pri,st named Joseph Auriol was convicted on Wednesday, at Perpignar, of the murder of two of his parishioners. Maria and Rose Fonda, who had shown him great kindness, and over whom he had acquired great influence. His obi 2ct was to procure funds for eloping with a schoolmistress of whom he was enamoured, and who, on account of her relations with him, had been removed to a parish at striae distance. He induced Maria Fonda to drink a decoction of hellebore root. She expired in a few hours, but her death was at first attributed to heart disease. A month after the other sister died, after making a will in the prisoner's favour. He had poisoned her with prussic acid. While in prisdn awaiting his trial Jae wrote a confession of both crimes, but at the trial he denied. his guilt. He was sentenced to imprisonment for life. ABYSSINIA AND EGYPT.—It is said that the King of Abvs• stubs has at present an agent in Berlin, communicating with the German Government, by whom he is said to have been favourably received, on the subject of being allowed direct access to the sea, his country having been shut in from the seaboard since the Abyssinian war. The King is willing to cede Massowah on the condition of obtaining 'in exchange the port of Zonlah, which is on the shores of Anesley Bay.

The British Government is understood to sve reggae(' .tollnigs suggestion unfavourably. but it is probabl the will that cleLeettub. will be shortly asked in the House of Cominone on ei.;„. ject, in view of the desirability of propitiating the the sinians, in case their aid should become accePtable in Egyptian campaign. A DECOYING AN ENGLISH GIRL TO TEN CONTlrigg` • TIMELY RESCUIC—A correspondent of the Press Association; writing from Paris, says:—Ou the arrival of the steame Marseilles, from Newhaven, at Dieppe on Sendai During,. ir the trig morning, an exciting incident occurred. across the Channel some of the passengers had the a picions aroused by seeing an Englieb girl, aPPerenti".. domestic fervent, in the company of a gang of disrepntaTe, looking foreigners, one of whom seemed to make her his sp€ charge. The general impression of those on board was that the girl was being decoyed from England for immoral pur- poses; and this idea being confirmed, a consultation tool! place among a number of the passengers, and it was decided to rescue the girl. A plan for carrying this intention' effect was speedily devised, and in a few minutes the ,gir At. nhi was made aware of the designs the fellows had uPomel: She at once claimed the protection of the Englieb' together with that of the other passengers, was readily AC. corded. Upon arrival at Dieppe the mat-ter wasp' aced in the hands of the police, to whom the ringleader of the gang vi 3 ,8_ given over; and he was subsequently taken before a Frenou justice of the peace, by whom he eras detained pending ie. quiries.

div.head: ARPIYAL OF CETEWAYO AT PLYMOUTH. DETAILS OF THE VOYAGE•

AMUSING INCIDENTS. , The ex-King of the Zulus arrived on ThnradaY Ce C- -1 mouth from Cape Town, after a protracted voyage. weo wayo is accompanied by his cousin UngemgewarmiLice officiates as the monarch's Prime Minister; a's° bYbein Councillors, Umkosana and Uegobozang, the former of w led a regiment at Isandula, and the latter one at Drift. The ex-King's personal suite consiste of a native 24. terpreter, a native doctor, and two native servant,d Henriquea Shepstoee has come to represent tbe Pro, Government, and this gentleman is.accompanied by au the terpreter. The party left-Cape Town in the Arab on vs. 12th of July, reaching ' Madeira in sixteen d3i,e, 'rhe voyage was occasionally stormy, especiellY tween the island and Plymouth.
