THE STRIKE IN IRE COAL TRADE,

The strike of the miners and day-wage-men em- ployed by Mes%rs. Eirens and Co., colliery proprietors, still continues, and not the least prospect presents that any immediate arrangement will be come to. The whole of the fourteen pits belonging to the firm are standing idle, and the mejority of the hands are 'still unemployed. A large number ef men have left the district, and, it is stated, that they have had no diffi ull'y in securing work elsewhere. The relief and .suppott of those who are left behind is now engaging tbe attention of the officials of the Miners' Society, who are doing their utmost to find the neces- saries of life for the teen. Subscriptions are rapidly: coming in from other districts, and with the aid of the funds of the society it is expected that they will be able to give each man on strike a certain sum per week until the dispute is settled. Mass meetings of the miin have been held at Ashton Heath and Newton Common, this week, and at both the men were very ho'peful and confident of winning the battle. No signs of any agreement are yet visible, though it is to bo hoped that some battlement will be come to before long.
MASS MEETINGS OF TliE MEN. ASHION HEATH.

A mass meeting of the men out on strike was held on Ashton Heath, on Monday afternoon. There was a large attendance, about 3,000 being present. Mr. John Cross, of St. Helens, was elected to preside, and he was supported by MreeSamuel Woods, of Park-lane. The Cuanteraer ohserved that be was glad to see there not so many men present at that meeting as.there were at their last watlierieg, (e's- Voice ; "They'n all getten work, Cross," and laughter.) It teemed that many of them had tied the country, and be was sure if all present would follow ' their example they would certainly win the battle. There was no other prospect in view for them, there was no other hope to be held out of any conciliatory measures being taken, and therefore they had nothing to do but to flee from the neighbourhood, leaving the collieries just as they were. He detailed a conversation he had had with Mr. Hall, the Government inspector, whom he (Mr. Cross) told that they were now getting below living point, and they could not live on what they were earning. Mr. Hall went down the mines of the country, and he (Mr. Cross) told him that he would see the men naked, but did he ever see or find any colliers asleep or lying idle ? Mr. Hall replied, "I never did." He thought they would all agree with him that Mr. Glover or Messrs. Evans's wished the public to understand that they had no hand at all in the strike—that it was brought about by the weakingmen's ignorance and by the presumption of their leaders. But they were working comfertably until the dispute arose, and until Mr. Glover wished to reduce their wages and undersold all other firms in the market. What they wanted was the colliery proprietors to advance the price of coal 21. per ton, give the miners Is. and keep is. for the shareholders of the company. (Hear hear, and "That's right.") He thought that would be one of the best things. But one of the largest firms in Lancashire was attempting to reduce their wages below anything ever in existence in this country. There had been nothing like it in the annals of the coal trade. They were fighting that fight on behalf of the whole of Lancashire. He know some of them were very sanguine about their support and were not uneasy, but only three weeks had gone yet. They had over £l2O diet day and had something like £45 in St. Helene, and he had no doubt if they could prolong the strike for about two months more—(laughter)—every man who was playing and was idle would be getting not less ! than 12s. or 138. per week, besides is. per week a bead for his children. They were increasing in funds everyday, and if all the miners in L incashire would contribute is. each per week Mr. Glover's pits would crumble into ruin, and Mr. ' Evans could go into Wales to his residence at Llandudno, and mourning over the waves of the Ocean, say "My mines are ell lost." (Laughter.) What would be the result (A voice: "He would be dorninoed," and laughter4They would all be working elsewhere. They had had many a severe struggle before that, but they had never conducted one more unitedly. They had never-had the day-wage-men recognis- ing colliers and the colliers recognising day-wage-men as they were doing at present. The pits could not long remain idle—they would be grinding and crumbling into dust, and lowering and tumbling before long. He hoped and trusted they would all be patient, trying to get work wherever they could. (Applause.) Mr. SAMUEL WOODS remarked that if there was anything which had a tendency to weaken the action of the men, it was by working in sections. While he was sorry to have to face so many men that day, at the same time he was exceed- ingly glad to see their united determination, and to see that one part was not going to work and the other stand out. He was glad to see the determined attitude of the men, in resist- ing the encroachment which Mr. Glover had thought fit to impose upon their rights, and he trusted n ail Mr. Glover succumbed, and until he came and told them that he was willing to withdraw the notice for a reduction and the alteration of the pay-day, that they would still maintain their present attitude. (Hear, hear.) He thought that if it was not for one thing, Mr. Glover would end the battle before they left that meeting. He did not want to submit, or lower his dignity; he did not want anyone to come and say that he was beaten by his workmen. He should be most glad if Mr. Glover would, in the face of the interests at stake, come, and like-a gentleman, say to his workmen, "Well I will withdraw the reduction, and allow you to resume work on the old terms." He did not think they wduld go to Mr. Clover and say to him that they would submit to the reduction. . He did not think it would be carrying out the intention of the whole of the men of the country, and he believed it would be a die- grace if they accepted anything which would not give satisfaction to the general mining population of the county. As it had been repeatedly stated at their meetings, they were not fighing their own battle. They were fighting on behalf of themselves in the first instance, and on behalf of the men of the county in the second instance. Ile trusted if any arrangement were come to that they would be suffi- cient to give satisfaction not only to themselves, but to all their fellow workmen throughout the length and breadth of the country. He .allioled -to Merchants and purchesersof the coal being able to dictate to the masters at what price they should be sold, contending that it was a great injustice. But the people of to-day were agitating, and raising as it were against the great capitalists—those who were con- sidered to be their superiors, on account of the despotic, and te rannical treatment to whatever they were subjected from time to time. The men in Haydock e•ere being treated as no other body of working men in Lancashire ever had, been. They were earning less wages-than any other body of men in the county, and yet, forsooth, Mr. Glover could think it to be his duty to come and say "I will reduce your wages ten per cent," and even when he said and admitted that one portion of the men could not live on what they were at present earning. But the men Were trying to teach him a lesson, and he hoped. the firmness which had been manifested by them would be continued. He advised the young men to flee away and get work elsewhere, and thus leave more assistance for those behind, the old and feeble, and those who had families. He hoped Mr. Glover would have the huraanity to censider the feelings of the men, their wives, and -their children. He (the speaker) did not want him to lose his dignity, and he did not think he would he humbled if he withdrew the notice and allowed 1 them to return to work on their old conditions. It would ' relieve the distress and show a great amount of sympathy

• with the workingmen, their wives, and children. He believed he would have to do it. The deputation would be glad to go and try to put an end to the fearful struggle, but until Mr. Glover sent for them he could not for the life of him see any termination of it. He thought it would be a pro- longed struggle unless Mr. Glover withdrew the notice, and he ivisLed to appeal to Mr. Glover, through the Press, that for the sake of the men and their families he would allow them to resume work on the old terms. He did not suppose that there was any mere weakness on the part of the men than there was at the last meeting. There was the same determination and strong feeling with respect to sticcumb- ing as when the strike commenced,and they were now at the end of the fourth week. The probability was that if Mr. Glover did not consent to withdraw the notice or make some arrangement, that would be one of this longest strikes that had ever been encountered in. this r,irt of Lancishire, Ho trusted they would all act honourably, as they had done up to the present; and he was glad to say that not in a single instance had any outrage been committed, though the strike had lasted four weeks. (A voice: "I hope there will not be.") He thought it was. the first strike on record where
the men had been out on strike for four weeks and ho depre- dations committed. There had been no case brought before the notice of tlie.police, and he trusted it would remain so.

W hatever they did let them respect the laws of their country, and not dis!zraee themselves by any outrage. Let them fight, as 1111:-. Glover asked them to Ott ut the outset, in an !, i honourableway, and" to theu they would not have anythir„-, regret he he enpnai united, flonuocownincl;i. coli:cgt,he dfiv he aelle( iiem to remain iC given to them, and then there was a prebabi! ity of them winning the battle. (Applause.) The meetilfig then concluded: MEETING AT NEWTON HEATH.

Mr. S. Woods presided over a meeting of colliers, at which it was estimated 2,000 were present, held on Newton Heath, on Wednesday morning. The CHAIRMAN, in addressing the meeting, remarked that miners were looked upan as devoid of knowledge, but he maintained that they were men who thought. Yet he was sorry to say they had not hitherto used their knowledge to the best advantage. He was impressed with the idea that a considerable number of those present who were not members of the society were men of knowledge, and yet they had not had the wisdom to become members of their own society. He was sorry to say that, and he hoped in future they would be able to use .their knowledge better, aiad that when the dis- pute terminated every man who was not at present a mem- ber of the society would join. (Hear, hear.) He proceeded to speak of the importance of self-reverence. Men, he stated, said miners did not respect themselves, and he was convinced that as so, because if they had respected themselves they would most certainly have been members of the society. alluding to the value of self-help, he remarked that he was eenvinced if the miners bad been helping themselves they , would have joined the society, and that day they would have been in a far better position than tipey were. If they had been members of the society there would have been no difficulty. As it was they had to send representatives from Haydoci; and St. Helens all over the country in order to obtain subscriptions to support those on strike. Miners ought to have the strongest trades' union in the country,and they would have if they were thoroughly organised. Both Mr. Cross and himself had gone through the district during the last eighteen menthe and had implored them as sensible men to consider their own interests. He had almost begged and prayed that they would become members of the society, bat they had not done so, and the dispute had arisen. Whatever might be the result of it let them in future, as they vatlued their own lives, and as they valued their families, become members of the society. He believed if they did so they would be helping themselves, and putting themselves in a position to be one of the strongest powers in the lini ed Kingdom. Mr. J. Cnoss rose to give a few words upon their position. He observed that he was glad to see the numbers were less every time they met. They kept going to obtain work some- where else. That morning 50 men left St. Helens for York- shire. After explaining a misunderstanding between the Havdock and Havannah men as to the payment of those on strike, he said they had passed another week of what was called passive resistance. They had passed another week of suffering and starvation, brought on not by themselves but by one of the greatest tyrants that ever lived in this country. (Hear, Hear.) Be did not remember during the last 50 years a greater imposition being attempted upon the workingmen of this country ; and he was happy to see that they were united in resisting this encroachment upon their homes. He was happy to say the masters were mourning and weeping over the destruction, that was increasing every day, of their plant. They had men wandering through the country trying to get coals. He thought the men had taught the masters such a lesson as they never had before ; and he hoped it would teach them that they had not the power in their hands to trample their workpeopla under their feet by reducing their wages without the men having a voice in the matter. The whole of the men in Lancashire were supporting the minces. There was one district where the men were only working three days a week, and yet they were paving the levy manfully to sup- port them in their resistance to a reduction. If the masters ' heat them they knew the tyrannical power they would have oyer them,

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. SATURDA.Y.-13ore Mr. Holbrook Gaskell. jun. Ellen Carey was fined 53 and casts for drunkenness. Owen Jones. for being drunk and disorderly on licensed pre- Raises, viz , the Queen's Arms, Moss Bank, Widnes, on the provioug day, was mulcted in lOs and costs; in default.l4 days' lanprisontnent with hard labour. MoN e ei,asrs F. H. Gassage (chairman) and Holbrook Gaskell, jun. Michael Glynn, charged with being drunk and disordely on the previous Saturday, was fined Is. and costs, with the usual alternativ. ; Sarah Cane was also fined 5s and costs for a slm'lar offence, the case being proved by P S Etrickland.— Mizabeth Bushell was brought up in custody on a charge of being drunk and disorderly in Irwell-street, and the Bench im- posed a penalty Of 105 and costs; in default, 14 days' imprison- want. Charlotte Doyle was charged with begging at Widnes on the previous day, and the Bench committed her to prison for seven da with hard labeur, 'Esther Dunn and Catherine Maloney was charged with steal- ing. on the previous Friday. a boiler door and frame, the pro- perty of Robert al'lntyre, Grrenfel-street. Inspector Barnet withdrew the charge against Nit:annoy, who was then put into the witness box. Lunn was sent to gaol for one month. W RDNEsnare —Before Edward Gibbons, and W. D. Holt, Esqq. AN CNJUST BALANCE —Edward Johstone, grocer and pro- vision merchant, at Sims Cross, ,Widnes, Pla charged with having in his possession a pair of scales, which were half an ounce against the purchaser.—Superintwdent Barker deposed to examining tha scales and finding them defective as stated in the charge.—Defendant denied all knowledge of the defect till Informed of it by the superintendent of police.—He was fined £1 and costs. I 15 OIST COVPLE.—George Taylor and John Rigby were sum- moned for fighting and meking a great noise and disturbaree on the 26th of last month. They both pleaded guilty.—P.C. 1,002 stated the facts of the ease.—They were both bound over to keep the peace fo • three month:, in default of sureties to be Imprisoned for one month. BREACH or PEACE BY WOMEN —Bridget Keenaghan and Margaret Connor were charged with committing a breach of Use peace, by making a noise and quarrelling with one apother. —P. 0. 1,009 said he was on duty in Pleasant-place, on the Ist of last month, when he found the defendants engaged in a mutual squabble. He ordered them to move on but they re- fused, and as they had attracted a large crowd, and were making a, considerable disturbance, he ascertained their names and addresses, and summons& them.—They wero bound over to keep the peace for three months. RE-APPEARANCE OF a. NLOOD."—michael Flood, an Irish labourer, residing in Widnes, was charged with esmtnitting a breach of the peace. He pleaded guilty.—P.O. 872 stated the facts of the MO, from which it appeared that the defendant had conducted himself he a manner far fram conducive to the peace of Her Majesty's subjects. Michael, who was then making his "third appearance for the season," was bound over to keep the peace DRIVING A 'MOWING IfacuriE ON THE FOOTPATII.—George Ramsay, a farm labourer, was charged with driving a mowing machine with two horses attached on the footpath of a public highway in Ditten. He pleaded guilty.—P.S. Coutts deposed that, when spoken to, the defendant said he did not know he was doing any ',arm. The road was perfectly good, and indeed, the ether side would have been better for the machine as it was grass grown_—A fine of 28. 6d. and costs was imposed. A DRUNK AND INCAPABLE CARTER.—Frederick Sankey. a carter, was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and lurry —He pleaded guilty.—P.O. 970 stated the facts -of the case. It appeared that the defendant had been in such an incapable condition that he lest all control of the animal he wastlriving. and before the constable came up had contrived to run into another vehicle, damaging the latter cocsiderably.— He was fined 7s. 6d. including costs. Scitoon ATTENDANCE CASES —The following parents were dealt with under the Education .Act for neglecting to send their children to school, 53 fines being inflicted In each case :—Peter Camay, Ellen Carnay, Thomas Molyneux, Thomas Welsh, Thomas Risley, Daniel Brown, Hugh Gallagher, John McDonald, John Keating. MORE DRUNKENNESS.—Thernas Eustace, who was repre- sented by his wife, was charge i with drunk and disorderly conduct, on the 26tIt. July.—PC. 130 proved the case.--at fine of Is. and costs was Imposed.—John Gibbon for a like offence, committed in Waterloo-road, was fined 5s and costs, —Patrick Hines who did not appear, was also fined for being drunk, on the 31st of last month —Thomas Curley, another absentee, was fined 53. and costs for misconduct. He seemed to have been of a bellicose disposition as he had attracted the attention of a police constable to him by the challenges t fight he was giving out. THURSDAY—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun.

- - A PAIR OF VAGRANTS.—Frederick Pritchard and James Hughes were charged with having been found sleeping out in Ditton-road.—P.O. Skinner said that he found both men in a tool house used by the backmakers about three o'clock that morning. They would give no account of themselves, and had only one halfpenny in their possession. He took them in charge and brought them to the Police Station.—They were Sent to gaol for seven days.

DRUNK AND DISORDFRLY.—John Piers was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Runcorn, on Tuesday.—He was ordered to pay the costs. A Cnorrres'-uNE THEFT.—AIice Deer was charged with steal- ing a shirt, a slop, and a flannel shirt, on the 21st July, from a house in Lock-street. She had been left to look after the ‘gothes, which were hanging on a clothes-line, but had instead lifted the articles stated, pawned them, and then absconded. Ebe was apprehended in Wolverhampton.—As the prosecutor did net appear, she was bound over to come ue for Judgment when called upon.

The prisoner was seen by the only lodger awake in the room, and the landlord haying been communicated wlth, a con- stable was called in, and the prisoner given into custody.—The prisoner, who dolled the charge, and said he was looking for a chamber utensil, was committed for 14 days' hard labour. ASSAULT —A young married man, named John Barnes, liv- ing at 56, Oliver-s,reet, was charged under a warrant with beating his wife Anne Barnes, en July 31st. Mr. P. Davies appeared Lir defendant. Compla'nant who is 20 years of ale, and who lila only been married to defendant four months, said tbat on Monday night when her husband came home she asked him if he wou d have his tea, and be said he would not have any more tea with her. He then struck her with his fist on the right ear, and knocked her into a fit on the floor. A fter hearing the evidence the magistrates recommended beth hus- band and wife to shake hands, and go home and be friends.

A YOUTHFUL THIEF.—A lad named William Whitfield, living at Penketh, was charged with stea 'mg Is. sd. from the pocket of a blacksmith named Frank Sampson, on Friday, ths 28th inst., Prosecutor hung his waistcoat up in the smithy at Penketh, the money then being in one of the pickets. About a quarter of an hour afterwards he went to put his waistcoat on and found on examining the pockets that the money had been extracted. The boy was in the smithy at the time the waistcoat was hung up, and he afterwards admitted having stolen the money. Prosecutor said he did not wish to press the case, and the prisoner was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod.

James Byrom 59., John Lowrey 79. 6d., Henry Hurst 55., William Perrins is., Patrick O'Dowd 55., Thomas McKeon 55., William Saggerson 79. 6d., and George Lydiatt is.. A SLEEPY CAETMAN.— Robert Low was fined is. and costs for having been asleep while in charge of a horse and cart at Ruyton, on the lath ultimo. -A VIOLENT DRUNKARD.—Thomas Fallon was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Viroolton, on the 31st Jaly,and also with isaving maliciously damaged a cape belonging to the officer, to the value of 3s —lt appeared that the prisoner had been drunk and disorderly, and when interfered with by an officer became violent and tore the lining out of his cape.— Prisoner was fined ss. and costs for having been drunk and disoraerly ; and 63 and costs for the damage, or 14 days' Impli- sonment.

A PALTRY CASE --A respectable looking lad was charged with having assaulted Mary Ann liockley, at Rainhill, on the 23rd ult.—Complainant said she was sitting at the window which was open, when the defendant came past and threw some mud at her, whi h struck the wall and dirtiec the bed-clothes. —Deendant said he had been prowled by the complainant and her sister, who commenced calling him names—Mr. Evans sad it seemed to be a very paltry case, and the Bench would dismiss it.

FRODSHAM. STATE OF THE CROPS AROUND FRODSHAM.—MT. John Challoner, Netherton, by Frodsham, writes as follows about Frodaham :—Corn Crops: Wheat, oats and barley are look- ing fairly well; but I am afraid will not be properly fed for want of more sunshine. Beans are looking well, they are full podded, but want more sun. Grass, clover, and rye grass, all cut, are good crops; but a deal damaged by the wet weather. Meadow grass on the marshes is a fair crop. Farmers are just in the midst of the hay making, though there are very bad roads to it for the want of dryer weather, and for the drainage board, and a few (say three Netherton farmers) would have been entirely impassible in several places. The board being a well selected body have taken the precaution to keep the water courses as low as possible to prevent the flooding of the said road's.—Root Crops: Early potatoes here have been the best in Cheshire, fair crops and good prices have been realised, but what is left for seed purposes is showing signs of disease. Late potatoes are looking very well, and there are every prospect of la,Ang good crops if we have dryer weather to check the disease. Mangle is doing better than for the last three years, being freer from the fly in the leaf. Turnips are doing very well. —Cattle: There are great complaints about milking cows giving a deal less milk than usual. My own are giving at least a fourth less owing to being so wet and cold and being short of the more nutritious grasses which hotter weather would bring forth. Owing to their having been six or seven such-like summers cattle does not last so long on the marshes. Several farmers are loosing two, three, and four per year through being graped, fluked, &c., all for the want of dryer and warmer weather. I had to sell four young cows last winter for £l3 the lot, and I am doubtful of two or three more going wrong this next winter, all from the same cause.—Sheep : There are very few kept round here owing, I believe, to so many wet seasons, and so many going Rotten and fluked.
ASHTON LOC IL BOARD.

A monthly meeting of the members of the Ashton-in- Makerfield Local Board was heti in the Board offices, Brynn-street, on Wednesday forenoon, when there were present :—Messrs. A. B. GOLBORNE. REMOVAL OF PAWNBROKER'S LICENCE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday morning, Martha Harrison, pawnbroker, Golborne, applied for the removal of the licence held by her as a pawnbroker, and Superintendent Jackson having no objection, the Bench granted the application. DRUNKENNESS.—At the Newton Petty Session, on Satur- day, John McDermot was charged with being drunk on the highway at Golborne on the 6th July, and was fined ss. and costs.—Peter Travis, a labourer, was summoned for a like offence, committed on the 15th inst., and he was fined 10s. and costs, having been previously convicted. ACCIDENT TO A GOLBORNB YOUTH.—On Thursday week, a sad accident occurred to a youth named Carlin. employed as a " sketcher " at the colliery of Messrs. Cross, Tetley, and Co., Bamfurlong. The accident occurred about half-past eleven o'clock, when Carlin, who resides at Golborne, was " conducting " some waggons loaded with coal. Whilst holding to one of these his elbow came in contact with the roof which is rather low, and before he could stop the vehicles the limb was doubled up and broken just above the wrist. He at once made his way to Golborne where he was attended by Dr. Mapei. STEALING STRAWBBRRIEa AND CUCUMBERS FROM A GARDEN.—Before J. Pearson, R. Houghton, and T. J. Gil- lespie, Esqs, at Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, James Stirrnp and John Anderson (the latter of whom did not ap- pear) were charged with stealing a quantity of strawberries and cucumbers trom a garden at Golborne, belonging to Annie Moon, on the 22nd Julv.—The evidence showed that on the date named the two men were seen in the garden. Anderson was Seen picking strawberries, and Stirrup, who was near the cucumbers was observed with a lot in his pocket. They afterwards ran away, but information was given to the police. Each of the defendants was committed to the House of Correction for one month with hard labour. COMMITTING' WILFUL DAMAGE IN A. COTTON MILL.— CHARGE AGAINST COLLIERS. —At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, John Chirton, Samuel Cottam, and Alfred Barton, three colliers, were charged with injuring a roller, the property of Mr. John Brewis, cotton matru- facturereGolborne, in the mill belonging to him, and doing damage to the extent of £3 18s.—The three defendants pleaded guilty. —Mr. Moore, solicitor, of Warrington, appeared to prosecute, and remarked that the defendants were trespassing in the mill between the hours of two and and three o'clock in the afternoon. They had no right to be there, and knew they were trespassing. In running out they knocked the roller over, after it had been placed on its end against a window. It was damaged to the extent of £3 18s. The defendants had expressed their sorrow for what had occurred, and had promised to pay the damage, although they were not able to pay it all at present.—After some conversation, the Bench said the summons would be dis- missed on the defendants paying £1 19s. in one month and the remainder in two months. 'PRACTISING FOR RUNNING": A CAUTION TO YOUNG MEN.—Two young men, named William Lawson and John Cunliffe, were charged at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, with obstructing the highway at Golborne by running races thereon, on the 24th July.—Lawson did not appear, and Ctualiffe pleaded not guilty as far as racing was concerned.—P.C. Smith said that about a quarter to nine on the evening of the day stated the two defendants were run- ning a race on the highway, in Cooper's-lane, Golborne. There was a crowd of 60 or 70 persons around the defend- ants, who were stripped, and had nothing on but drawers. Several persons on either side of the road could not get clown the lane without some difficulty.—Canliffe: Was I in drawers? P.C. Smith: You were.—How far were you off me? Fifty yards away. We were watching you for 20 minutes before you started running.—Cunliffe : I was prac- tising for running.—Corroborative evidence wan givPn by another constable.—P.C. Smith added: They were running for a wager of sc.—Cunliffe: We were practising for run- ning in sports and we were both running in sports' costume, and were not naked.—The Chairman: We cannot allow this sort of thing on a public footpath. There is no harm in practising for sports, but you ought to get permission to practise in some field. You cannot obstruct people. Cun- liffe, you will be fined 2s. 6d. including costs; but as Law- son does not appear he will be fined ss. including costs. HALTON. ODDFELLOWS' ANNIVERSARY.—The anniversary of the Halton Rising Sni Lodge of Oddfellows took place on Mon- day. As a befitting commemoration of the event, the members, numbering about 135, assembled in Halton at ten o'clock, where they farmed in procession, and, preceded by the village brass band, marched into Runcorn. The mem- bers as they walked through the town, in the full regalia of the Order and headed by the charter of the lodge, presented a capital spectacle and attracted much favourable attention and comment. After staying a short time at the Anchor Inn, processional order was re-established, and a return made to Halton. Dinner of a sumptuous nature was furnished at the Castle Hotel, and an enjoyable evening was spent, the "light fantastic " being engaged in shortly after dinner. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES OF WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. —The anniversary services of this school took place on Sunday, the Rev. C. Wright, of Manchester, preaching the sermons. There are, we are informed, some 207 scholars connected with the school, for which there are 25 officers and teachers. The average attendance is, merning 79, after- noon 147. Vestries were erected a short time ago, on which there is due £32, and the school funds are short about £l5. A debt of this nature considerably hampers the man- agement, and in order to have it,Cleared off as speedly as possible a strong appeal was made on Sunday. The services were weil attended on both occasions, the evening service being crowded. At both Mr. Wright represented the neces- sity for liberality on the part of the congregation, and the announcement made at the evening service that over £32 had been collected was very gratifying. Mr. Robert Shaw addressed the children in the evening. WIGAN. THEATRICAL MANAGERS AND COPYRIGHT PIECES —On Wednesday, at the Wigan County Court, Mr. George Wood, trading as J. B. Cramer and Co., Regent-street, London, sued Mr. Barry Stuart. manager of the Theatre Royal, Wigan, for £l6, penalties incurred through performing Offenbach's opera" La Fille du Tambour Major " for one week, in Wigan Theatre, without the written permission of the plaintiff, the assignee of the words and music of the opera. The opera was performed for six nights by Mr. R. W. South's company, and plaintiff claimed £2 10s. damages for each night. For the plaintiff it was contended that the defendant had permitted the opera to be performed and had "provided a band and full working staff requisite for the thorough and complete representation of the opera on the stage ;" that he bad no written. permission to do this. and was therefore liable for damages. It was con- tended for the defendant that no proof had been given that South had not the plaintiff's permission to perform the piece, and, secondly, that the defendant was not responsible. The defendant provided the theatre, band, gas, scenery, printing, advertising, and servants, but he did not represent or cause to be represented this opera. His act was simply that of a landlord who let his theatre and servants at a rent, or an equivalent to a rent—a proportion of the receipts.— His Honour (Mr. W. W. Ffoulkes) held that defendant was not liable, there being no evidenceof joint action and control or anythiug in the nature of a partnership. WIN WICK. TRR,PASSING IN PURSUIT OF GAME AT WINWICK.— Matthew England and Samuel Mains, the latter of whom did not appear, were summoned at the Newton 'Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before J. Pearson, It. Houghton, and T. J. Gillespie, Esqs., with trespassing in pursuit of game on lend at Winwick, belonging to Mr. Stone.—The defendant England pleaded guilty. Henry Smith, keeper for Mr. Stone, deposed that he was coming out of his house between 18 and 9 o'clock on the night of the sth July, when he heard the report of a gun. He went into the road and saw the two defendants, who carried a gun, coming up the road. He then secreted himself behind a fence and the men passed by and turned down a private road known as the "Ladies' Walk." England went first and Mains followed. They afterwards got on to the public road again, but turned into the fields and went towards some rabbit burrows to see if they could get another shot. Witness followed them on to the field and met them as they were returning. England carried the gun and witness got hold of it and found that both barrels were loaded. He asked England if he had got a licence, and he replied that he bad and produced it.—The Chairman: Was the licence in his name? Witness: Yes, sir. Mr. Stone (who was present in court) observed that he did not wish to press the case unduly. He simply brought it as a warning in the case of England, who bad a wife and two children. In the case of the other man, who was an old offender, he must press the case.—The Chairman (to England) : Mr. Stone has spoken in your favour asking us not to press the case. 'We will be lenient with von this time, but be more careful in future. You will be fined 2s. 61. and costs.—The witness Smith was then sworn and gave similar evidence against Mains, adding that the latter had a dog with him.--saains was fined 12s. and costs.

div.head: SHOCKING FATALITY AT EUNCIIRN.
div.p: SHOCKING FATALITY AT EUNCIIRN.

On Saturday, the annual excursi.n of the Runcorn employs of the Bridgewater Navigation Company took place to Liverpool on the steamer "Queen of the Mersey." The steamer arrived at the 0!d Quay Pier on its return journey about 10-30 p.m., and after the passengers had landed an accident of a shocking character, anti one which termi- nated fatally, occurred to the engineer of the steamer, Joseph Ashley Yates, aged 44, of Greek-street, Runcorn. The un- fortunate man had been standing on the paddlcbox, and was stepping on to the planks by which the passengers had left the boat when one of them turned a little, and Yates fell between the steamer and the wall of the pier into the water, his head in the L.ll striking the sponson beam of the steamer. He was immediately picked out of the water by a young man, named Isaac Lowe, the stoker of the steamer, but was apparently lifeless. S. Robinson was at once sent for, and he, on examining him, gave it as his opinion that death had been caused ;from injuries sustained in the face and not by drowning. The deceased was the son of Mr. Yates, formerly a deacon of Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Runcorn. He was very much respected, and leaves a wife and several children.

div.head: 'NEWEST.
div.p: THE 'NEWEST.

The deputy coroner (Mr. J. E. Worsley) held the inquest on the body on Monday, at the Devonshire Hotel, Ashridge- street. Mr. Wm. D. JoWife, of the firm of Ashton and Jolliffe, appeared on behalf of On deceased's relatives; and Mr. Mea:iloweroft represented the Bridgewater Navigation Company. The first witness called was Thomas Ellis, who said he lived in Brackley-street, and was employed as a letter carrier by the Blidg;,water Diaviga- tion Company. The decased was his brother-in-law, and was 44 years of age. He was employed by the Bridgewater Navigation Company as engineer on board the Queen vf the Mersey.

Wm. Dobson, a boatbaiider, living in Irwer.-lane, said that be stood on the pier known as the Old Quay on Saturday night, the 29th instant, having arrived by the Queen of the Mersey. He saw the deceased on the paddle laL,x sitting on the lampstand whilst the passengers were being landed. He saw him get up and start over the gangway to come on shore, when he fell upon the gangway on his stomach, turned over, and fell head foremost down towards the water between the steamer and the pier. He could not see whether deceased struck against anything as he fell. He saw the body recovered from the water by Isaac Lowe, a few seconds after it was immersed, apparently lifeless.—Mr. Jolliffe : What sort of a plank was it that was placed for the pas- sengers to step upon? Witness : There were two loose planks.—Mr. Jolliffe : How was it he managed to slip? Did the plank give way ? Witness: I cannot say how he slipped ; it is a mystery to me.—Mr. Meadowcroft : Do you know whether he had any occasion to come on shore? Witness : I don't.

Isaac Lowe stated that he lived in Poole-lane, and was a stoker on the Queen of the Mersey. He was present when deceased met with the accident. He saw de- ceased coming off the steamer. He bad made one step on one of the planks, when it turned a little and deceased fell down between the steamer and the wall. Witness sub- sequently found blood upon the sponson beam of the vessel. He got down between the steamer and the wall, and got deceased's body out of the water immediately. Blood was flowing from the back of his bead, and he was dead. He did not think deceased had had any drink whatever —By Mr. Jolliffe : The to of the paddle box was round, and the planks did not lie quite level upon it.—By the Coroner: The Passengers came across the planks and were handed on shore by four gentlemen. The steamer would be about three feet from the wall.—By Mr. Meadowcroft : It was dark at the time the passengers were Aping landed.—By Mr. Jolliffe : There was a lamp about 20 feet away from the steamer, and they could see everything very clearly. The Coroner, in addressing the jury, obsen ed that if they were satisfied deceased met his death by injuries which he received when he fell off the planks they would have to return a verdict of accidental death; but if on the other hand they thought his death was not accidental, but was directly attributable to negligence on the part of his em- ployers, they would have to return a verdict to that affect. The jury returned a verdict of "accidental death," and recommended that abetter way of landing passengers he provided by the. Bridgewater Navigation Company. The conduct of the witness Lowe was highly commended.

div.head: INSPECTION OF THE NINTH LANCASHIRE (WARRINGTON) RIFLE
div.p: INSPECTION OF THE NINTH LAN- CASHIRE (WARRINGTON) RIFLE
VOLUNTEERS. -

In splendid weather, and in the presence of a large num- ber of spectators, the annual inspection of the 9th Lanca- shire Rifle Volunteers took place on Saturday afternoon, in a field near St. James's church, Wilderspool-road, Latchford. The attendance of the public would have been much larger but for a change being made at the last moment in the in- spection ground. It was intended to hold the inspection in the field off Longford-street, but the bad condition of the ground rendered the selection of another site necessary, and the field at Latchford was chosen. It proved an admirable place for the inspection as the ground was very even, and allowing the on-lookers a splendid view of the whole manoituvres. On the ground devoted to the spectators were drawn up several carriages, in one of which were the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) and the Mayureas, and Mr. and Mrs. Pickmere, and a number of gentlemen, to whom the evolu- tions were a source of admiration, the steadiness and smart- ness of the corps having been wonderfully improved by the week's training. At three o'clock the "fall in" was sounded, and the members commenced to assemble in the field to the west of the Post-office, where nearly an hour was taken up, some of the men being unable to get away from their work in time to be present at the hour fixed for assembling. The Newton Company was early on the field, and at a quarter past four o'clock 544 men were present out of an enrolled strength of 578. The number showed a decrease on last year, when there were present at the inspection 582 men out of an enrolled strength of 611; and it may be stated that this is the first time for the past eight years that the attendance at the inspection has been below what it was in the previous year. Thus in 1875 there were present 425 men, in WI 441, 1877 482, 1878 502, 1879 574, 1880 581, IgBl 682, and on Saturday 544. However, as an illustra- tion that the men have been more attentive to their duties this year, it must be stated that nearly every absentee obtained leave of absence, whereas last year the greater number were absent without leave. The officers present on parade were Col. Greenall in command, Col. Bertram, adjutant, Captains Lister, Bolton, Litton, Bridge, Ridgway, Hepherd, and Widdows ; Lieutenants Thomson, Gooch, and Buckton ; Surgeon Gornall, assistant surgeon Watkins, acting chaplain the Rev. A. Siddall, and Sergeant Major O'Brien. The men were divided into eight companies of 25 files each, and after being inspected by the company officers, and proved ready for battalion drill, were marched to the field at Wilderspool, where line was formed facing the saluting base. The inspecting officer was Col. Bell, commanding the South Lancashire Begimental District, and he was received punctually at the appointed hour—five o'clock—with a general salute, the band playing the National Anthem. After inspecting the use, column was formed to the right, and the march p ist took place, com- pany after company passing the flag in a remarkably regular manner. It is doubtful whether the marching was ever better than that which was shown on Saturday, when the men appeared to step well at a smart swinging pace. Quarter column was formed after passing the saluting point, and the regiment returned in that formation. Changing I ranks again they went past for the third time at the double, and on this occasion the fall of three, owing to the slipperiness of the ground and the length of grass, caused some amusement amongst the spectators. Column was then wheeled to left and advanced in double time. and, wheeling to the left again, line was formed to the left on the rear Com- pany on the ground from which they started previous to the march past. The senior captain (Captain Lister) was then called to the front to put the men through the manual and firing exercises, which were creditably gone through, the men being very steady and attentive. Quarter column was formed by the right on the No 1 Company, and the inspect- ing officer desired Colonel Greenall to put the battalion through a few movements. Line was re-formed on No. 2 Company, covered by No. 1 in skirmishing order. The battalion then left retired in eschelon from the left, re-fofmed left, changed front to the left, and the skirmishers were recalled. Captain Bolton then took command, formed com- pany, changed front, and re-formed line, deploying one company to the left and the remainder to the right. The front of the line was then changed to the left of the right company. Captain Litton was then ordered :0 dri'l the battalion, and after the men had been pat through a few movements column was re-formed.

Col:mel BELL here addressed the men, and expressed his satisfaction at the manner in which they. had assembled, the number being exceedingly large, and at the careful and steady way that they appeared to have gone through all that they had been asked to do. It would give him much pleasure to report favourably upon the battalion; and though that was going to be the case he'proceeded to point out— though not in a fault-finding spirit—that there were a few points to which they would do well to give their attention. Firstly, they ought to try to do without AO much talking. It was necessary there 4hould be silence if the drill was to be carried on carefully and well. Secondly, they should try to acquire the habit of looking straight in front of them when they were marching. He noticed a few men looking down when marching past, and that was a fatal defect. If only a few men practised that habit it would be sufficient to mar the effect and spoil anything like good marching. However, it would be his dut.) to report favourably, and he hoped on future occasions to see amendment in the matters he had mentioned.

Colonel GREENALL afterwards congratulated the men upon the favourable remarks made by the inspecting officer. He poin:ed out that the very points in which Colonel Bell had said there was room for improvement had been referred to by himself during the week, and it was to be hoped they 'you'd now endeavour to rectify these matters. He would not detain them long, Cut he would like to draw their atten- tion to the necessity of sticking by the colours. They should try te hold on as long as it was possible. He knew, however, that business and domestic engagements very often pre- vented, men from standing by as long as they could wish, but he thought that when a man had once put his shoulder to the wheel he ought to endeavour to stick to it as long as possible. He wailed to make those remarks from the fact that it was over twenty years since the regiment bad been inspected on that field before. Then they consisted of only one company, and when their inspection took place they had the corps from other districts and the strrounding gentry present, and!they were congratulated upon what they did then, and particularly upon their skirmishing drill, which was thought to be very good. But out of that company only three members were present that day. He himself was one; Captain Litton, who at the time he referred to was a sergeant, was the second; and Colour- Sergeant Hutchinson, who was then with his men, was the third. Those three had found it convenient to hold by the colours for over 20 years—nearly 23—and be thought he could point to those cases as examples that might be copied in that particular by every member of the corps. He urged that they would lay the matter to heart, and endeavour to uphold the corps by their constancy and attention. In con- clusion, the Colonel requested the men to proceed to head- quarters, and let it be seen as they went up Bridge-street that they could bold their heads up.

Headed by the band, under Sergeant Ne"ens, the regiment then marched up Bridge-street and along San.ey-street to the bead-quarters, Where, after lodging their arms, the men sat down in the Drill Hall to the usual substantial dinner, and the officers adjourned to the Town Hall for their inspec- tion mess. On the whole the inspection was as good as any there had been for the past three years. On Monday evening the ball, with which the year's pro- ceedings are brought to a close, took place in the Drill Hall. About 150 couples attended, and until 12 o'clock enjoyed •the pleasurOs of stepping to the music of the excellent band of the corps (under the leadership of Sergeant Newns), Sergeant-Major and Mrs. O'Brien haying made ample arrangements for the comfort of the dancers.

Tit MAN WllO CAN'T PUT TIP WITIC A. VirOILAN. Thomas Ward was charged on a warrant, at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, before the ex-Mayor (Councillor Fairclough) and Alderman Webster, with having run away from the blrough , leaving his wife and three children chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—The prisoner , pleaded guilty.—Mr. Harbourne, relieving officer, who proved the case, said the prisoner went away on the Ist May and nothing was seen of him until he was apprehended by P.S. Spinks —Prisoner, on being asked if he had anything to say, stated that he "could not put up with that woman. When he gave her money she went and spent it, and what she did not spend she lost."— The Bench remarW that if the prisoner could not trust his wife, it was his duty to see the money was properly sp,nt.—Mr. Harbourne said the wife had been in several workhOuses, and she was now in Wigan; and it appeared she was going from one work. house to another.—The prisoner was sent to gaol for a month's hard labour.

div.head: misciiLLAlquors CORRESPONDENCE.
div.p: misciiLLAlquors CORRESPONDENCE.

The CLERK read a letter from the Board of Trade enclos- ing copy of the Act of Parliament, and other notices with respect to boiler explosions, and askirt that he would cir- culate them among persons interested.—lt was decided that the Clerk should send a copy to each of the persons whom he thought were interested. The CLERK rensarked that he had received a letter from the Local Government Board in answer to one sent by him on the Bth ult. As they would know from the minutes of the last meeting it was decided that ,he should reply to the letter containing an abstract from the assistant district auditor's report. He had done, explaining that the work in question was done under pressure, that it was very necessary from a sanitary point of view, and that the Board did not , expect any loss. The work was in connection with the streets at Stnloshaw Cross. He read the letter in reply which stated that the Local Board had no power to mort- gage the rates without the sanction of the Local Government Board, nor were they empowered to pay interest on advances except where mortgages were actually entered into. In cases where loans for the execution of private improvement works were required, application should be made to the Board for their sanction, and they requested that that course might be adopted for the future. He (the Clerk) had also forwarded, as instructed, the particulars of the surcharges on the Board but had not as yet received any reply. He had received a letter from the Local Government Board, dated the 21st July statimr that in the statement of accounts the amount of interest due on the Sinking Fund had not been added. He (the clerk) explained that on the date when the return was called for the interest was not due until two or three days afterwards. The members would rememb:r that at the last meeting an authority was signed for Mr. Ffarington to get the interest and deal with it. The interest had not beet received, and they could not comply with the request made at the time. He had written to the Local Government Board to that effect. He stated that at the last meeting he was instructed to fill up a return to the House of Commons relating to the gas works. He had done so and had for- warded it.

div.head: HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.

A meeting of the Highway and Sanitary Committee was held on the 26th ult., at which the Surveyor laid before,the meeting a plan of so much of the main street of Ashton as included the lengths of roadway belonging to the County in connection with the Town Bridge and Jack Bridge (176 yds. in length), and showing the suggested improvements of• widening, &c. It was resolved thai a copy of the plan be forwarded to the County Surveyor, and that he be requested to inspect the suggested works.—The Nuisances at "Ten Houses": It was reported to the meeting that the work required to remove the nuisance had been completed.-4nalysis of Milk: The Aesistant-Clerk reported that he had along with Mr. Cham- bers on the previous Thursday taken three samples of milk; and had tot warded these to Dr. Campbell Brown for analysis. —Medical..officer's Report: The Medical Officer reported that during the month there had been 10 deaths; of these 2 were from consumption, 2 from premature birth, 1 measles (pneumonic complication), and the remainder from other causes not requiring classification. The births during the same time had been 36. Dr. W. Latham called the attention of the meeting to the existene of scarlet fever at Steam Engine cottages, Stubshaw-cross. and Unsworths' cottages, and the Inspector was instructed to visit and disinfect those places.—The Sanitlry Inspector's Report :—Mr. Chambers reported the existence of nuisances j at cottages in Bolton-road and Wigan-road, and notices to i abate the same were ordered to be served on the respective owners.—Mr. SIDDALL brought before the notice of the com- mittee an objectionable iron gutter ,in Wigan-road which I was ordered to be rectified.—The question of throwing stones, I brickbats, breaking lamps, and raeleg on the highways was considered, and the Surveyor was requested to post notices and inform the police on the subject. Alluding to the minute that three samples of milk had been forwarded for analysis, the CLERK remarked that when the committee meeting was held an answer had not been re- ceived. Since then, however, Dr. Brown had forwarded his analysis, from which it appeared that one sample was genuine milk, a second was exceedingly rich milk, contain- ing twice the ordinary proportion of cream, and the third which was "skimmed" milk, and which was sold as "skimmed milk," contained 0.23 per cent of fat, 9 2 of other solids, making a total of 9.43 of total solids. Nine-tenths of its cream had been removed, which was the whole that could be removed by "skimming." Mr. BIRCHALL proposed that the minutes of the Highway Committee be adopted, and Mr. LOWE seconded the motion, which was carried. THE PROPOSED NEW HOSPITAL. At a meeting of the Hospital Committee held On the 26th nit., the plans of the site for the new Hospital were laid be- fore the meeting. The quantity of land required was shown to be 3,204 squire yards, ard the price was stated as £2l per annum for this area. It was resolved that the Board be , recommended to accept the offer of Mr. Moubert, acting for Lord Gerard, of 3,304 square yards of land for the site of an Infectious Hospital at the rate of £2l per annum. Mr. GASKELL moved that the minutes be passed. Mr. RICHARDSON seconded, and the motion was earrieth

div.head: FINANCES OF THE BOARD.
div.p: THE FINANCES OF THE BOARD.

A meeting of the members of the Finance and General Purposes Committee was held on the 26th ult., when the SURVEYOR reported that he had examined the accounts of the treasurer, collector, and assistant surveyor, awl that they were correct. The following is a summy of the Clerk's financial statement for tile month :—General district rate account: Receipts, £351 6s. 81 ;-expenditure, £235 17s. 5d.; balance due to bank, £315 19s. 3d. Gas works account: Receipts, £47 65. 9d. ; expenditure, £l5l 15s. id.; balance die to bank, £865 14s. 41. Water works account : Receipts, £69 12s. id. ; expenditure, £458 is. 01.; balance due to bank, £2,297 lie. 7d. Accounts amounting to £397 65. were examined and recommended for payment. They included : Public Works Loan Board, interest, &c., £163 25. 6d.; Thompson and Co., pipes, £126 16s. 3d. The Assistant Surveyor presented an estimate of the amount required for wages for the five weeks ending let September, 1882, as follows :—Gereral district ratc, £9O ; gas works, £l6; water worke, £lB ; total, £124. itt was resolved that the Board be recommended to sign cheques for these sums at their next meeting.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board with respect to the money borrowed by the Board for the purpose of making the new streets at Stubshaw Cross, the substance of which appears above under the head of " Miscellaneous correspondence." On the motion of Mr. GASKELL, seconded by Mr. GRIMKE, the minutes were adopted. THE GAS WORKS AND THE PRICE OF GAS.

The members•of the Gas and Water Committee held a meeting on the 26th ult. The Clerk reported that 347,000 cubic feet of gas had been made from 37 tons of coal, giving 9.380 feet per ton. The Surveyor reported that the depth of water in No. 1 reservoir was 9 feet 814. inches, as against 9 feet 0 inches at last meeting; Nos. 2,3, and 4 were run- ning, over; No. 1 tank had a depth of 6 feet 6 inches, and No. 2 tank 5 feet 6 inches. The Surveyor read an extensive report which he had drawn up, on the state of the gas works. The report stated that several circumstances had arisen during She financial year just terminated which had brought forward the necessity of submitting for their con- siderat,on a report on rhe gas works. Having regard to those several subjects, he endeavoured to place before them all the facts he had been able to gather so as to enable them to judge and decide on the points under consideration; and he thought he could best do so by formulating them under the heads of (1) the financial position of the gas works; (2' the state of the distributing portion of the works; and (3rd) the condition of the manufacturing position of the works. Pro- ceeding to speak of the financial position of the undertaking he pointed out that the present financial position of the account showed debits amounting to £1,047 5s Bd, against £1,170 lie 101141 as assets. He then alluded to the progress of the works from the time the Board took them in 1876, giving statistics from which, he said, it would be seen that the financial progress might be said to be satisfactory. But another item was to be noted, namely, that under the Act of Parliament and under their provi- sional order, a sinking fund for the extinction of the debt on the works had to be established. The first payment for that purpose had to be made for the year ending March last. The sum then put aside was £221 2s 3d, and after paying that sum a loss of £159 15s lid on the year's work- ing was experienced. He concluded that it was evident the contingency of dealing with any surplus profits in the reduction in the price of gas was not likely to arise for some years, but incidentally it might be stated that he did not think it equitable to transfer any part of it to the credit of the District Rate, because a number of the ratepayers were not gas consumers, and it would be taking the gas profits received from a section of the ratepayers to benefit the whole. He pointed out several " wants " in connection with the undertaking, remarking that if after they had been provided it might appear that the the price of gas could be lowered, it would then be fair and reasonable to make a further reduction. Proceeding to speak as to the works and plant for distributing the gas, he re- marked that he had prepared a plan for the district showing all the lines of gas pipes. On that plan was also shown all the sizes of the pipes, the position of the syphons, the number of burners in certain districts, and the present maximum cpsumption. He stated that the present means ' of distribution were just sufficient for the consumption, although it would be advisable to increase the sizes of the I pipes in certain localities in a gradual manner. Ile pro- ceeded to recommend the re-laving of larger pipes in various streets. In his report of the works for manufacturing gas, the Surveyor explained the position and sizes of the retort house, purifying house, condensers, gas holders, tar and ammoniacal fluor tanks, dec. Several important appliances were wanting, including a photometer, and apparatus by which to test the illuminating power and pressure of the gas. The dealing with residual Products was in a somewhat unpatisfactory posi- tion, while plant---such as a "scrubber" or washer, and an exhauster, were required to complete and perfect their works. The committee decided that the present ft-inch pipes in the street from the works to the main street be taken up, and that Bt.4nch pipes be laid instead, and that the 6-inch pipes in stock (468 yards) be laid in place of the 4-inch pipes, so as to extent the pre- sent 6-inch pipes in the direction of Bolton, Wigan, and Liverpool-roads as far as they will extend.—lt was also resolved that Mr. Paterson, of Warrington, be—as advised
in the report—called on to report on the appliances yet required for the completion of the Gas Works, and that the report of the Surveyor be adopted hnd printed in the minutes.

Mr. LIDDALL said he noticed that it was not thought equitable to transfer any part-of the profits to the District Bate, and asked if that had not already been done. He was under the impression that it had been, but he was not quite sure of the fact.

A MEMBER: Certainly not, it is illegal. Mr. LIDDALL (resuming) observed that he had been try- ing to find out, but did not do so, how it was that their gas was more expensive than at other places, such as Nawton for Instance. He was in favour of a reduction in the price of gas if it could be properly managed, but he did not see that It was so evident as Mr. Goldsvrorth did. Mr. Goldsworth read "it was thus evident," but he (the speaker) did not see that it was. Properly speaking they were prevented by law from making profit out of the gas for the benefit of the rates or anything.

The CHAintrAN ; That has been done, has it not? Mr. SIDDALL replied in the affirmative, but it ought not to have been. There was no reason why those who paid for gas ought to pay the rates of those who did not buy gas. That wap what they were doing if the Board transferred the profits of the gas to the district rates.

Mr. PAII•TTER re—marked that that subject was alluded to at the last meeting. Mr. SIDDALL : It still gees on. The CLERK: Certainly not. I think it has been trans- ferred for two years. Mr. SIDDALL : If 40, where is it?

_ Mr. GRIMEE : It is the sinking fund. Mr. GASEELL remarked that they had five years allowed after they took the Gasworks before they commenced a sinking fund. The " transfer " was made with an igtention to ease the rates.
Mr. SIDDALL : Precisely so. We did it then as we thought for the best, and now as we know better we shall not do it again._ _ _

—Mr. ROBERTS pointed out that there were special reason 9 why they could not compete with Newton in the price of gas. One great difference between them was the distance in the "service," arta the area over which the gas had to be carried. Another reason was their works were not corn. plated. The whole of the parish of Newton, he thought, was only about 2,000 acres in extent, while the township of Ashton was something like 6,000 acres. That made a very great difference in the carrying of the gas. Suppose they had to carry a main pipe a mile or a mile and a half, and only had eight or ten consumers, all that amount of capital would be expended to supply the eight or ten consumers, but in Newton they might have 50 or 60 in the same length of pipe. If they had had a length of pipe one mile long costing £l,OOO they had t 9 pay interest on it, and only had about 10 consumers bringing in £2O. They would actually be at a loss. If at Newton they had 100 consumers bringing in an income of £lOO it would make all the difference.
Mr. SIDDALL asked if the consumption of gas at Ashton was not as large as that at Newton? _ _
Mr. ROBERTS: No, I think it is far less than it is al Newton.

Mr. SIDDALL : I am under the impression that it is. Mr. C. LATHAM remarked that gas had been served at Newton longer than it had at Ashton. Mr. RonnuTs thought that had nothing to do with the question at all. After some further conversation, and inspection of a plan prepared by the surveyor, the matter dropped. •Mr GASISEI L then moved that the minutes be passed. __ _ _
Mr. KNOWLES secondo.d the motion, which was.cArried.
PRINTING OF TILE BALANCE STMT.
Mr. ROBERTS observed that some time ago a resolution was come to that the balance sheet for 1881 should be printed and distributed. He, however, had not yet received a copy of it.
The CLERK stated that it was in the hands of the printers at present. _ .
The CHAIRMAN: It is not forgotten, Mr. Roberts. This was the only business, and the Board then djour ned
THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY AND GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT,
PUBLIC MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.

About two months ago a temperance movement, under the auspices of the "Blue Ribbon Army and Gospel Temper- ance Mission," was commenced in EarlestOwn, and for a week or two appeared to progress very satisfactorily. For about a month past it has been lacking the energy which it displayed at the commencement, but since then its pro- moters have re-organised themselves, and an unusual activity has been imparted to it. On Wednesday evening a public meeting was held in the "Mission Tent," Legh- street, and there was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by the Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar of Earlestown, and among those present were Mr. E. J. Weaver, of Earle.s- - ; Mr. Cordingly, of Manchester ; and Mr. Houghton, of Earlestown. The meeting :was opened with singing, reading of the scriptures, and prayer by the rev. Chairman. Mr. WEAVER as secretary of the movement, then read a report, from which it appeared that the Blue Ribbon Army and Gospel Temperance Mission had been at woik in Earlestown for about two months. During that period no less than 446 ribbons and pledges had been taken. (Applause.) In that number was included 120 from the Vulcan, which was the very lowest estimate, because they had bad about 200 pledges in all, and 20 from Gorse Green. By a course of visitation he had found that out of the 446 there were 49 belonging to other societieg, leaving a grand total of 397 in connection with the Blue Ribbon movement alone.

I The CHAIRMLN then addressed the meeting., remarking ! that he was sure they would all be pleased to hear the very ! good report that had just been given. He had heard of i people complaining of the existence of that movement, and ; when they did so they could depend upon it that it was a ' living' standing protest against certain things, systems, and I i persons. They had heard of the aggressive action, and that I the movement was spreading. They would no doubt be glad to know that it was, and he thought they had occasion for rejoicing that the work was going on so prosperously. He thought they would all agree with him that the report wasi a very satisfactory one, and he hoped they would have greater success in the future than they had had hitherto. (Applause.) Mr. CORDINGLEY, of Manchester, said that the work of the Blue Ribbon Aamy was one of the first importance in the present day. It was one that not only bad for its object the raising of the fallen, but also the bringing upwards of those that had already rgceivd a knowledge of the Gospel of Christ and the Grace of God. The term Gospel tem- perance was, he believed, employed, to denote that its object was to reach those that already belonged to the -Church of Christ, but still took what was termed their " little drop "in moderation. It had for its object also to induce every man who bore the name of Christ to depart , not only from evil, but that which lead to evil. (Hear, hear). The question of "temperance versus drink" lay at the root of our national progress. If we were to become a mighty , people, and if we were to become a people that should he held up as an examplgto the nations around, and one thet should be great and noble, we must cleanse and purge ourselves of that national evil which had eaten into the very core of society. (Hear, hear.) What was drink doing for all classes of society ? Did ministers of religion escape? He said, no. Did men of learning escape? No. No matter what position they had in society, when once they- had entered en the downward path of intemperance it was almost an impossibility that they should stop until they ended in a drunkard's grave. and sunk into a drunkard's hell. Let then) look at it from another aspect—what was it doing for religion? He pointed out that many who bad once been members of the Christian church had been led astray by drink, and maintained that by taking it drink took away entirely the action of the brain. Therefore they found that a man in a state of in- toxication was ready for everything that was vile and unholy. If they could only do away with it, the time ',would soon come when instead of a decrease taking place in ! Christian churches Christ should reign unto the end of the earth. The struggle in which they were engaged concerned every one of them, and he hoped every man and woman throughout the length and breadth of the land would " don" the blue ribbon and stand firm so long as God should give them breath. (Applause.) Mr. HOUGHTON briefly addressed the meeting, impressing upon all the necessity of being earnest in the CAUSE) they had • taken up. , During the evening a number of songs, ko. were creditably given, and a very pleasant gathering was held.
